en: Supplement to the *Mahāyāna-dharmayukti-vana-alaṃkāra*, Scroll Four, composed by the Śramaṇa Huizhao of Dayun Monastery. Chapter on the Three Categories;
Chapter on Attainment and Non-attainment; Chapter on the Meaning of Emptiness.
Chapter on the Twelve Links (12), Chapter on the Two Kinds of Birth and Death (2), Chapter on Seeking (3), and Chapter on the Three Categories (3).

The Dharma-gate of the Three Categories is divided into five sections: first, defining the essence; second, explaining the names; third, establishing the system; fourth, determining the provisional and the real.
There are five categories of difference.

Regarding the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), there are three [approaches]: first, according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); the ten and twenty-eight [bases] are both conditioned and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If distinguished according to the gate of outflows (*sāsrava*) and non-outflows (*anāsrava*), the five aggregates pertain to both natures. If distinguished according to permanence and impermanence...
Analysis by way of gates: Only the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) consists of a small portion of the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) among the twelve bases (*āyatana*);

the remaining eleven bases and one small portion of the dharma-base consist of both natures. Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), only a small portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) consists of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);

the remaining seventeen elements and a small portion of the dharma-element consist of both natures. Second, defining the essence by way of the five phenomena (*pañcadharma*): the five aggregates (*skandha*).

Among these, a portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is called "characteristic" (*nimitta*). A portion of each of the aggregates of consciousness, feeling, perception, and formations (*vijñāna-vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-skandha*) is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).

A portion of the aggregate of formations and a portion of the aggregate of form—namely, names, phrases, and syllables—are called "name" (*nāman*). A portion of the aggregate of formations is called "correct knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*).

The twelve bases (*āyatana*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the four objects (*viṣaya*), and a portion of the base of mental phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) are called "characteristic. The [remaining] portion of the base of mental phenomena is... [the text continues].

A portion of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and the entirety of the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) are called "name" (*nāman*). The entirety of the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and a portion of the sphere of mental objects are called "discernment" (*vikalpa*).

A portion of the sphere of mental objects is called "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*). A portion of the sphere of mental objects is called "suchness" (*tathatā*). Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), [these are included].

The nine [sensory] forms and the entirety of the dharma-dhātu in its partial aspect are called "signs" (*nimitta*). A partial aspect of the dharma-dhātu, which is the entirety of the sound-dhātu, is called "name" (*nāman*).

The seven mind-elements in their entirety and a partial aspect of the dharma-dhātu are called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*). A partial aspect of the dharma-dhātu is called "correct knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*). A partial aspect of the dharma-dhātu is called "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Regarding the third point, the determination of the essential nature according to the hundred dharmas: within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), only [the following are included]:...

There are eleven types of form (*rūpa*). Consciousness consists solely of the eight mind-kings (*citta-rāja*). Feeling (*vedanā*) is the aggregate of feeling; perception (*saṃjñā*) is the aggregate of perception;

and the remainder of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) includes all [mental factors] except for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the five sense organs and the five objects each occupy their own respective bases.

The eight mind-kings are subsumed under the base of mind (*mana-āyatana*). The remainder are all subsumed under the base of mental phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*). Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the five sense organs and the five objects...

Each has its own sphere. The six consciousnesses are called the six bases-spheres (*ṣad-āyatana-dhātu*). The seventh manas and the eighth [consciousness] are called the mind-sphere (*mano-dhātu*), as well as the immediately preceding mind.
The remainder are subsumed within the phenomena-sphere (*dharma-dhātu*).
Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of accumulation; thus it is called an aggregate. "Base" (*āyatana*) has the meaning of source of production.
"Element" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it maintains its own essence; this is also the meaning of "element."

Regarding the third point, the establishment [of the aggregates]: it is asked, for what reason are all material forms combined into one aggregate? Why are all consciousnesses combined into one? Why are feeling and perception divided into two separate aggregates?
And why are all other mental factors combined into the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)? The answer is: it is for the purpose of eliminating five kinds of notions of self (*ātman*).

First, in order to eliminate the notion of a self as an agent equipped with instruments, the five material aggregates are established; this is because the five sense organs and the five sense objects are the instruments employed by a self.

For this reason, the aggregation of form is established as one aggregate; it is merely form and not the self. Second, to eliminate the notion of a self that experiences, the aggregate of feeling is established;
it is merely feelings such as pleasure and pain and not the self. Third, to eliminate the notion of a self that speaks, the aggregate of perception is established;
it is merely perception and not the self. Fourth, to eliminate the notion of a self that acts, the aggregate of formations is established; it is merely...
Volition is not the self. Because it serves to eliminate the causes for [the notion of] a self through five pairs, consciousness alone is not the self. Question:
Why, among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), are material forms divided into ten while consciousness is combined into one? Answer: It is for the purpose of eliminating the notion of a unified self.
Regarding the teaching of the twelve bases (*āyatana*): why is form (*rūpa*) divided into ten, while consciousness (*vijñāna*) is combined into one? Question:
Within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), for what reason is form divided into ten and the mind divided into seven? Answer:

It is in order to eliminate the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) and to cause [practitioners] to know that the roots and objects are the basis from which consciousness arises, rather than consciousness being able to produce the objects and so forth. This is explained according to the provisional gate (*anuvartana-mukha*) of the Hīnayāna.
Another explanation: For those who prefer a concise treatment of form (*rūpa*), the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are taught, with the mind (*citta*) divided into four and form combined into one.

For those who prefer a more extensive treatment of form, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are taught, with form divided into ten and the mind combined into one. For those who prefer an equal treatment of form and mind, the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are taught, with the mind divided into seven. Furthermore, another explanation:

according to whether the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings are superior, middling, or inferior, for those who are sharp, the five aggregates are taught; for those of middling capacity... [text continues].
The former refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*); the latter refers to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

Regarding the distinction between the conventional and the real: among the aggregates (*skandha*), the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) comprises both the conventional and the real. The five sense faculties (*indriya*) are real; the five objects (*viṣaya*) comprise both the conventional and the real.

Within the aggregate of form, blue, yellow, red, and white are real, while the rest are conventional. Among sounds, light and darkness are both conventional and real. As for odors and tastes, both... [are conventional].

Regarding the types [of objects]: although there is no explicit textual passage in the *Śāstra* concerning this, we shall now determine it by means of reasoning. These also encompass both the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the substantial (*dravya*). Among the six kinds of odor, the three categories of "good," "bad," and so forth, are provisional with respect to their nature;
however, when discussing their substance, they are substantial. The single type of "blended" odor is exclusively provisional, while the remaining two are substantial.

Within the sensory object of taste (*rasa*), those categorized by nature are provisional, whereas when discussing their substance, they are substantial. As for the tactile object (*spraṣṭavya*), it encompasses both the provisional and the substantial: the primary derivative elements (*mahābhūta*) that act as the creators are substantial, while the rest are generally [provisional].

These are conventional. Among the dharmas of form (*rūpa*), five types—such as those arising from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) and so forth—are merely conventional; those produced by meditative mastery (*samādhi-vaśitā*) are real. The form that is the object of meditative concentration is conventional;

consciousness (*vijñāna*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*) are real. Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), twenty-four dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) [are conventional].

Furthermore, vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), the minor, medium, and major anuśayas (latent tendencies), as well as the fundamental and other types of anuśayas, should be understood as both provisional and substantial.

Among the twelve bases (āyatana), the five sense-faculties (indriya) are substantial; the five objects (viṣaya) are like the aggregates (skandha). Within the base of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana), twenty-four factors of the dissociated class (viprayukta-saṃskāra) are provisional, while vitarka and vicāra are also provisional.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is real. The remaining [factors] are, as appropriate, the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), which is exclusively real. Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), they are explained as in the case of the bases.

There are ten categories of the fivefold classification of distinctions. First, the distinction of the untainted (*anāsrava*) has three grades; this will be analyzed in its proper place in the tenth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Second, the wholesome through application (*prayogika-kuśala*): the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) includes that which is wholesome by application, while within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), there is form...

The two objects, sound and [tangible objects], are both [morally] wholesome through application (*prayoga-kuśala*). This is because the five sense-faculties and three objects are not so. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Two dharmas are not wholesome by their own nature;

they become wholesome or unwholesome through manifestation (*vijñapti*). The three objects are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), that which is derived from feeling (*vedanā-samgṛhīta-rūpa*) and that which is produced by meditative mastery (*samādhi-vaśa-janita*) are wholesome through application;

the remainder are not. The two aggregates of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) are both wholesome through application. Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), applied thought (*vitarka*)...

Investigation (*vicāra*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), sleep, the eleven wholesome [factors], the five universal [mental factors], the five object-specific [mental factors], the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), and so forth, are all preparatory wholesome states.

Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the two bases of form and sound (*rūpa-āyatana* and *śabda-āyatana*) include preparatory wholesome states. Within the phenomena base (*dharmāyatana*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and others include preparatory wholesome states.

The remainder is as explained under the aggregates (*skandha*). Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) and the two elements of sound and form (*śabdadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*) [include preparatory wholesome states].

A small portion of the *dharmadhātu* consists of the wholesome [states] acquired through application (*prāyogika-kuśala*). The remainder is as explained in the section on the bases (*āyatana*). Three [bases] consist of the wholesome [states] acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*):

a small portion of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*), the two [bases] of form and sound within the form aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*), and the form derived from the mental continuum (*samādhi-nirmita-rūpa*) and the form produced by conceptualization (*parikalpita-rūpa*) within the form category of the *dharmāyatana*;

the two aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*); and eleven wholesome [factors] within the formation aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*), namely: the universal (*sarvatraga*), the object-specific (*viṣaya-niyata*), and the four—vitarka, vicāra, kaukṛtya, and middha.

They are unwholesome (*akuśala*). Among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the two bases of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) and sound (*śabdāyatana*) are unwholesome; thus they are called unwholesome.

Within the category of form belonging to the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), the form derived from volition (*samādāna-rūpa*) and the form of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-rūpa*) are also called unwholesome. Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) all pertain to the unwholesome.

Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the universal (*sarvatraga*), the object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), the major and minor *anuvartin*, the indeterminate (*aniyata*), and the four types of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) all pertain to the unwholesome.

Regarding the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), they are as appropriate: five are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). Among the five aggregates (*skandha*), the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of bodily and vocal karma;

for example, the form arising from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) when Brahmā engages in deceit is entirely obscured-unspecified. Feeling, perception, and consciousness are also entirely obscured-unspecified.

Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viniyata*) mental factors, as well as the fundamental afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*)—excluding the ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as anger, resentment, vexation, envy, and harmfulness—are for the most part obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Among them, two are also unwholesome (*akuśala*), and the eight major ones are all common to both the obscured-unneutral and the unwholesome.

Regarding the twenty-four dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*), they correspond accordingly; the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*) all pertain to the spheres (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) as appropriate. There are six [categories].

Within the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) category: among the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the entirety of the five material faculties (*pañcendriya*) and their corresponding objects (*viṣaya*) that support them are born of maturation (*vipākaja*). Sound is indeterminate;

according to the *Abhidharmakośa* (Small Vehicle), it is not retribution, but according to the *Yogācārabhūmi* (Great Vehicle), it is also retribution. Within feeling, perception, and consciousness, with the exception of the manas-consciousness:

within the formations aggregate (*saṃskāraskandha*), the universal (*sarvatraga*), object-specific (*viniyata*), and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)—excluding those associated with non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*)—as well as the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the three types of non-perception retribution (*āsaṃjñikavipāka*), are all [born of maturation].

This is born of maturation (*vipākaja*). It corresponds to its respective bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). Among the seven modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*), it is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) among the five aggregates; among the five objects (*viṣaya*), it excludes sound and those lacking sense faculties;

and within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it includes that which is induced by meditative absorption, that which is projected by karma, that which arises from conceptual construction (*parikalpa*), and so forth—all of which pertain to the modes of deportment.

Among feeling, perception, and consciousness, it is that which takes conditions and initiates activity. Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), it consists of the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viniyata*) mental factors, as well as applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and consciousness.
All of these are included accordingly within the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). The eight types of craftsmanship belong to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) among the five aggregates;

they consist entirely of the five objects (*viṣaya*), excluding the five sense faculties (*indriya*), and include the matter of mental factors (*dharma-rūpa*), the matter resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), and pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-rūpa*). They consist of the three [aggregates] of feeling, perception, and consciousness.

Regarding those that arise by taking conditions as their object, within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the universal (*sarvatraga*), the object-specific (*viniyata*), and the investigative and analytical (*vitarka-vicāra*) mental factors, along with torpor (*middha*) and so forth, are all included. These are assigned to the bases and elements as appropriate. The nine types of transformation (*nirmāṇa*) belong to the five aggregates.

Among these, only form (*rūpa*) is taken. Within the classification of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) include those produced by transformation (*nirmāṇa*). Among the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), only the sixth and the [consciousnesses] of the eye and ear are included.

Excluding the five faculties, the results of karma, and the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), within the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), there are the five sense objects in their entirety and a small portion of the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*)—namely, the form produced by supernormal power (*abhijñā-rūpa*) and a small portion of the mind base (*manāyatana*). The remainder are not. Within the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), the five...

The entirety of the *dhūta* (dust/defilement) [realms] and a small portion of the *dharmadhātu*. Among the six consciousness realms, three—those of the eye, ear, and mind—are [included]; the remainder are not. Ten have an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature by their very essence.

Within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), there are two types: those that are maturation (*vipāka*) and those that are both outflow (*niṣyanda*) and nurtured (*aupacayika*). One location is pervasive and nurtured.

The two perceptions continue, flourish, and are nurtured. There are four types of outflow (*niṣyanda*): first, the outflow of maturation (*vipāka-niṣyanda*); second, the outflow of nurturing (*puṣṭi-niṣyanda*); third, the outflow of transformation (*vikāra-niṣyanda*);
and fourth, the outflow of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-niṣyanda*). Only the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is generally categorized as intrinsically neutral (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*).

This refers to the five external sense objects and the four sense objects that support the faculties, which are not [the result of] karmic retribution (*avipāka*). Question: Various treatises state that there are four [types of neutral], yet some do not mention them. Why is this?

Is it not said that there is an indeterminate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*)? Answer: Apart from the indeterminate that is maturation (*vipāka-avyākṛta*), there is no separate indeterminate intrinsic nature.

The statement regarding the "basis of the self" (*ātma-vastu*) is made in accordance with its increase; it is for the purpose of establishing the basis, the objects of activity, and the maintenance of the aggregates, whether extensively or briefly. There is no separate basis.

That which is the object-condition for the "mine" (*ātmīya*) refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), because the aggregates are the basis of the "mine. This refers to the objects of enjoyment of the "mine."

The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) refers to the objective basis for the conventional expression "I. The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) refers to the objective basis for the conventional expression "mine," because it gives rise to such expressions.

The substance of volition (*cetanā*) refers to the objective basis for "what is created by me," because it performs the act of conditioning and because it is that which is acted upon by me. To dismantle these five attachments, the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are taught; the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are taught as that which is obtained [by them].

Since the faculties are identical in their capacity as graspers, while the objects are what is grasped, the latter are kept implicit and not explicitly mentioned. The section on maintaining one's own nature consists of ten parts.

The Eight Elements (dhātus). Question: Why are the elements distinguished immediately following the [discussion of] the uninterrupted [sequence]? Why are the eight consciousnesses designated merely as "elements," while the objects are divided according to the elements, which would result in twenty-four?
Answer: Because there is no distinction between the support (āśraya) and the object (ālambana), twenty-four are not established.
Chapter Sixteen: Attainment and Non-attainment.
The meaning of attainment and non-attainment is analyzed by way of ten gates: first, clarifying the basis; second, clarifying the derivation of the name;

third, clarifying the distinctions; fourth, analyzing according to consciousness; fifth, analyzing according to stages; sixth, analyzing according to internal and external; seventh, analyzing according to the [great] elements... [text continues].
Minor Analysis. 8. Analysis according to the three periods of time. 9. Analysis according to whether [the attainment] has been previously acquired or not yet acquired.
10. Analysis by way of question and answer.
First, clarifying the basis: all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) obtain a basis; if the basis is wholesome, the attainment is also [wholesome].

If the basis is wholesome, the acquisition (prāpti) is also wholesome; if the basis is unwholesome, the acquisition is also unwholesome. If the basis is bound to the desire realm, the acquisition is also bound to the desire realm;

likewise, if the basis is indeterminate, the acquisition is also indeterminate. If the basis is bound to the form or formless realms, the acquisition likewise depends on being bound to the form or formless realms.
If the basis is unbound, the acquisition is also unbound. The acquisition of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) belongs exclusively to the Noble Path. It is not...

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) belongs to three categories: 1. When defilements are temporarily not produced because they have been suppressed by the six worldly paths of practice, this acquisition belongs to the six worldly paths.

2. If it is an ultimate cessation, it belongs to the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which serves as its support. 3. If it is a temporary non-arising due to the absence of conditions, it belongs to the seeds.
There are two types of supports for non-acquisition (*aprāpti*): first, that which relies on the noble path; second, that which relies on conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

Regarding the seeds of dharmas: if all defiled dharmas are not acquired, this non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is established based on the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), depending upon the Noble Path and the six paths of action.
If there is non-acquisition of any untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, it is established based on those two [obstacles].

If there is non-acquisition of tainted wholesome or neutral dharmas, it is established based on their own respective seeds. If all defiled dharmas do not arise as active manifestations, this is termed "non-acquisition in function. If...

When the seeds are also severed, it is called "not attaining the essence. If all contaminated (sāsrava) wholesome and neutral states, at the time of being separated from their conditions and fetters, are called "not attaining function," then in the ultimate state of Buddhahood, non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is called "not attaining the essence."

Regarding the non-acquisition of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas: if they do not arise in actual manifestation, it is termed "non-acquisition of function. For those who possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), there is no non-acquisition of the essence.

For those without the spiritual lineage, there is non-acquisition of both essence and function. If one compares those of fixed nature within the three vehicles, each has non-acquisition of the essence and function of the untainted dharmas belonging to the others.
Second, regarding the explanation of the names: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks, "What are 'attainment' (*prāpti*), 'acquisition' (*lābha*), and 'accomplishment' (*samanvāgama*)?

The answer is: they refer to the causes that are intensified through the gathering of conditions for birth. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, there is a distinction between attainment and accomplishment:

if one first acquires [a dharma], it is called "attainment"; if one has possessed it for a long time, it is called "accomplishment. In the Mahāyāna, however, seeds remain as they were from the beginning.

Abiding [in this state] is called "attainment" (*prāpti*). When the fruit becomes increasingly abundant and flourishing, it is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). There are three types of accomplishment: First, the accomplishment of the seed (*bīja-siddhi*):

when the causal conditions follow their natural course as they were previously, it is called the accomplishment of the seed. Here, "seed" is itself the "accomplishment," which is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Second, mastery (*vaśitā*):

when accomplishment is attained through the application of effort and cultivation, it is called the accomplishment of mastery. "Mastery" is itself the "accomplishment," which is likewise a *karmadhāraya* compound.
"Accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*) is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. Furthermore, "mastery" (*vaśitā*) is itself accomplishment; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Regarding "active manifestation" (*samudācāra*): it is called active manifestation because the manifestation of the fruit appears and adheres. Active manifestation is itself accomplishment; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Regarding the distinctions of the three knowledges (*vidyā*): all phenomena (*dharma*) are, in brief, of two kinds.

First, existence; second, non-existence. Here, we take existence and not non-existence. Within existent phenomena, there are two types: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Here, we take the conditioned and not the unconditioned. Why? Because the unconditioned is eternally abiding and does not perfume to form seeds. Therefore, we proceed with respect to the conditioned.
Briefly, there are three types: first, defiled phenomena; second, wholesome; and third, indeterminate.

Within the defiled, there are two: first, unwholesome; and second, obscured-indeterminate. Within the wholesome, there are two: first, acquired through application (*prāyogika*); and second, acquired by birth (*upapattilābhika*).

Within the indeterminate, there are four: first, born of maturation (*vipākaja*); second, pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*); third, pertaining to craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*); and fourth, pertaining to transformation (*nairmāṇika*).

All defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) of the three realms are termed "possession of seeds" (*bīja-samanvāgama*). Among the wholesome, those that are innate (*upapatti-labdha*) are termed "possession of seeds.

Within the four types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena, the entirety of the maturation-neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) and a portion of the deportment-neutral (*airyāpathika*) and skillful-neutral (*śailpasthānika*) are termed "possession of seeds."
The remainder are all accomplished through mastery (*vaśitā*). These two types of seeds, when they arise as actual manifestations (*samudācāra*), are termed "accomplishment by manifestation.
Why is this? Because seeds are latent and difficult to discern, they are divided into two [categories]. Manifestations are evident and easy to discern; therefore, they are discussed collectively.
Within the three types of accomplishment, regarding the initial accomplishment of seeds, it is established in relation to defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*).

Regarding non-attainment (*aprāpti*), there are two aspects. First, within the context of the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*), it can only suppress the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and cannot suppress those of vision (*darśana-heya*).
Within the [afflictions] of cultivation, it can only suppress those within the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) and cannot suppress those of the seventh consciousness (*saptama-vijñāna*).

Within the six consciousnesses, it can only suppress the four delusions regarding objects (*vastu-moha*)—namely, greed, hatred, and so forth—and cannot suppress the two views of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Regarding greed...

Among the four [afflictions] beginning with hatred (*dveṣa*), it can only suppress those four that are associated with hatred and so forth; it cannot suppress those that arise in association with the two views (*dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the four [afflictions] beginning with attachment (*rāga*), one selects whichever nine grades (*navaprakāra*) exist within the three realms and eight levels—excluding only the level of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*).
Within each of these eight levels, there are nine grades, and for each grade, one performs the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantaryamārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

It subdues them. Speaking in terms of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), both the seeds and the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are rendered non-existent. Speaking in terms of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), it only subdues the active manifestations without severing the seeds and so forth.

Regarding each category [of afflictions], the subduing of the active manifestations is termed "non-attainment" (*asamanvāgama*) of the manifestations, while the seeds are termed "attainment" (*samanvāgama*).

This continues until the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are entirely subdued, at which point it is termed "non-attainment" of the desire realm's active manifestations; as for the higher [realms]...
Both the seeds and the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the two realms are accomplished. Within this, according to what is appropriate:

regarding the second point, which concerns the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), if the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are those that arise from conceptual discrimination (*parikalpita*), then in the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the three vehicles, neither the seeds nor the active manifestations are accomplished.

Regarding those [obstructions] to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*): if we consider the Bodhisattva’s ten stages (*bhūmi*), up to and including the seventh stage, the active manifestations still exist.

Regarding accomplishment and non-accomplishment: the seeds of the *samādhi of certainty* are accomplished. From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they never manifest; manifestation is termed "non-accomplishment.

The seeds of the *vajra-anantara-samādhi* are not accomplished. Among the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), those arising from conceptual discrimination—both in terms of seeds and manifestation—are certainly not accomplished upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). As for those that are innate (*sahaja*), they are [eliminated] at the sixth stage of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Regarding the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), whether as seeds or as active manifestations (*samudācāra*), there is non-attainment throughout each stage (*bhūmi*).
As for those associated with the seventh consciousness, the afflictions (*kleśa*) have active manifestations that are sometimes attained and sometimes not within the first seven stages;

however, their seeds are never attained until the Vajra Path. Regarding the cognitive obstructions, within the eighth stage, their active manifestations are sometimes attained, while their seeds [are not].
The essential point is that they are ultimately never accomplished. Regarding the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) present within the six consciousnesses:
among the ten stages (*bhūmi*), both the afflictive and cognitive obstacles are not accomplished. As for the seventh [consciousness], it requires the Vajra-like [samādhi].

Within the context of the Two Vehicles' abandonment of the afflictive obstacles, the seeds and active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are certainly not accomplished; however, regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there is...

Regarding those who transcend the fruits: there are those who proceed gradually. If one proceeds gradually, then within the three realms, as each respective category of seeds and their active manifestations are no longer accomplished, one attains the ultimate fruit.
According to what is appropriate, there are three ways of transcending the fruits. Regarding the transcending of two intermediate fruits:

this involves the vertical abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the three realms—specifically, the abandonment of one grade in the desire realm and one grade in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
[They are] abandoned. According to what is appropriate, there is the accomplishment or non-accomplishment [of these]. Regarding those who suppress afflictions through the six stages of practice:
if one who has suppressed the six grades [of afflictions] turns their mind and enters the Path of Seeing, the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) were previously not accomplished;

as for the seeds (*bīja*), at the time of entering the Path of Seeing, according to what is appropriate, those previously suppressed—whether few or many grades—are not accomplished. The latencies (*vāsanā*) are certainly accomplished. As for the defiled [afflictions]:
Thus, within the category of wholesome [states], there are two types: first, innate wholesomeness (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*); second, acquired wholesomeness (*prāyogika-kuśala*).

Regarding innate wholesomeness in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), if one does not give rise to the seeds or the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of wrong views, it is certainly established as present.

If one gives rise to wrong views, the active manifestation is certainly not established. Regarding acquired wholesomeness, it is established through mastery; however, for one with wrong views, the active manifestation is not [established].

Accomplishment. When born in the higher realms, one necessarily accomplishes the seeds of the wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*), as well as those arising from hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*), and those produced through application (*prayoga*).

Regarding their manifestation (*samudācāra*), there may be accomplishment or non-accomplishment. As for the abandonment of bondage (*bandhana-vigama-prahāṇa*), when these various wholesome states enter the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), some may not be accomplished in part.
Non-accomplishment of the seeds occurs only upon the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); [this applies to] the untainted (*anāsrava*) seeds of the wholesome states of application.

The seeds of the *nirmāṇa-citta* (transformation mind) are definitely established; however, its actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) is not necessarily established. It is not included within this classification of the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), such as deportment (*airyāpathika*).

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the seeds of deportment and craftsmanship are definitely established, while their actual manifestation is not necessarily established. The same applies to those who possess mastery over preparatory effort (*prayoga-vaśitā*):

there is both establishment and non-establishment. As for the transformation mind, it is definitely not established [as a seed]; regarding that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), the seeds— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is accomplished. Regarding its active manifestation (*samudācāra*), there are cases where it is accomplished and cases where it is not. With respect to entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) by way of liberation from bondage, there is also a portion for which the active manifestation is not accomplished;
however, the seeds (*bīja*) reside in the Path of Liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and thus the meditative absorption is definitely not accomplished [in that state].

Fourth, distinguishing the realms (*dhātu*) in terms of consciousness: within the five sensory consciousnesses, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is only the possession (*samanvāgama*) of seeds, but no mastery (*vaśitā*).
Regarding the two [faculties] of eye and ear, there is both mastery and possession. In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is only the possession of three seeds;

in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is none at all. As for the others, they pertain to all three realms: in the desire realm, there are seven—namely, two defiled, two wholesome, and three neutral. In the form realm...

Within the realms, there are six [types of mental factors]: the defiled (kliṣṭa), the wholesome (kuśala), and the neutral (avyākṛta)—the latter being of three kinds, excluding the skillful (śailpasthānika).

In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are four: the defiled, the wholesome, and two kinds of neutral, including the neutral of non-conceptualization (anabhisamskāra-avyākṛta). Regarding mental concomitants (caitta): in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), they are complete, with the exception of *praśrabdhi* (serenity).

In the form realm (rūpadhātu), those associated with defilement are present; however, among the "great" [universal] factors, eight are absent, and among the "minor" [particular] factors, three are absent. Within the indeterminate (aniyata) factors, *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) are present. The formless realm follows this same pattern, established according to what is appropriate for each case.
It is established. Within the sixth [consciousness], there is mastery over the three realms; if it is untainted (*anāsrava*), the seventh [consciousness] likewise possesses mastery.
Regarding the eighth [consciousness], it consists solely of seeds. Discussing this in terms of cause and fruit: the fruit of the eighth is exclusively mastery, while its cause consists only of seeds.

The sixth and seventh causes possess all three [natures]. As for the fruit, it belongs exclusively to the sovereign (īśvara). Among the causes, the five consciousnesses—eye and ear—possess sovereignty; this is also possible.

From the eighth stage upward, the five [consciousnesses] together also possess sovereignty. Regarding the three types of wisdom: in the desire realm, there are wisdoms derived from hearing and reflection;

in the form realm, there are wisdoms derived from hearing and cultivation; in the formless realm, there is only wisdom derived from cultivation. If one is a bodhisattva established in meditative concentration, is the fruit necessarily fixed?
Fifth, regarding the stages: in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), the manifestation of afflictions is suppressed by means of hearing and reflection;

however, there are cases where it is not suppressed, such as with the non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) and so forth. In the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), among the afflictions, the manifestation of both the conceptual (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*) views is entirely absent.
As for the seeds of innate virtue (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) and applied virtue (*prāyogika-kuśala*), they are certainly present; as for their manifestations, they may or may not be present.

In the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), all conceptualized defilements (*kliṣṭa*) belonging to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—both their seeds and their active manifestations (*samudācāra*)—are necessarily not established.

As for innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), their active manifestation is necessarily not established; likewise, the active manifestation of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is necessarily not established.

Within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), prior to the seventh ground, the active manifestation of defiled, wholesome, and indeterminate states does exist. From the eighth ground upward, the defilement of the seven consciousnesses (*vijñāna*)... [is absent].

Regarding the manifest activities (*samudācāra*): among the six types [of seeds], those that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), those acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*), and those that are wholesome (*kuśala*) are not established as manifest.
In the state of a Buddha, all impure (*sāsrava*) wholesome and indeterminate seeds, as well as inferior pure (*anāsrava*) ones, are entirely non-existent in both their seed and manifest forms.

Sixth, regarding the distinction between internal and external: in the Hīnayāna, "attainment" (prāpti) is established internally but not externally; in the Mahāyāna, it is established both internally and externally.

Seventh, regarding the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles: in the Hīnayāna, one attains the great through the attainment of the small, and attains the small through the attainment of the great.
One does not obtain any dharmas; yet the Mahāyāna establishes the "great obtaining.
Regarding the eighth point, the distinction according to time: the Sarvāstivādins establish that there is obtaining throughout the three times.

For past dharmas, they establish that obtaining occurs after [the dharma has arisen]. Although past dharmas no longer function, their essence is obtained and not lost, remaining attached to the practitioner.
That which is named "subsequent attainment" (pṛṣṭhalabdha) pertains to the past; that which is named "simultaneous attainment" (sahaja-labdha) pertains to the present.
When a dharma exists in the present and there is an attainment (prāpti) that co-exists with that dharma without being lost, it is called "simultaneous attainment.

Regarding future dharmas, there is "prior attainment," whereby one attains those future dharmas and causes them to belong to the practitioner. Such present conditions shall now result in the attainment of dharmas without loss; there is an attainment of those dharmas now.

In the Mahāyāna, both the establishment of phenomena and their acquisition are possible. If seeds possess the capacity to give rise to manifest states, then it is permissible to provisionally establish [the category of] "previously acquired" prior to those phenomena.

Regarding the ninth [category], that which was previously acquired is termed "previously acquired," while that which was never before acquired is termed "previously unacquired"; this applies to innate virtue (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), whereas applied virtue (*prāyogika-kuśala*) is termed "previously unacquired."
It is obtained. Furthermore, it is explained that contaminated wholesome dharmas are called "previously obtained," while uncontaminated dharmas are called "not previously obtained.

Regarding the analysis of the tenth question and answer: the interlocutor asks, "If the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes an object as its condition, there must be a 'realization' (*prāpti*) that comes to take that seeing as its condition;

likewise, one should obtain the dharma through an obtaining. Is there a distinct obtaining that comes to obtain this obtaining? The response is: "The seeing-part is dependent on others; it is the fruit of the ultimate valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
Realization is attained through conditions; this is its conventional designation. There is no separate "attainment" that comes to bring about the attainment. Question:

If the dharmas attained are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and the dharma that attains them is also conditioned, then it should follow that if the dharmas attained are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the dharma that attains them must also be unconditioned. Answer: Conditioned entities are mutually compatible;

thus, both the attainment as the agent and the attainment as the object are conditioned. Unconditioned phenomena are not mutually compatible; therefore, they cannot both be unconditioned in the same way.
Question: Is the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) established based on the seeds of the various categories [of afflictions] that pervade the three realms?

Answer: It is co-existent with the same level (*bhūmi*) as the maturation (*vipāka*). It is just like other [dharmas]. Why? Because there is no accomplishment (*samanvāgama*) of the nature of an ordinary person belonging to all three realms simultaneously.

Question: For a person who lacks the [noble] nature, there is no fruit to be obstructed; upon what basis is the nature of an ordinary person established? Answer: Because it is extremely heavy, it is established based on both obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) in general.
[This section] is established.

○ Regarding the "Chapter on the Meaning of Emptiness" (Kongyi Zhang), the meaning of emptiness is briefly analyzed by means of five sections: first, the difference in enumeration; second, the determination of its essential nature (tixing); third, the clarification of its establishment and sublation.
Fourth, it is attained by the three vehicles. Fifth, it reveals the stage of realization.

Regarding the first point, the difference in number: some speak of one emptiness; the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says, "The five aggregates are all empty," referring to the gate of emptiness among the three gates of liberation.
Some speak of two emptinesses; this is taught everywhere as the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Or it is said...

The four emptinesses are explained at the end of the fifty-first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: "Furthermore, existence is empty by virtue of the emptiness of existence; non-existence is empty by virtue of the emptiness of non-existence;
the self-nature of emptiness is empty by virtue of the emptiness of its own nature; and the other is empty by virtue of the nature of the other. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter twelve, states:

"There are four types of emptiness: first, analytical emptiness (*vibhāva-śūnyatā*); second, the emptiness of that realm (*tad-dhātu-śūnyatā*); third, internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*); and fourth..."

External emptiness. Or, seven kinds of emptiness are taught. In the first fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Buddha told Mahāmati: "Mahāmati, 'emptiness of emptiness' refers to the locus of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Mahāmati, the attachment to the imagined nature is further empty; it is the non-dual nature, free from the characteristics of self-nature.

Mahāmati, those are briefly explained as seven kinds of emptiness: namely, the emptiness of marks (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of non-existence..."

Emptiness. It is the emptiness that is free from all verbal expression; it is the great emptiness of the ultimate noble wisdom; it is the mutual emptiness (*itaretara-śūnyatā*). Alternatively, eleven kinds of emptiness are taught.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what is meant by 'emptiness'? "Good son, as for emptiness:"
That which is called internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, beginningless emptiness, essential emptiness,

the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of emptiness, and great emptiness— as elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā Śāstra*, and the *Yogācārabhūmi Śāstra*.

The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* [explains] the sixteen emptinesses, namely: internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the beginningless and endless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*), emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), and emptiness of essential nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

The emptiness of marks (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*). Alternatively, seventeen kinds of emptiness are taught;
as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, these sixteen are augmented by the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). Alternatively, eighteen kinds of emptiness are taught;

as stated in the eighth and ninth [chapters] of the *Prajñā[pāramitā]*, these seventeen are augmented by the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Alternatively, nineteen kinds of emptiness are taught; as stated in the *Prajñā[pāramitā]*, [these are the aforementioned plus] the tenth.

Above the six emptinesses, one adds the emptiness of the object of focus (*ālambana-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of increase (*upacaya-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of mutual non-existence (*itaretara-śūnyatā*). Alternatively, twenty emptinesses are taught.

Among the eighteen emptinesses, the emptiness of detachment (*vigata-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*) are combined as the emptiness of dispersal (*vibhava-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of non-alteration (*avikāra-śūnyatā*).

The emptiness of the absence of characteristics is the emptiness of self-characteristics and the emptiness of common characteristics. Alternatively, twenty-two kinds of emptiness are taught, as also explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (and so forth).

Second, regarding the essential nature [of emptiness]: Now, in discussing emptiness, there are two aspects: first, the object of emptiness (*śūnyatā-viṣaya*); second, the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-caryā*). As for the object...

Third: First, it is called "empty" because it does not exist. For example, that which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*) exists only as a mental object but lacks reality; thus, the two selves—of persons and phenomena—are all termed empty.
Based on this meaning of emptiness, one speaks of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in characteristics and the absence of arising.

This is like entering a deer-woman’s hall and not seeing horses, oxen, or the like; those characteristics are the fruit, just as when one attains the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), poverty and such are already severed. That realm is empty, and so forth.

Alternatively, those whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist are all subsumed under emptiness. Because the two types of emptiness are manifested, they are called "empty," as in the case of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Although in principle sentient beings do not exist, its intrinsic nature is not empty; yet, when one contemplates this dependent nature and does not perceive the grasped object (*parikalpita*), emptiness is manifested, and it is likewise called "empty.

Based on this meaning, it is said that the absence of production (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*) is termed the absence of self-nature (*svabhāva-niḥsvabhāvatā*). The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also says: "That is to say, the aggregates (*skandha*) are devoid of..."
The notions of "I" and "mine" arise through the application of the means for accomplishing karmic actions; this is called the emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*).

The essence of formations is not non-existent, yet it is empty in the sense that there is no grasping at what is imagined (*parikalpita*) and no manifestation. It is called empty because it possesses the three natures of emptiness, just like the nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, although sentient beings do not exist in principle, their essential nature is not empty. By contemplating the inherent nature of these grasped objects, one performs the practice of emptiness.
Only by contemplating the emptiness of the two selves does one realize the true principle. This true principle is itself emptiness; it is called "emptiness" because its fundamental nature is empty.
Based on this meaning, it is said that there is no nature in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāva*). The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* also states:

"For those who have attained the noble knowledge of self-realization, all [phenomena] are empty of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); this is called the Great Emptiness of the Noble Wisdom of Ultimate Truth regarding all dharmas.
This is identical to various treatises. Alternatively, it may be described as the non-arising of suffering. In brief, the first two types of emptiness are termed the emptiness of Śūnyatā (the void).
It is called "empty" because it does not exist. It is called "empty" because the essence of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent.

Upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the absence of the imagined nature is revealed as emptiness; thus it is called "empty. The former [the imagined] is truly empty; the latter [the dependent] is empty by way of designation.

The final type is the fundamental nature of *śūnyatā* (the space-being); through the gateless gate of emptiness, one realizes the principle of emptiness. Its essence is a real existent nature, for emptiness is revealed therein.

It is called "emptiness. For this reason, it is said that the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are termed "existence," while the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) are termed "empty.
One who is able to contemplate the practice of emptiness contemplates these three objects as appropriate; this too is termed "emptiness.

However, in their essential nature, they are not actually empty, because they are subsumed within the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). When these various texts speak of emptiness here, they do not give rise to an objective field of emptiness, nor...

Regarding the coexistence with emptiness: within this single emptiness, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* state that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all empty, yet they speak of conventional five aggregates as being the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Now, following the Mahāyāna and based on the object of emptiness, the *Madhyamaka-vibhāga* identifies three types of five aggregates:

first, the five aggregates of imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); second, the five aggregates of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and third, the five aggregates of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Now, based on...

This emptiness is briefly explained in three ways. First, regarding the aggregates as they are grasped [by the deluded]: the intrinsic nature of all phenomena does not exist; their characteristics do not arise of themselves. Therefore, they are called "empty.
Ordinary beings falsely grasp at the five aggregates as being real, yet these very aggregates are empty and are not form; they are empty only after they have ceased.
As for the five aggregates that depend on others, they are like a mass of foam, bubbles, a mirage, a plantain tree, or a magical illusion; they do not exist in the manner [in which they appear].

Because it is grasped as having an inherently produced nature, it is also called "empty. The *dharmatā* of the five aggregates is called "non-existent" because one realizes their true empty nature only after observing that what was grasped is empty and non-existent.
Because it is the true nature as it was grasped, this ultimate lack of intrinsic nature is also called "empty.
It is called "empty" because, by observing emptiness, the causes and effects of birth and death, or suffering, do not arise. Therefore...
It is taught that the three objects all establish the meaning of emptiness. Furthermore, that which is empty is solely the nature of true thusness (tathatā), which is neither empty nor existent.

It is manifested by means of emptiness; it is designated as "empty" only as a conventional expression because it is the nature of emptiness, intended to negate the attachment to it as being existent. Fools do not understand this.

The grasping at the five aggregates and so forth as being truly distinct from reality, giving rise to various conceptualizations of association and dispersion, is now refuted by tracing them back to their source and subsuming them within the nature of reality.
Their essence is precisely *tathatā* (suchness). Since phenomena are inseparable from principle, they possess no separate substantiality;
therefore, it is said that the five aggregates are entirely empty, and all sentient beings are the *tathāgatagarbha*. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva pervades his own very body.

Therefore, all phenomena are likewise empty of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these aggregates; it is not that the aggregates must first be extinguished and cease to exist for one to return to true nature.
Among the three gates of liberation, that which is called the gate of emptiness refers to taking the practice of contemplating emptiness as its object.

It is therefore described as emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, fascicle 8, states: "Regarding the objective spheres of the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), how are they subsumed within these three natures (*trisvabhāva*)?

In principle, they all apply; according to their specific characteristics, each corresponds to one. One should know that emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*) correspond respectively.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74, and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fascicle 6, state: "The gate of emptiness is established on account of the first nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*)."
The door of liberation [is established] by observing that "self" and "what belongs to self" are empty.

Because of the second nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the door of wishless liberation (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) is established, because one does not give rise to wishes regarding all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena.

Because of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the door of signless liberation (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) is established, because one observes that all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are signless (*animitta*). Since consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) relies on each of these [natures] individually, it is so stated.
Each characteristic has its own corresponding [emptiness]. One should understand emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*) in their respective order.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the twelfth [chapter], states: "If, in this place, that thing does not exist, by this principle one contemplates it as empty;

therefore, it is called emptiness. That which is contemplated as empty is such that nothing can be wished for; therefore, it is called wishlessness. One contemplates this as being devoid of all modes of activity (*saṃskāra-nimitta*). Therefore...
It is called "signless" (*animitta*). It relies upon the observation of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and constitutes three practices.

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (73), among the five dharmas, the characteristic of "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) corresponds to the three [gateways to liberation]: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*).

Since these are also the three types of objects, it should be known that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) likewise possesses three objects: namely, the dependent nature devoid of the imagined nature, and the two selves—of persons and phenomena—which are established through the manifestation of causes.

The *Tattvasiddhi* explains that these two are manifested by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and thus they constitute the objective sphere of emptiness. Because one does not generate aspirations (*praṇidhāna*) regarding them, they are the objective sphere of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Because there is no mental focus (*ālambana*) upon this objective sphere of emptiness and wishlessness, it is the objective sphere of signlessness (*animitta*).
Therefore, the three natures all pervade the three objects, as explained in the "Chapter on the Three Doors of Liberation" and in the *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra-ṭīkā* (Shuyao).
Accordingly, the three types of objects—whether non-existent or existent—are themselves the three modes of practice, which together are termed "emptiness.

Regarding the essence of these two emptinesses, the essence of the two emptinesses of the objects consists briefly of two kinds: first, the essence that is non-existent, namely the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
The two natures of sentient beings and phenomena are both non-existent; yet their two essences are not non-existent, namely the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

Because its essence is manifested by the absence [of the two natures] and its nature is existent, various treatises speak of the two selves (*ātman*). In reality, the two selves do not exist, yet there is the practice of contemplation. Its essence is truly not empty.
The minds of the two types of contemplation—impure and pure—realize that [object] in accordance with conditions, serving as the wisdom of the two emptinesses. 4.
Regarding the essence of emptiness, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* subsequently explains it itself: "Existence is empty of existence.
Here, "existence" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). These five aggregates are empty of existence because their nature of arising cannot be apprehended.

With the exception of a single dharma that lacks existence—namely, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—this lack of existence is empty of lack of existence, because the essential nature of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and so forth is entirely non-existent.

It refers to the fact that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). This emptiness is not produced by wisdom, nor is it seen as something produced; it is not produced by anything else either.

This is their intrinsic nature. By virtue of this emptiness of intrinsic nature, whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, all phenomena abide in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), equality (*samatā*), the state of being free from birth (*anutpāda*), suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity (*avitathatā*), and non-alteration (*ananyathā*).

The nature of transformation and the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are both empty because they are of a dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). This does not mean that the essence of suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth is itself empty;
rather, it is called "empty" because it is devoid of the grasped dependent nature, thereby revealing this suchness as being of a dependent nature. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:

To observe emptiness means to observe that all phenomena are empty of permanence, pleasure, self, and what belongs to a self (*ātmiya*), up to and including being empty of a self and what belongs to a self.

If one clings to phenomena as having permanence, pleasure, self, and purity, one will sink and wander in saṃsāra; now, by observing them as empty, one eliminates the pervasive conceptual grasping (*parikalpita*).

This is not an emptiness of existence, but rather the destruction of the object of that grasping. That which is the emptiness of the realm (*dhātu*) refers to the unshakable liberation of the mind (*ceto-vimukti*).

It is empty of all afflictions such as greed; because one has attained the dharma of dual liberation and the delusions of greed and so forth have already been severed and extinguished, it is called "empty" due to their absence.

Regarding the essence of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*): it refers to the emptiness within one’s own person of the conceit of a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), as well as all perverse attachments such as pride (*māna*).
The severance of these within the internal body and the elimination of the grasping mind that conceives of a self is termed "internal [emptiness]."
Emptiness. Regarding the essence of external emptiness: it refers to being empty of and free from desire and craving for the five objects of sensual pleasure. As it is said:
"Because I have already transcended the marks of form, I dwell having realized and perfected external emptiness," and so forth, as explained at length.

In this context, the mark of the excellent objects of desire is called the "mark of form. Because the greed and desire arising from that mark are severed, it is called "external emptiness"; it is also [severed].

The conditions of enumeration, such as craving for the five sensory desires, are called "external emptiness. According to the meaning of the preceding text, because of internal and external emptiness, there is the observation of emptiness.
If the grasping mind of "I" and cravings such as desire were not extinguished, by what means would there be the observation of emptiness regarding objects?
It is precisely because of internal and external emptiness that there is the emptiness of their results—the grasping mind of "self" and so forth.
If the mind of the five desires is not severed and extinguished, how could the accomplishment of the emptiness of that realm be attained? The treatise states:
Furthermore, the practitioner, by means of the emptiness of those fruits, at times directs the mind to contemplate external emptiness, or contemplates internal emptiness through observation;
or at times contemplates the emptiness of both the internal and external. By the power of this, the mind realizes and attains them together, namely: again...
Regarding this emptiness of the internal body, one who has not yet realized it should direct their attention to and contemplate immovability.
"Immovability" refers to the perception of impermanence or the perception of suffering. By contemplating in this way, one is no longer moved by such things as the conceit of "I am.
Because one is not moved by the mind through such notions of self and conceit—and so on, as explained at length—one then [attains]...

The two types of emptiness are both realized through mental engagement. Among these four kinds of emptiness, the first—investigative emptiness—is the emptiness of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

The latter three kinds of emptiness are the emptiness of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature); they are termed "emptiness" because they eliminate the grasping of delusions. In total, these are the emptiness of the object.

The untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that can contemplate these four is the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-caryā*). Regarding the essence of the seven kinds of emptiness, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "What..."

What is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)? It refers to the contemplation that all natures are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Because they belong to a collection of successive accumulations, they are devoid of intrinsic nature when analyzed.

Since self-characteristics and common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) do not arise, and because there is no intrinsic nature in terms of self-nature, other-nature, or both, characteristics do not abide.

Therefore, it is said that all natures and characteristics are empty; this is called the emptiness of characteristics. This meaning explains that when one contemplates all phenomena, they are merely a succession of accumulated aggregations.
It arises because it is illusory. It differs from the two characteristics—specific and general—that are conceptually constructed; they lack reality and are not identical.
Since the specific and general characteristics grasped as real by ordinary beings and followers of the Lesser Vehicle are fundamentally non-existent, these two characteristics do not arise.
Whether in terms of self-nature, other-nature, or both, there is no such thing as a specific or general characteristic; therefore, the two characteristics do not abide. Self-...

The two characteristics [of arising and ceasing] do not manifest as having birth or abiding; how, then, could they possess an intrinsic nature? Therefore, they are called "empty of characteristics. As it is stated in various treatises:
"All phenomena are not born from themselves, nor are they born from another; they are not born from both together, nor are they born without cause. For this reason, they are said to be unarisen."
When this meaning is explained according to one’s own inclination, there is likewise no abiding. Since abiding and arising exist equally, only non-existence is mentioned;
cessation by way of difference is omitted because it does not exist. What is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)? It means that [a phenomenon] does not arise from itself;
this is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. Therefore, it is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature. As previously stated, all phenomena are merely...
This arises through successive accumulation; thus, one clings to it as having real existence. This successive accumulation is now refuted:
this dharma of accumulation has no reality in its own nature; its self-nature is unarisen. There is only a succession of semblances of dharmas;

what appears to be an accumulation is fundamentally non-existent, yet there is a conventional designation of arising, which is called "existence," and a conventional designation of remaining for a brief moment, which is called "abiding. It is designated as "cessation" when it is entirely gone.

Because they lack substantial reality, the nature of all phenomena is said to be empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). This is not the same as the refutations found in the two [non-Buddhist] schools regarding things that appear to be produced by causes and conditions.
What is the emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*)? It means that the aggregates (*skandha*) are devoid of a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).

Because they are accomplished through causes and function as effects produced by conditions, they are collectively termed the emptiness of formations. The meaning of this is to say that the formations of the five aggregates are accomplished by causes and are also produced by conditions. By...
The fruit arises from causes; it is entirely neither "I" nor "mine. Beyond these formations (*saṃskāra*), one is free from "I" and "mine" and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);

therefore, they are called the emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*). Mahāmati, this very emptiness of formations is a dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in succession, lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Although there is no [intrinsic] formation, if one speaks of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as being established through causes and conditions and produced by the skillful means of karma, [this is so].

Free from the characteristics of "self" and "what belongs to self," there are those who grasp at the aggregates (*skandha*) as causes and conditions, thereby establishing them as having a substantial reality.

Now, we refute this grasping at the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these dependently originated aggregates; since they lack a real intrinsic nature, it is called the "emptiness of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

This emptiness of the unconditioned does not negate existence, for the conventional dependent origination of intrinsic nature is different [from substantiality]. Regarding the two schools that refute the phenomena of dependent origination: the former refutes the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), which is explained generally.

All these are accumulated through mutual succession. Because this [teaching] shatters the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and explains the internal aggregates (*skandha*) as dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is thus taught.
What are all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) that are beyond verbal expression and empty? It refers to the fact that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is ineffable;
because all phenomena are free from verbal expression, they are called "all phenomena beyond verbal expression. What is the ultimate noble wisdom regarding all phenomena (*paramārtha-āryajñāna*)?
The Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). This refers to attaining the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), wherein all boundless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are empty.

This is called the Great Emptiness of the Noble Wisdom of the Ultimate Meaning of All Dharmas (*sarvadharma-paramārtha-āryajñāna-mahāśūnyatā*). This emptiness is precisely the emptiness of *tathatā* (suchness), which is realized through the noble wisdom of the Buddha’s own self-realization.
At the time of such realization, all conceptualizations, the faults of the perceiving mind, and their habitual tendencies [are eliminated].

Evil is entirely non-existent. This emptiness is precisely the emptiness of the non-arising of delusion and suffering, the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Furthermore, this consists of two types of emptiness; briefly stated, there are two kinds of emptiness:

first, the distinction between the false and the real. The former refers to that which is grasped as an object of attachment; the latter is the emptiness of the nameless *tathatā* (suchness). Second, the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate.
The former refers to conventional phenomena such as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); the latter is the supreme truth (*paramārtha*), the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

The nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The former is emptiness beyond verbal expression; the latter is the profound internal realization of wisdom. Because it is beyond verbal expression, it is called the "nature of emptiness," and thus it is termed "emptiness.
What is "emptiness of this in that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*)? It refers to the emptiness of something being absent within another; this is called "emptiness of this in that."

For example, in the house of Migāramātā there are no elephants, horses, oxen, or sheep; yet it is not that there is no community of bhikṣus, for both [the house and the bhikṣus] are empty [of those respective things].
It is not that the nature of the house is heavy, nor is it that the nature of the bhikṣus is empty; it is simply that in other places there are no elephants or horses.

This is called the self-characteristic of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-svalakṣaṇa*). That [characteristic] does not exist in that [phenomenon]; this is called "emptiness of this and that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*).
For example, when there are no sheep, horses, or the like within the Mṛgāramātuḥprāsāda, it is called "emptiness of this and that.

It is not that because there are no monks and so forth in that hall, or because the nature of the house itself is non-existent, that it is called empty. Both of these types of emptiness constitute the emptiness of the Mṛgāramātuḥprāsāda, which is devoid [of those things].

There is no need for further investigation. Among the six preceding emptinesses: the first two are the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); the next two are the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); and the final two concern the two truths (*satya-dvaya*).
Within the first two pairs, the former in each pair refutes the two types of grasping that arise initially in ordinary beings and followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

The latter in each pair successively refutes the two types of grasping that arise later in those on the path of training (*śaikṣa*) within the Mahāyāna. Within the final two truths, the former is the opposition between the false and the real, and the latter is the opposition between existence and non-existence.
This emptiness is as follows: first, that which is grasped and realized by ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle at the stage of initial practice is already called "emptiness.

Subsequently, in contrast to the conventional, it is the emptiness of principle; this is taught as "emptiness" for the sake of what is deluded about and what is awakened to by the subsequent stages of the Mahāyāna practitioners in training.
