These six types of emptiness above all dispel what is grasped and are thus explained as "emptiness. The Sūtra speaks of "emptiness of emptiness" because true reality is the locus of the self-nature of deluded thought.
Each respective emptiness is generally termed "emptiness of emptiness," not for the purpose of removing attachment.

Regarding the contemplation of the essence of the eleven types of emptiness that transcend [duality], the traditional interpretation of the ancients holds that the first ten are the emptiness of the object (境空) and the final one is the emptiness of wisdom (真空).
Emptiness. True wisdom is empty because it differs from the deluded mind that perceives external phenomena as existing; by refuting this [delusion], emptiness is revealed.
Thus, the first ten types clarify emptiness in relation to objects. When sought according to reality, there are no phenomena outside the mind;

all dharmas are fully endowed with true suchness (*tathatā*), for the essence of true suchness is quiescent. Therefore, the latter type explains emptiness in terms of wisdom. As the *Bhūmi* states: "All suchnesses..."

To say that its own essence (*svabhāva*) is empty is called the emptiness of the nature of wisdom itself; however, this current explanation is not so. The ten [emptinesses] previously observed are empty because they are false and non-existent;

since they lack existence, they are empty. The latter [emptiness], the Great Emptiness, is the emptiness of *tathatā* (suchness); it is called "emptiness" because the nature of emptiness is itself empty by virtue of *prajñā*.

This "Great Emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā) is not the same as the emptiness of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) taught in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, nor is it the same as the fifty-one types of emptiness in the ten directions taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;
therefore, it is named "Great Emptiness. According to ancient commentaries on the first fifteen [emptinesses], the first eight use non-existence (*abhāva*) to refute existence (*bhāva*).
It is termed "emptiness. The ninth [stage] dispels existence by means of non-existence and is termed the "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*).

The tenth stage, by means of that which is neither existent nor non-existent, simultaneously refutes both existence and non-existence; this is termed "the emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Thus, this is existence, and this is the absence of non-existence;

therefore, it is identical to the ten equalities taught in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. Now, I shall explain the emptiness observed by the first nine cognitions, while the tenth is the cognition that observes.
The wisdom of emptiness is also empty; it is explained in terms of both the middle and the extremes. This wisdom that is able to perceive is not [itself] within this emptiness;

because the wisdom is also empty, it is called "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). For this reason, a sutra says: "Such emptiness of emptiness is not the same as the samādhi of emptiness of emptiness attained by the śrāvakas.
This is called "this is emptiness, this is existence, this is non-existence," and so forth. The mind that is able to contemplate is likewise illusory.

Therefore, the wisdom that observes delusion is also designated by the name "emptiness. However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, chapter fifty, states: "Emptiness refers to the emptiness of all phenomena.
Because this emptiness is itself empty, it is called 'the emptiness of emptiness. Since this emptiness is non-existent due to [the absence of] emptiness, it is named 'emptiness.
While the referents of these meanings differ, they are not mutually contradictory. Within the preceding nine [types of emptiness], the first eight are conventional, while the ninth is ultimate.
Meaning (*artha*). Because it does not exist as it is grasped, it is called "empty. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) refers to the state of nirvāṇa;

it is empty by virtue of being the ultimate truth. Within the preceding eight [emptinesses], the first seven clarify that sentient beings and phenomena are empty because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The last one clarifies that sentient beings and phenomena are empty because they lack marks (*animitta*). Within the provisional middle of causes and conditions, there is no...

"True nature" is called the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*). Within ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), there is no characteristic of causes and conditions; this is called the emptiness of signlessness (*animitta-śūnyatā*). Now, [your] explanation is incorrect.

Among the first eight types of emptiness, the first seven are emptinesses of that which is apprehended (*upalabdha-śūnyatā*), while the latter one is the emptiness of that which is not apprehended (*anupalabdha-śūnyatā*).

*Prajñā* is named the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). Within the first seven, according to the ancient exegesis, the first six concern the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of sentient beings; these are precisely the [emptinesses of] arising...
[The opponent claims: "The last [emptiness] clarifies that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; this is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Now, [the author] explains that this is not so.

Within the emptinesses of the internal, external, and so forth, it is stated in each case that there is no Tathāgata, Dharma, or Saṃgha, nor any possessions, nor the conditioned and unconditioned, as well as the beginningless emptiness.

Having universally examined persons and phenomena, why is it that one only attains this emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*)? That is to say, within the first six emptinesses, there is no such thing as a phenomenon."

Regarding the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-śūnyatā*), which is the realization of the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states that there are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) which are neither produced by the noble ones of the three vehicles nor by anyone else.
Because this is their fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), it is called "fundamental nature. It is not something created by oneself, by another, or by both together.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts state that intrinsic nature is the untainted lineage (*anāsrava-gotra*).
Because this lineage attains purification, one contemplates emptiness; thus it is named "emptiness of intrinsic nature. This is not the same as [the emptiness of] nirvāṇa.

Regarding the first six [types of emptiness], the ancient commentaries explain that the first five contemplate the emptiness of the present, while the last one contemplates the emptiness of the past. This current explanation is not so. All...

As for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), because they are not subsumed under the world (*loka*), one should say that the first five contemplations observe the emptiness of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-śūnyatā*), while the last one observes the emptiness of their having no beginning (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*).

Among the first five, the first three distinguish emptiness based on internal and external phenomena, while the latter two distinguish emptiness based on the difference between conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) categories.
The commentary states: "Among the first three, 'sentient beings' (*sattva*) are termed internal; [the rest] are not..."

Sentient beings are called "external. The absence within of a self (*ātman*), a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-force (*jīva*), or a lifespan (*āyus*) is called "internal emptiness" (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).

The essential nature of external phenomena is that these external phenomena are neither the self nor what belongs to the self; this is called "external things. Furthermore, when one contemplates external phenomena as being merely provisional and lacking substantial reality, this is also called "external emptiness";

the emptiness of the essential nature of phenomena—this alone is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which is termed "external emptiness. Now, through contemplation, one realizes and knows that these [phenomena] return to...

The mind, and so forth, up to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), being neither self nor belonging to a self, is called "emptiness of the unconditioned. All of these constitute the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*);

they do not yet empty the essence of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva*), and thus are not called "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Question: Why are the internal and external observed through the combination and separation of existence and non-existence regarding the conditioned and unconditioned? Is it not otherwise?
Answer: It is not incorrect to say that it was not stated [explicitly]. Both internal and external phenomena are equally conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); thus, observing them together is easy.

However, observing the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) together is difficult; for this reason, it was not mentioned. Furthermore, one clings to internal and external phenomena as being separate or combined, and conceives of a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).
By observing their separation and combination, this [teaching] refutes that clinging. As for the two types of phenomena—the conditioned and the unconditioned—[the same applies].
Thus, there is no conjunction. Question: Regarding the emptiness of having no beginning, why is the emptiness of having no end not mentioned?

It should logically follow from the meaning; therefore, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, all three periods of time are observed together. Now, it is clarified that the past gives rise to faults because it is the locus of attachment from the beginningless [past].
As for observing the future, one understands it by analogy with the way the mind arises in the past; it is simply not mentioned here for the sake of brevity. At [the present],...

Among the sixteen kinds of emptiness, the "emptiness of non-dispersal" (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*) is taught, which refers to the fundamental and its subsequent manifestations; the "emptiness of no-end" (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*) is not mentioned.

The seven types of emptiness discussed above constitute the "emptiness of the absence of intrinsic nature" (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Regarding "the absence of anything" (*abhāva*): when one perceives the characteristics of causes and conditions as being distinct from "anything" (*bhāva*), this is called the "emptiness of the absence of anything.
This is the "emptiness of signlessness" (*animitta-śūnyatā*). Therefore, it says below: "Just as a person has no [independent] distinction, it is named 'empty. This is external..."

This is called the emptiness of non-nature (*abhāva-śūnyatā*). It is like a person being called "empty" because they possess nothing; it does not mean that one clarifies the emptiness of non-nature by referring to the objects themselves.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of emptiness which negate existence with non-existence, and a ninth, the emptiness of oneness, which negates non-existence with existence.
These preceding eight kinds of emptiness are termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). All phenomena are empty yet eternally existent; they are not actually non-existent.

Because they are not real and do not exist, there is no ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) can be apprehended; this is called the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

The nine types of emptiness discussed above individually refute the distinctions between existence and non-existence, while the tenth emptiness simultaneously dispels both existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, while the preceding nine emptinesses eliminate the nature of existence and non-existence, the tenth eliminates their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Since both the prior existence and non-existence are empty, it is so called.

Emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*): The phenomena of dependent origination have the same essence whether they exist or do not exist. Because they share the same essence, non-existence is treated as existence, and existence is treated as non-existence;

thus, there is no distinction between them. Since they are neither existent nor non-existent, they are "emptiness of emptiness. These ten gates of emptiness refute and eliminate prior characteristics by means of the principle of emptiness.
The eleventh emptiness, however, establishes emptiness based on reality. This is taught in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* from the perspective of concealment.

The *ālaya-vijñāna* is considered the "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*) because it manifests as supreme. Prajñā is also considered the "Great Emptiness," for that very true consciousness manifests as prajñā;

it is not the wisdom of objective reflection. Because the essence of prajñā is quiescent, it is called the "Great Emptiness. My current explanation differs slightly [from others], as has already been demonstrated above.

Objective realms do not follow the mind; purely projected images arise solely from the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*); and those with substantiality involve both the subjective and objective aspects.

The essence, such as the nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) and so forth, according to their respective capacities, consists of the consumer and the consumed (the emptiness of the external). This abides in the body (the emptiness of the internal and external).

It is that which can see (the emptiness of emptiness). It is the suchness of this (the emptiness of the ultimate). It is the emptiness of the two truths sought (the emptiness of the conditioned and the unconditioned).

It is for the constant benefit of sentient beings (the emptiness of the absolute). It is for not abandoning *saṃsāra* (the emptiness of the beginningless and endless). It is because it is inexhaustible (the emptiness of non-dispersal). Therefore, the Bodhisattva...

Contemplating emptiness serves to purify one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*); [contemplating] the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) serves to attain the primary and secondary marks; and [contemplating] the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) serves to purify the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Because all phenomena are empty, the Bodhisattva contemplates the emptiness of both the *pudgala* (person) and phenomena (*dharma*).

Since their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and actual reality (*tattva*) do not exist, and because this absence of nature is itself a nature, two distinct types of emptiness are established. The commentary states: The "eaters" are the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).

Because one clings to these six faculties as being able to experience objects, one now contemplates their empty characteristic; there is no real agent of experience. Thus, the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is emptied.

Therefore, it is called "internal emptiness" (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*). This refers to the six objects of sensory experience (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Because one clings to these six objects as being real entities that are actually experienced, one now contemplates that the six objects lack reality;

since their imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is emptied, it is called "external emptiness" (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). This "basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the sense-fields that support the faculties (*indriya*).
It is not "internal" because it is not the internal faculties themselves, nor is it "external" because it is not like the external container-world (*bhājana-loka*). Thus, it is neither external.

Therefore, these are internal; because they are not internal, they are external. Due to grasping them as real, one now contemplates them as empty. Regarding the delusion concerning the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), there is the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*);

therefore, it is called "internal and external emptiness" (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). That which the body dwells within is "great emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*). The vessel-world possesses great and superior function;
it is the support for the "great external" and for many classes of sentient beings, and is thus termed "great. Therein lies the great...
Because it is that wherein mental objects abide, it is called "Great" (*mahat*); now, observing it as empty, it is called "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).

That which is able to see is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), which is precisely the wisdom of the observer. Because one previously observed that its object was empty—emptied of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)—the wisdom of the observer was held to exist;
now, observing that the wisdom of the observer is also empty, it is called the "Emptiness of Emptiness. This is what accords with reality.
It is also the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Truth is the object of wisdom that accords with conditions; it is called "ultimate" because its meaning is supreme.

Alternatively, truth transcends the conventional, and thus it is called the ultimate. Because the principle is manifested through conceptual construction, and now one contemplates that the emptiness of such construction reveals the truth—since the principle is that which is revealed—it is called the emptiness of the ultimate.
As for the emptiness of the two truths sought [here], it is the emptiness of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Furthermore, because one clings to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as being real, they are now observed as empty; thus, it is called "emptiness of the conditioned" (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

Because one clings to the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and the nine unconditioned phenomena and so forth as being real, they are now observed as empty to eliminate that pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*);

thus, it is called "emptiness of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), which is precisely suchness (*tathatā*). Another explanation states: Bodhisattvas [practice this] in order to seek all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). There are bodhisattvas who seek...

For the sake of enlightenment, one empties the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Because one seeks the imputed nature of true emptiness and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is said that both the conditioned and the unconditioned are empty.
Regarding "constantly benefiting sentient beings," this refers to the emptiness of difference;
because one contemplates the ultimate emptiness of sentient beings, one perceives no distinction between self and others, and is thus able to constantly benefit them. As for "not abandoning saṃsāra":

This is the emptiness of the limitless (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*). Through wisdom one contemplates reality and eliminates pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*); through compassion one extensively transforms sentient beings.

Because sentient beings are limitless, there is the emptiness of the limitless. That which is virtuous and inexhaustible is the non-dispersal emptiness (*asaṃbheda-śūnyatā*), which is also called "non-empty."
The stores of merit and wisdom accumulated by Bodhisattvas shall never be exhausted throughout the limits of the future; therefore, it is called "the emptiness of non-dispersal.
For those whose lineage is pure, it is the "emptiness of intrinsic nature," for phenomena are fundamentally undefiled, though they are obscured by afflictions;

now, by contemplating the limit of emptiness, the afflictions reveal the lineage of the intrinsic nature, and thus it is called "the emptiness of intrinsic nature. For those who seek the primary and secondary marks, it is the "emptiness of marks" [as follows]:

It is emptiness. Because one seeks the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) by contemplating the limit of reality (*tattva-paryanta*), it is called the "emptiness of marks and signs. To purify all Buddha-dharmas, there is the "emptiness of all dharmas" (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
This is because, having conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*) all Three Jewels, one now contemplates their removal and the purification of all Buddha-dharmas;
therefore, it is called the "emptiness of all dharmas. Furthermore, "all dharmas" is also applicable not only to the Buddha-dharmas, but also to the person (*pudgala*).

The Dharma is emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Because the two attachments to arising and to phenomena lack an intrinsic nature in their essence, it is called "emptiness of non-nature" (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
As for "neither existing," this refers to the emptiness of the nature of non-nature; it is attained through the non-nature of arising and phenomena.

This clarifies that attachment to non-apprehension as being existent merely exacerbates the illness. Now, observing that even non-apprehension is empty, it is therefore called "emptiness of non-apprehension" (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the eighteen emptinesses: within the previous seventeen emptinesses, the "emptiness of non-nature" (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) is divided into two, with the addition of the "emptiness of self-nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

This refers to the very essence of the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). Furthermore, there are three explanations for this: first, it is called "birth" (*jāti*) in its general sense, and "phenomena" (*dharma*) in its specific sense.

Because it has two aspects, it is called "dharma" (phenomenon); because it is a derivative, it is called "arising. Because it has three essences, it is called "dharma"; because it is a function, it is called "arising.

Furthermore, because it possesses both essence and function, it is called "dharma"; because it is not [substantial], it is called "arising. Regarding the nineteen emptinesses: from among the previous seventeen, excluding the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), three additional emptinesses are added:
first, the emptiness of the object of cognition (*ālambana-śūnyatā*), wherein all objects cognized by consciousness are empty; second, the emptiness of the dominant condition (*adhipati-śūnyatā*)...

Emptiness. Emptiness of the object of cognition (*ālambana*). Emptiness of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). All are simultaneously empty. Third is emptiness through mutual non-existence (*itaretara-abhāva-śūnyatā*).

The various types of emptiness previously explained were said to be emptiness through mutual non-existence, such as there being no horse within a cow; now, observing that all things are empty in this way is called emptiness through mutual non-existence.

Regarding the twenty emptinesses: one takes the first nineteen emptinesses, excluding the final three emptinesses, to obtain seventeen emptinesses. By means of non-apprehension, these constitute eighteen emptinesses.
Within these, the non-diffusion is divided into two: the emptiness of diffusion and the emptiness of non-diffusion. These refer to the wholesome dharmas of the two vehicles.

Because there is that which is empty, it is called "emptiness of dispersion" (*vikiraṇa-śūnyatā*). Another explanation is that the untainted (*anāsrava*) is named "non-dispersal emptiness," while the tainted (*sāsrava*) is named "dispersal emptiness.

Furthermore, the "emptiness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) is divided into two: the "emptiness of specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the "emptiness of common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). Because the thirty-two marks are distinct, they are termed "specific."

Because the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) are shared [with ordinary beings], they are termed "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) and "empty. Now, regarding the sixteen aspects of the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), fourteen are entirely [aspects of] phenomena (*dharma*), and one is partially so.
That which is now distinguished as the "arising" is truly only the object. Question: If it is said that there is only "true emptiness," do all seven [aspects] necessarily involve consciousness-only?

Answer: Yes, they are indeed consciousness-only; however, they must be accompanied by the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*). There is an inherent emptiness of arising, though it need not necessarily [be explicitly present].
The contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) for the two vehicles.

Regarding the section on the twelve links of dependent origination, within the explanation of how name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) act as mutual conditions, there are two types of contemplation of the twelve links: first, the contemplation of the establishment of defilement (*saṃkleśa-pratiṣṭhāna*); second, [the contemplation of purification].
The pure non-conceptualizing contemplation (*anabhisamskāra-vipaśyanā*). Within these two types of contemplation, both progressive and regressive orders exist.
"Conceptualizing contemplation" (*abhisamskāra-vipaśyanā*) refers to that which is coarse and superficial in its mental aspects (*ākāra*), being established through conventional designations;

thus it is called "conceptualizing. When a Bodhisattva is about to eliminate [the afflictions], they first contemplate them in their progressive order: from ignorance (*avidyā*) arise volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); from volitional formations arises consciousness (*vijñāna*); from consciousness arise name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Name...

From form arise the six sense bases, and so on, up to birth, which leads to old age and death. In this way, one contemplates the succession of birth and death in forward order to engender weariness and detachment.
Having thus contemplated in forward order, one then contemplates its results in reverse order to determine from what they arise.
Within this, there are two parts: first, contemplating by whom the result of old age and death exists—namely, through birth; and second, contemplating by whom birth itself arises.

There is existence. Existence exists by means of what? Existence exists by means of clinging (*upādāna*). Thus, one contemplates each of the links up to the factor of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) through the four noble truths:

the suffering of aging and death, the origin of aging and death, the cessation of aging and death, and the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death; and so on, up to the origin of volitional formations.
This is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). One cannot further ask by what ignorance exists; therefore, there are only forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*) when subdivided therein.

If one contemplates only the truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), there are two causes for the fruit of suffering that is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*): first, the coarse and proximate cause, which is birth (*jāti*);

second, the distant and subtle cause, namely craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*). One thus contemplates how these produce the fruit of suffering that is old age and death in the present life.

This means that one contemplates how craving and grasping give rise from afar to the fruit of suffering—old age and death—in the future. Having thus contemplated the fruit of suffering as arising from its accumulation, one then contemplates from what that accumulation arises:

namely, from suffering. One then contemplates from what the fruit of suffering arises: namely, from the five [aggregates] beginning with consciousness. One then contemplates from what those fruits of suffering further arise:
they arise from volitional karma (*cetanā-karma*), which is to say, from craving and grasping; beyond this, one does not contemplate anything else.

Ignorance and volitional formations are not different from craving, grasping, and becoming. Therefore, the contemplation of the two truths of suffering and its origin ceases at consciousness and turns back.

Having thus contemplated the truths of suffering and its origin in reverse order, one knows this to be the source of birth and death; wishing now to sever it, one then proceeds to the contemplation of cessation and the path.
First, one contemplates the cessation of old age and death; next, one contemplates by what means old age and death are brought about—namely, by the path—and thus contemplates.

The Path is able to realize cessation (*nirodha*). Thus, one contemplates the two truths of Cessation and the Path. Starting from old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) and proceeding back to the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), there are forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*).

Question: For what reason does the contemplation of Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) revert at the stage of consciousness (*vijñāna*), whereas the contemplation of Cessation and the Path transcends consciousness and reaches the link of volitional formations?
Answer: The continuity of Suffering and its Origin completes a single cycle and then reverts. Cessation and the Path involve the severance [of that cycle]; therefore, they proceed until...
Regarding the practice: "Pure non-conceptualizing contemplation" refers to the essence of non-discriminative wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) being conjoined with suchness;

it is the profound union of the subjective mind and the objective realm, not a mere conventional designation. It is designated by the name "non-falsely established" to indicate that all afflictions are eternally extinguished, and it is shown by the term "pure."

Within this, there are two [methods]: first, the direct order (*anuloma*), and second, the reverse order (*pratiloma*). First, regarding the direct observation: through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one perceives that the ignorance (*avidyā*) to be abandoned by seeing the truths (*satya-darśana-heya*) is extinguished.
Because ignorance is extinguished, formative forces (*saṃskāra*) do not arise; continuing in this manner until old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) no longer exist.

Because ignorance is extinguished, there is liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*); because the associated afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished, there is liberation of the mind (*citta-vimukti*). Because ignorance is extinguished, there is no further impelling activity; because the afflictions are extinguished...
Therefore, there is no present birth; because karma and afflictions are absent, subsequent results do not continue. One attains the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Having attained no-more-learning, one retrospectively contemplates the fruit of suffering—birth and death—which has been extinguished: by what was it extinguished? It was by the cessation of formative forces (*saṃskāra*). And by what were the formative forces extinguished? And so on.
Due to ignorance, there are three kinds of dependent origination regarding arising and ceasing. Furthermore, one performs seventy-seven types of knowledge by contemplating the twelve links;

within each link, there are three knowledges: first, the knowledge that contemplates the cause; second, the knowledge that scrutinizes the cause; and third, the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*).

The wisdom that contemplates causes refers to contemplating from whom old age and death arise; they arise from birth. Next is the wisdom that scrutinizes the cause, which further scrutinizes how old age and death arise from birth.
These two types of wisdom separately contemplate the three periods of time. Within a single link [of dependent origination], there are six types of wisdom combined.

The wisdom of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*) contemplates the three periods of time in general, meaning that old age and death arise from birth. There is one such instance for each link, excluding ignorance.
In the eleven links, there are eleven knowledges (*jñāna*). Combined with the previous sixty-six knowledges, there are seventy-seven knowledges.

Regarding the twelve links, each link is observed both in direct and reverse order, and each possesses the four truths (*catuḥsatya*). For example, when observing old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), there is the suffering of old age and death.
The origination of old age and death; the cessation of old age and death; and the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death—these comprise forty-four knowledges in total.

One contemplates the eleven links in reverse order, and within each link there are two causes: the knowledge that investigates the cause and the knowledge that scrutinizes the cause, which serve to bring about knowledge of the root.

This is likewise for the past and the present. Because one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, it is called the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*). In total, there are seventy [knowledges].
The Seven Knowledges.

(Above, on the sixteenth day of the first month in the fifth year of the Kaiyuan era, the monk Xuanyan read this in Zizhou. By means of this merit, may it extend universally to all living beings, so that together they may attain the fruit of Buddhahood, etc.)
The above concludes the fourth fascicle of the Fayuan Yilin (Forest of Meanings from the Garden of Dharma).
Chapter Two: The Two Kinds of Birth-and-Death.

The meaning of the two kinds of birth-and-death is analyzed through eight sections: first, defining their essence; second, explaining their names; third, distinguishing their characteristics; fourth, [distinguishing their] differences...
1. Distinction; 2. The five bases according to stages and levels; 3. The inclusion of the four types of birth and death; 4. The interpretation of the three kinds of mind-made bodies;
5. Questions and answers for detailed analysis.

First, regarding the nature [of birth-and-death]: it is *paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa* (segmented birth-and-death). Its nature consists of the five fruits (*phala*) among the twelve links, as well as the seven links of birth, death, and old age;
the remaining links serve merely as causes and conditions for birth-and-death and do not constitute the actual nature of birth-and-death itself.

In this stage, one takes only the *vipāka-avyākṛta* (maturation-neutral), which pervades both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), encompassing both general and specific retributions. If it were merely a single, specific retribution, it would not constitute the [actual] nature.

Therefore, the treatise states: "Segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*) refers to the coarse resultant fruits of the three realms produced by the power of the auxiliary conditions of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), acting upon various contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome and unwholesome karmas.

Transformational birth-and-death (*pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa*) likewise takes as its essence the collective and individual retributive fruits of the resultant form and mind (*vipākaja-rūpa-citta*); it does not take ignorance (*avidyā*) or uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*) as its essence. This...
Its nature is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), as it possesses only outflows (*sāsrava*).

The treatise states that "inconceivable transformation-death" refers to the subtle and superior matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) produced by uncontaminated karma with conceptual differentiation, through the auxiliary power of the conditions provided by the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Second, regarding the explanation of the names: the term "birth and death" (*saṃsāra*) is a *dvandva* (coordinative) compound, as birth and death are mutually distinct and separate.

The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "To arise by receiving retribution is called 'birth'; to perish by receiving retribution is called 'death'. This explains the general name. Next, the specific names are explained.
Regarding "segmented" (*paricchinna*), the treatise says: "The length of body and life follows the power of causes and conditions."

Because it has fixed limits, it is called "segmented" (*paricchinna*). If "segmented" refers to the cause and "birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra*) refers to the result, then because it is the birth-and-death of the segmented [cause], it is an *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
If "segmented" refers to the result, then because the segmented itself is birth-and-death, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
As for the term "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), the treatise states: "By the power of compassion and vows, one transforms the body and life-force; thus, there are no fixed limits."

It is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). As with the preceding "segmented" (*bheda*) [birth], it applies to both explanations; for the term "transformation" can be understood to apply to both cause and fruit. Third, regarding the analysis of their characteristics, there are two parts:

first, the analysis of the characteristics of segmented birth; second, the analysis of the characteristics of transformation. Within this, [the first] is divided as follows: [The text continues: Regarding the analysis of the characteristics of segmented birth... [and so forth].

Within this section, there are two distinctions: first, the provisions of the dispersed [state]; second, the provisions of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The provisions of the dispersed state are further divided into two: those that accord with experience (*anuloma-vedanīya*) and those that are experienced crosswise (*tiryag-vedanīya*).
Regarding "those that accord with experience," these refer to the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), beginning from ignorance (*avidyā*) and proceeding in succession up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

One revolves through the cycle, undergoing the fruits of spontaneous karma, dwelling according to the cultivation of one's actions, with lifespans being either long or short. These do not depend on hearing or reflection as conditions; they involve the relinquishing of wealth.
Because it serves as a support, it is called "receiving in accordance" (*anuloma-vedanīya*). As for "receiving crosswise" (*pratiloma-vedanīya*):
one observes that their life-span is short and limited to only thirty or fifty years, yet that person’s meritorious conduct is extremely superior.

Taking the two types of wisdom—derived from hearing and reflection—as the cause, they either give away clothing and goods to the Saṃgha, or rely on recitation, the production of scriptures, and the creation of images. By the power of this merit, they vow to attain longevity.
In all cases, because the two types of wisdom—those derived from hearing and reflection—serve as the means (*upāya*), one causes [the lifespan] to extend according to one's wish;

this is therefore called "transverse acquisition" (*tiryag-upabhoga*). These two together are termed "scattered requisites. Regarding the second, the "concentrated requisites," there are three types: first, external requisites; second, internal requisites;
and third, the requisites for the mixed cultivation of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). As for the external requisites, they range from those of a person who has attained the first fruit up to...

Regarding the person who has attained the fourth fruit (*caturthaphalaprāpta*): having entered the meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*), they subsequently emerge from that absorption and relinquish their robes and alms bowl.

This serves as the condition for sustaining the present body and causing it to endure for a long time until the fruit is fully realized. Whether this person first enters the absorption and subsequently relinquishes the robes and bowl, or first relinquishes them and subsequently enters the absorption, neither case is prohibited.
As for the second type—those sustained solely by internal conditions—this refers, for example, to a person who has attained the third fruit (*tṛtīyaphalaprāpta*) relying on the *anāgamya* stage.

Concentration (*samādhi*). Either the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) or [accessory concentration] supports the karma of the body, enabling the bodies received in each stage (*bhūmi*) and each location (*sthāna*) to attain long life.

However, it is correct to rely on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration; yet, what harm is there if one attains the fundamental [concentration] before providing such support? Regarding the third [type], the support of the mixed cultivation of *dhyāna*:
first, by means of the contaminated (*sāsrava*), one supports the four karmas below the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*); next, by means of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)...

Regarding outflows (*āsrava*): they assist an initial moment of tainted consciousness (*sāsrava*), a middle moment of untainted consciousness (*anāsrava*), and a subsequent moment of tainted consciousness;

or an initial moment of untainted consciousness, a middle moment of tainted consciousness, and a subsequent moment of untainted consciousness. In this manner, whether more or less, they assist past karma of the lower realms to cause the acquisition of that body;

therefore, it is called "mixed cultivation" (*miśra-bhāvanā*). All of the above are termed "discontinuous transformation" (*paricchinna-pariṇāma*). Next, the "transformative transformation" (*pariṇāma-vipariṇāma*) is distinguished; therein are two parts. First:

There are two types: those who turn back (*āvartaka*) and those who go straight on (*anivartaka*). Regarding the first, among those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have turned their minds toward the three fruits:
although they have not yet attained a purely untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), when they employ this [mind] to support their karma, they do not use that which is tainted (*sāsrava*).

Therefore, the body thus refined is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*); it is not like the karma of mixed cultivation where taints are interspersed. That is to say, if a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) turns back...

Regarding the mind: as stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, there are those who, upon turning their minds [toward enlightenment], immediately suppress the remaining afflictions and undergo the transformation of death (*pariṇāmikī cyuti*);
there are also those who do not undergo this transformation until the seventh birth. The other two fruits should be understood accordingly. This applies within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Since noble ones who have already undergone rebirth cannot possibly receive a body from a higher realm again, it is known that they sustain the body received within the desire realm.
With this very body, they reach the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*); thereafter, although their actual body may travel to the Palace of Sovereignty (*Vaśavartin*), the body they leave behind—

It is subsumed within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This eighth untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousness of the bodhisattva likewise takes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) of the desire realm as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
If, however, one is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who receives a body in a higher realm, they receive a body accordingly within the four stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

One then disciplines this body until it reaches the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*). As for those who have turned their minds toward the path after attaining the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), they likewise employ the untainted (*anāsrava*) to support tainted karma (*sāsrava-karman*).
Although they have not yet attained a purely untainted mind, at the time of supporting their karma, it is not mixed with the tainted;

therefore, this is not called "mixed cultivation" (*miśra-bhāvanā*) of karma. Among those who proceed directly among humans, there is a class of bodhisattvas who, prior to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), [proceed in this manner].

Regarding the transformation of the body through change (*pariṇāmika-śarīra*): although these [bodhisattvas] have not yet attained a purely untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), at the time they sustain their karma, they employ only the untainted;
therefore, the body they receive is also called "transformed. A certain class of bodhisattvas attains this transformed body only upon reaching the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*).
Because at this stage they sustain themselves solely by means of the untainted, the body thus refined is certainly a transformed one. This refers to the sustaining of the [eighth] stage...
Regarding the four dhyānas and past karma, one may still utilize this very body until reaching the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*).

Although it is the final body, one further utilizes the superior, untainted (*anāsrava*) provisions of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and does not pass away; rather, one undergoes further births for the sake of taming [beings], as explained by Guṇaprabha.

As for the claim that bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage experience both fragmented and transformational death (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*) alternately, there is no authoritative textual evidence for this in the *Dharmapāla-śāstra*.

Fourth, regarding the distinction between types: The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "With the Tathāgata as the condition and tainted karma as the cause, those who seek future existence are born within the three realms.
This distinguishes the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).

"With the ground of the latent tendencies of ignorance as the condition and untainted karma as the cause, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and autonomous Bodhisattvas produce the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). This clarifies the transformation [birth-and-death].

It is easy to undergo birth and death. According to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, when ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) within the internal dharma are not heedless, the meritorious and immovable formations they produce do not have ignorance as their condition;
that is, [formations such as] the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and so forth. Such individuals do not create this karma for birth and death.

Furthermore, it says that even ordinary persons within the internal dharma who possess the four roots of goodness and so forth may also create this karma that brings about birth and death. If this were not what is brought about [by karma], [it would be contradictory].
How, within this cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), can one obtain the merit of immovable karma? Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Such a factor of warmth (*uṣmagata*) is both a conditioned phenomenon (*dharma*) and a conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) thing. This factor serves as the root for obtaining the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).

It is like a person riding a horse: he both loves it and urges it on. The mind of warmth is likewise: because of love, one undergoes rebirth; because of aversion, one practices contemplation. Thus, although it is indeed a conditioned phenomenon,"

It is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and can serve as a characteristic for that right path. Furthermore, while the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts state only that noble ones (*ārya*) do not create new karma, they do not say that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) likewise do not create new karma. If this is so, why does the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* not state that ignorance (*avidyā*) is a condition?
It simply states that it is not a condition with respect to non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*); therefore, there is no contradiction. This...

The "body of feeling" (karmic body) varies in length according to one's karma; because it is the realm known by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is called "segmented" (*paricchinna-bheda*).

It is not inconceivable (*acintya*). As for the birth of transformation (*pariṇāma-ja*), for those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) downward—whether they are those who turn back (*vivartana*) or those who proceed directly (*anugamana*)—it all takes manifest ignorance (*vṛtti-avidyā*) and its seeds as conditions.
From the eighth stage upward, whether turning back or proceeding directly, it all takes the seeds of ignorance (*bīja-avidyā*) as conditions.

Because it is supported by the superior outflow-free (anāsrava) states, it does not follow the force of karma; its duration is limited and it cannot be measured by ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles.
Therefore, it is called the inconceivable transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Before the seventh stage, that which is received remains coarse.
From the eighth stage onward, it becomes increasingly subtle.
Regarding the five stages and the levels: segmented birth and death is the dharma experienced by ordinary beings, having proceeded from beginningless time through the nine stages of the three realms.

Regarding the four modes of birth and five destinies, their respective states of retribution differ according to their karmic causes. As for those of the two vehicles, they abandon [birth] upon entering the realm of nirvana without remainder;

as for the various bodhisattvas, they may abandon it at the first stage or the eighth stage. This refers to the transformation of birth and death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*); however, for those who have turned their minds back toward enlightenment, [the situation differs].
Regarding the stages of training and beyond-training, one receives [the fruit] initially according to what is appropriate, as in the case of a person who has attained the first fruit.

If the karma for seven births is entirely determinate, one will only undergo the transformation-rebirth (*pariṇāmi-kāya*) upon reaching the seventh birth. If the karma for seven births is entirely indeterminate, it occurs in the very body of the first birth.

They undergo transformation and rebirth. Among those who have seven births remaining, there are both those for whom it is fixed and those for whom it is not fixed. Those for whom it is fixed all undergo it; those for whom it is not fixed do not.
According to the body they receive, they immediately undergo transformation. There are three grades of persons in the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin): some undergo one more great birth.
If one's karma is fixed, one undergoes this birth and only then undergoes the transformation of death (parināma-cyuti).
If it is not fixed, because of the aversion to taking birth, one undergoes the transformation of death within this very body. Regarding those who have attained the third fruit:

if they are to undergo further births, because of their aversion to taking birth, their superior karma is not fixed and they may undergo the transformation of death within this body; if they do not undergo further births, they may instead be born in the Form Realm. Only then...
They undergo transformation (parivṛtti) because their superior karma is fixed. For those whose karma is not fixed, it is possible to undergo transformation within this very body.
If it is the fourth fruit [of Arhatship], then regardless of which of the two lower realms one is in, one undergoes birth through transformation within that very body.
As for Pratyekabuddhas, they reside exclusively in the desire realm; although they may appear in worlds where no Buddha exists, it is nonetheless due to the power of their spiritual lineage (gotra).

Because they rely [on conditions], they will inevitably receive the Buddha’s transformative teaching and turn their minds [toward enlightenment], with the sole exception of those of the lineage who are exclusively inclined toward quiescence (*śamaikāyana-gotra*).

As stated in the sūtras, those who have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* will give rise to the bodhicitta after eighty thousand *kalpas*, and even those who are *pratyekabuddhas* will give rise to the bodhicitta after ten thousand *kalpas*.
Some say they attain *bodhi*, while others say they reach *nirvāṇa*; however, because they have given rise to...

The mind is that which attains concentration. This means that after turning the mind [toward enlightenment], one passes through eighty thousand *kalpas* up to ten thousand, before finally reaching the first stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*).

Some say that even upon reaching the beginning of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), although the mind has already been turned, because one cannot relinquish the mind that delights in tranquility, one must pass through eighty thousand *kalpas* up to ten thousand while practicing the preparatory stages (*prayoga*).

They practice with negligence and fail to progress. After such kalpas have passed, they finally awaken and advance in their preparatory practices until they reach the beginning of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle eighty, states: "Question: If one dwells solely within the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*),"
Regarding those who are able to set forth: how is it that they can realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through only a single lifetime? Why is this so?
Because even for Arhats and others, there is no longer any remaining lifetime, let alone a succession of many lifetimes.
The answer is: because they must increase their practice and observance before they can achieve accomplishment; for the most part, the World-Honored One [teaches this].
Based on this dedication toward enlightenment, the Śrāvakas were spoken of with intentional meaning as being "of the same category.

Son of good family, if there are those who have well-cultivated the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), they are able to remain for an eon or even more than an eon. Regarding the phrase "more than an eon," the intended meaning here is that it exceeds one eon.
Although they thus augment their life-force (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*) and are able to proceed toward enlightenment, that which they have cultivated...
Their practice becomes extremely sluggish because they delight in nirvāṇa; thus, they do not equal those who have begun their initial practice.

Having thus increased their life-span through such practice, they leave behind their physical body with its sense faculties (*sārūpyakāya*) and separately manifest a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Before fellow practitioners, they employ skillful means to demonstrate entering parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu*). By means of that which they have left behind—the physical body with its sense faculties—...
As for his body, he dwells in seclusion within this very world-system, in Jambudvīpa, wherever he pleases;
even all the gods cannot behold him, let alone other sentient beings.
Because he delights greatly in dwelling in nirvāṇa, among those who travel throughout various worlds to approach, serve, and make offerings to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and in his cultivation...
Among the various noble paths for accumulating the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), when one is negligent, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas repeatedly awaken them.
Having been awakened, they become able to practice without negligence. The commentary explains:

because they delight in *nirvāṇa*, regarding their extensive travels and the cultivation of the provisions, the time of negligence lasts for eighty thousand *kalpas*, and so forth, up to ten [thousand].
This refers to a period of a thousand kalpas. Once awakened, those who are not negligent are at the time for generating the resolve and advancing in practice.
Even though a *pratyekabuddha* (directly-advancing bodhisattva) possesses afflictions, they will reach the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in at most ten thousand kalpas.

Those who turn toward the Two Vehicles, although they have severed eighty thousand and ten thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), only reach the stage of the Ten Faiths; therefore, they are said to be "dull-witted.
This is not like those who begin their practice from the start. Thus far has been the analysis of those who turn toward [the Mahāyāna].

As for those who proceed directly, all Bodhisattvas from the eighth ground (*bhūmi*) upward invariably and definitively receive the body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*). Prior to the seventh ground, there are two types of persons: the first is...

First, an abundance of wisdom; second, an abundance of compassion. While the former undergoes transformation and change, the latter does not, because they intentionally accept birth and death in order to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Regarding the sixth point, the inclusion of the four types of birth and death, according to the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, there are four kinds of birth and death.

First, the birth-and-death of skillful means (*upāya*); second, the birth-and-death of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); third, the birth-and-death of existence (*bhava*); and fourth, the birth-and-death of non-existence (*abhava*).

Regarding the birth-and-death of skillful means, that sūtra states: "Just as among the twelve links, ignorance gives rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), so too does the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) act as a condition to give rise to the first birth-and-death of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*). Regarding the birth-and-death of causes and conditions, that [sūtra]...

The Sūtra states: "Just as the various formations (*saṃskāra*) produced with ignorance (*avidyā*) as a condition are called 'birth-and-death through causes and conditions' (*hetu-pratyaya-jarāmaraṇa*), so too are the untainted karmas (*anāsrava-karma*) produced with the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) as a condition.
Regarding "birth-and-death involving existence" (*bhava-jarāmaraṇa*), the Sūtra states:

"Just as the fruits of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu-bhava*) summoned by formations are the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) obtained through untainted karma, this is 'birth-and-death without existence' (*abhava-jarāmaraṇa*)."

As for that, it is said that "birth conditions old age and death" refers to the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*), with the final body serving as the condition for inconceivable retrogression.
According to the sutras and their corresponding metaphors, although four types are mentioned, only one is truly the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*).
These four are spoken of collectively based on the causes and conditions of birth-and-death as well as its essence; it is not that the essence of birth-and-death itself consists of four types.
Why is this so? The first is the condition for birth and death (*saṃsāra*); the second is the cause; the third is precisely the fruit of retribution that is produced;
and the fourth consists of the two characteristics of change and cessation at the very end. Furthermore, within that [segmented] division, there are four kinds of difficulties:

first, the difficulty of afflictions (*kleśa*), namely ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*); [the difficulty] within the transformational [birth and death], namely the birth and death of expedient means (*upāya*). There is no...

The same applies to the stage of clear abiding (*vidyā-sthiti-bhūmi*). Second is the difficulty regarding karma: this refers to the wholesome and unwholesome karma of the practitioner, which serves as the causal condition for birth-and-death within the transformational realm (*pariṇāma-vaśika*).
The same applies to the untainted (*anāsrava*). Third is the difficulty regarding retribution: this refers to the five fruits and the branch of birth (*jāti-aṅga*).
In the *nirmāṇa-cyuti* (transformative death), there is birth and death. The mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) produced by untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) is also like this.

Regarding the difficulty of the four faults: these are namely old age and death; furthermore, the three types—afflictions, karma, and birth—all possess the sense of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) due to their transience.

In the transformative [death], there is no [ordinary] birth and death; even the final falling away is likewise [without ordinary birth and death]. Or, it is simply the preceding three types of transience.

The suffering of conditioned existence (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) is a fault. However, the term "birth and death" (*saṃsāra*) applies generally to both cause and effect, as both are part of the process of transmigration;

yet it applies specifically only to the retribution of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). The above has distinguished the two types of birth and death solely according to their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), focusing exclusively on retribution.

The Sūtra, however, speaks of them collectively according to their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), stating that afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and retribution constitute the four types of birth and death. This is the view of the ancient masters.

It is incorrect to assign the stage of "birth-and-death with outflows" (*sāsrava-jāti-maraṇa*) to the first, second, and third stages; to assign "birth-and-death through causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-jāti-maraṇa*) to the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages;
to assign "birth-and-death with existence" (*bhava-jāti-maraṇa*) to the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages; and to assign "birth-and-death without existence" (*abhava-jāti-maraṇa*) to the tenth stage.

However, regarding the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, what is the meaning of its correlation of twenty-two types of ignorance with eleven kinds of coarse retributions (*dauṣṭhulya*) and their distribution across the four births and deaths?
It means that in the first four stages, one has not yet attained the vision of the truths; thus, although untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) exists as a causal condition, its name is obscured.
Consequently, the designation "birth and death" is established based on conventional skillful means (*upāya*). The fifth, sixth, and seventh stages are supramundane (*lokottara*).

The stage [of the tenth bhūmi] is manifested through its untainted causes; within it, there is still that which has not yet received its fruit. Therefore, by virtue of its causal conditions, it receives the name "birth and death.

From the eighth, ninth, and tenth bhūmis, one has already received the *pariṇāminirvāṇa* (transformative rebirth). Although within these three stages one has already received the fruit, there is subsequently a further eleventh retribution.
For this reason, they are specifically termed "birth and death with existence" (*sabhava-jāti-maraṇa*). The "emergence portion" (*niṣkrānta-bhāga*) of the tenth bhūmi is the supreme...
Regarding "subsequent existence": because there is no further reception of karmic retribution thereafter, it is called "the absence of birth and death.

Thus, the meaning of the assignment of stages differs, and the meaning of the discernment of nature differs. Therefore, the four types of birth and death, when correlated with the eleven retributions, correspond to the distribution of four, three, one, and one;
this is not contradictory to principle.
The seventh assembly explains the three types of mind-born beings (*manomaya*). Regarding these three types of mind-born beings, there are two approaches.

First, the general approach concerning the three vehicles, as cited above in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), which relies on the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* to refer to arhats and pratyekabuddhas.

And there are bodhisattvas who have attained mastery (*vaśitā*). Regarding these bodhisattvas who have attained mastery: some are on the first stage (*bhūmi*) because they have already attained mastery over birth through the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state;

some are on the seventh stage because they have entered the stage of the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and some are on the eighth stage because they have attained the state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* states:

"From the first stage onward, one has already departed from birth-and-death with limited segments (*paricchinna-bheda-maraṇa*). Thus, it is known that [the transformation body] receives its intention at the first stage.
Regarding the birth-body (*janmakāya*), the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, fascicle four, states:

"O Mahāmati, by preaching the Dharma of tranquility, one attains the realization of the characteristic of pure non-self and enters the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*). Having entered the Far-Reaching Stage, one attains mastery over immeasurable samādhis."
Because of the body born of mastery (*manomaya-kāya*), it is known that the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) also attains the body born of mastery; however, this is not yet universal.
Second, regarding the ten stages of the bodhisattva universally, three types of bodies born of mastery are established. As stated in the fifth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
"There are three kinds of bodies born of mastery. What are the three? First, the body born of mastery through the attainment of the bliss of samādhi."
First, the physical body (*janma-kāya*). Second, the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) that realizes the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are.

Third, the mind-made body that arises spontaneously with its kind and acts without effort. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, the Bodhisattva practices according to reality and attains the signs of realization of the progressively higher stages.
What is the mind-made body that attains the bliss of samādhi and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*)? It refers to the third [stage].
In the fourth and fifth stages, one’s own mind becomes tranquil and performs various activities.

The ocean-like mind, the waves of the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), and the bliss of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) are called the arising of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). Because one perceives the objects of one’s own mind, one knows, as they truly are, the characteristics of existence and non-existence;
this is called the characteristic of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*). What is the mental faculty that realizes the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are?
The "body born of birth" refers to that within the eight stages where, through observation and realization, one attains the signlessness of all phenomena;
as explained at length, this extends up to attaining mastery over the will and entering the assemblies in the lands of all Buddhas according to one's inclination.

This is called the "mind-made body born of the thorough realization of the characteristics of all phenomena. What is the "mind-made body born of the spontaneous activity of the same class"? It refers to one's own realm...

Internally self-realizing all phenomena as having the characteristic of bliss according to reality, because the characteristic of phenomena is bliss—this is called the "manomayakāya born of the same category, spontaneously arising, and without effortful activity.
The commentary explains: within the first two stages (*bhūmi*), one also attains the "manomayakāya of the bliss of samādhi."
However, because they have not yet attained mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are omitted and not explained. Another interpretation states:

regarding the first two types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*), the middle one is cited to include both the preceding and succeeding ones. That is to say, the first mind-made body cites the third, fourth, and fifth stages, which thereby includes the first and second stages as well as the sixth stage.
The second body cites the eighth stage, which thereby includes the seventh and ninth stages. If...

If it were not so, what would be the meaning of the term "mind-born" (*manomaya*) for those not explicitly mentioned? Since the first two [stages] have already been mentioned, they subsume the middle;
as for the third mind-born stage, its non-mention makes its existence self-evident. Therefore, these stages are not enumerated in the sutra.
The eighth question-and-answer section on *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) consists of four questions and answers. Since these are fully elucidated therein, they will not be recounted here again.
III. Seeking the Forest of Meanings (*Arthavanam-paryeṣaṇā*):

The three seekings are briefly analyzed through five gates: first, name; second, essence (*svabhāva*); third, torrent (*ogha*); fourth, the mutual inclusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-saṃgraha*); and fifth, the seven [categories].

Regarding the *anuśaya* (latent dispositions), there are five different explanations in various treatises: First, as for the name: "seeker" (*anuśayin*) means "one who seeks. This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Second, as for its essence:
it consists of all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, along with the simultaneous mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as well as bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*).

Excluding those arising through the power of false teachings, as well as those associated with right view, or those that are innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) and so forth—just as described above—all such factors that seek an essential nature (*svabhāva*) belong to the realms of desire and form, excluding the formless realm.

Furthermore, excluding those that are untainted (*anāsrava*), those that are wholesome by way of preparation for right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi-prayoga-kuśala*), those that are conducive to the untainted (*anāsravānulomika*), and those arising through the power of false teachings, all remaining phenomena possess an essential nature. If one speaks only of Brahmā...
The pursuit of conduct (*brahmacaryaiṣaṇā*) consists of the right view regarding the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as innate virtue and untainted bodily and vocal actions;

these are all the essential nature of the pursuit of pure conduct. If one speaks of the "pursuit of false pure conduct," this refers to that which arises through the power of false teachings within the three realms, along with its associated bodily and vocal actions;
this is the essential nature of the third pursuit. The current explanation differs [from others], and it has already been reconciled and explained as follows.
There is a textual passage for this at [Treatise on the] Sixty-Five [Dharmas], but I could not find it upon searching;

the text has been mis-collated. Regarding the three floods (*ogha*), there are four: namely, the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*). The commentary explains:

all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding ignorance and views, constitute the flood of desire. This can be understood by examining their essential natures, excluding ignorance and views, as listed under the five gates.

This is the substance of the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*). As for the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), it consists of the five gates of the form and formless realms; its substance is to be reckoned as above. The remainder, with the further exclusion of hatred (*dveṣa*), is the substance of the outflow of existence.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) refers to the ignorance of the three realms. Views (*dṛṣṭi*) refer to the five views of the three realms. As stated in the *Mahā-śāstra*, fascicle 89:
"The superior-grade greed of the desire realm arises in those who have not yet abandoned desire; this is the outflow of the desire realm. Those who have already [abandoned it]...

Excluding those who have abandoned greed for the upper realms, these are the *āsravas* (outflows). According to the discourse on the gateways of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there are two remaining types of arising outflows:
the outflow of evil views, which refers to the sixty-two views; and four of the five views, which are the views regarding causes and conditions.

How are these? Ignorance (*avidyā*) alone is called the outflow of ignorance; this is the perception of consciousness. This is stated according to what is predominant and most frequent, as in the case of knowing the preceding [factors] as they truly are.
It is said that there are sixty-five types of existence (*bhava*). Now, regarding the distinctions among these three types of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*):

according to the beginning of the seventh fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the first flow is the seeking of sensual desire (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*); the second flow is the seeking of existence (*bhava-paryeṣaṇā*), which encompasses both the form and formless realms;

and the latter two flows constitute the seeking of false holy life (*mithyā-brahmacarya-paryeṣaṇā*), which encompasses all three realms and so forth. Does the "seeking of sensual desire" mentioned in this present text include the flow of sensual desire?
When [the category of] "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) is established, the three evil destinies are excluded, because it encompasses only those born within the three realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

As for "existence-seeking" (*bhavārthika*), it does not encompass the fourth dhyāna or the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-āyatana*) and so forth. Nevertheless, there is no logical contradiction; as stated in the seventh fascicle of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, these two categories have mutual differences in breadth and narrowness.

While that [text] includes the five destinies above the desire realm—thereby excluding ignorance (*avidyā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*)—this [category], although pertaining to humans and devas, nonetheless...

To take both ignorance (*avidyā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) [as causes] would mean that while the *gati* (destinies) are broad, the *vastu* (entities) are narrow; however, in this treatise, the *gati* are narrow while the *vastu* are broad.

Nevertheless, when distinguished by way of *gati* and *dhātu*, both sides are acceptable. As stated in the sixth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, there are five *gatis* within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Because one seeks all types [of existence], the treatise states that by the power of seeking, one does not escape the desire realm; that which invites the suffering of the desire realm is "existence-seeking" (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*).
This treatise does not apply to the fourth dhyāna, the formless realms (*ārūpya*), or the seventh [consciousness].

The first [category] includes the fourth dhyāna and the four formless realms, thereby excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) of those levels. Those levels are broad while the destinies (*gati*) are narrow; this, however, refers to the destiny.
The ground is broad and the space is narrow, as in the sixth section at the end [of that treatise], which discusses the elements of earth (pṛthivī-dhātu).

It is precisely due to the power of seeking existence (*bhava-icchā*) that the two realms are not mentioned as bringing about the suffering of the form and formless realms. Regarding the discussion on the Brahma-seeking, according to this treatise, it refers exclusively to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) in the fourth [dhyāna].
Thus, all afflictions that seek externally in accordance with [the world] have the nature of false seeking, as in the seventh fascicle.

Furthermore, the ignorance and views of the three realms all have the nature of false seeking, as in the sixth fascicle. Consequently, the invitation of birth and death within the three realms is entirely of the nature of false seeking.
In that [Abhidharma], the seventh realm is broad while the destinies (*gati*) are narrow; in this treatise, the destinies are broad while the realms are narrow, existing only in—
The fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) do not exist in the lower realms; as stated in the sixth fascicle, all three realms are thus included. This is the definitive treatise.
Although this treatise mentions the four formless states, it does not necessarily imply that all [aspects] are taken up.

While there are distinct types of seeking, such as craving and pride, these exist in the lower realms; therefore, they are categorized as "three" based on their types. The first stream [of beings] seeks desire. The second...
The second stream is the pursuit of existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*). The third and fourth streams are the pursuit of false holy life (*mithyā-brahmacarya-tṛṣṇā*). Speaking in terms of the realms (*dhātu*):

the pursuit of desire (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*) resides in the three destinies (*gati*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), though in reality it pervades all five destinies. The pursuit of existence resides in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), excluding the fourth dhyāna, though in reality it also pervades it.

The pursuit of false holy life and so forth reside in the fourth dhyāna as well as the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The treatise states that they are not excluded [from the fourth dhyāna]; thus, they include the fourth dhyāna.
Distinguishing the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): this treatise discusses it in relation to the arising of the three types of sensual pleasure (*kāmarati*), and thus it differs [from other systems].

This [treatise] treats the third flood (*ogha*) and yoke (*yoga*); since the yoke clarifies the essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is no different from the flood. In the initial passage of the sixty-fourth [section], there is again this difference:
that [other system] speaks of the three outflows (*āsava*).

Regarding the classification of the forty-nine latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): those seeking sensual pleasure (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*) comprise two, namely the two latent dispositions of sensual craving (*kāmarāga*) and hostility (*pratigha*).

Those seeking existence (*bhava-paryeṣaṇā*) comprise one, namely the latent disposition of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), which likewise extends throughout the two upper realms. Those seeking erroneously (*mithyā-paryeṣaṇā*) comprise four latent dispositions: pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Regarding the fifth point, the differences in the interpretation of the text: according to this passage, the "pursuit of false brahmacarya" (mithyā-brahmacaryaiṣaṇā) encompasses all three realms.
As for pride (māna), views (dṛṣṭi), and ignorance (avidyā), these are all distinct from the aforementioned floods (ogha).

Within the flood of desire (kāma-ogha) and the flood of existence (bhava-ogha), they are all categorized as "false pursuits" (mithyā-paryeṣaṇā) in terms of their types, because the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of pride and doubt are subsumed under false pursuit. These [categories] represent the actual inclusion [of the defilements]. This is from the seventh fascicle.

Regarding the summary of the outflows (*āsrava*): there is such a summary of existence (*bhava*). Now, in this context, since the pride and doubt arising from non-Buddhists must also subsequently lead to wrong seeking (*mithyā-paryeṣaṇā*), they are subsumed under wrong seeking.
However, their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not [wrong view], because their individual natures are not of the nature of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
