If that is so, how about ignorance (*avidyā*)? Ignorance is necessarily concomitant with views, whereas doubt and pride are not fixed [as being so]; therefore, they do not serve as an analogy for the former, which are all [fixed].
Restated. *Supplement to the Mahāyāna Dharma Garden Forest Chapters*, Scroll Four;
*Supplement to the Mahāyāna Dharma Garden Forest Chapters*, Scroll Seven.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Huizhao of Dayun Monastery.

The Forest of Meanings on the Elements (Dhātu) and Bases (Āyatana). The Forest of Meanings on the Five Aggregates (Skandha). (Combined to clarify the differences in breadth and narrowness among the three categories; hence they are treated separately. The Forest of Meanings on the Five Objects (Viṣaya).

The *Dhātu-āyatana-artha-vana* (Forest of Meanings of the Elements and Bases) is analyzed through seven gates: first, the explanation of names; second, the determination of essence; third, the establishment of the intent; fourth, the sequence; fifth, the refutation and establishment;
sixth, various categories; and seventh, questions and answers.

First, regarding the explanation of the names: first the enumeration, then the explanation. The enumeration of the names may be understood [from the text]. As for the explanation of the names, there is first the general and then the specific.

The general name is *dhātu* (realm) and *āyatana* (base). Regarding *dhātu*: in Sanskrit it is called *dhātu*, which in the language of Tang (Chinese) means "realm" (*jie*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga Practice), fascicle 56, asks:

"What is the meaning of *dhātu*? It answers: "The meaning of cause; the meaning of seed; the meaning of intrinsic nature; the meaning of lineage; the meaning of subtlety; the meaning of... [and so forth].

The meaning of "sustaining" (*dhṛti*) is what is called the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*). These six meanings are all termed "elements. The older interpretation that it means only "sustaining" relies on a single meaning and does not exhaust the full principle.
As for "locus" (*āyatana*), in Sanskrit it is *āyatanam*, which in the language of Tang (Chinese) is translated as "locus.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (56) states: it has the meaning of being the gateway through which the various minds and mental factors arise and grow; the meaning of "condition" (*ālambana*); the meaning of "expedient means" (*upāya*); and the meaning of "the nature of conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*).
The sense of being a basis, and the sense of being a place of residence—these are called the meaning of "āyatana" (base). These six meanings are all termed *āyatana*.

The old translations rendered this as "entry" (*praveśa*). However, the commentary states: "The meaning of 'entry' refers to the Śrāvaka. Why? Because of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*)."
Because consciousness arises therein, it is called an "entrance" (*āyatana*). If that were so, when consciousness actually arises, it should not be called an "entrance.
This is because these [bases]—the faculties and their objects—are what can produce consciousness. Furthermore, if one says "entrance," the Sanskrit original should be *āyadvāra* (gate of arising);

since it is stated as *āyatana*, one cannot call it an "entrance. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Chapter 14), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Chapter 1), and the *Pañcaskandhaka-prakaraṇa* clarify the *dhātus*.

The meaning of their respective locations is identical in this regard. The numbers eighteen and twelve are merely numerical designations; they follow the "appositional compound with a numeral" (*saṃkhyāpūrvapada-dvigu*) among the six types of grammatical analysis (*ṣaṭ-vibhakti*).
To explain their individual names: that which illuminates is called the eye; that which hears is called the ear; that which smells is called the nose;

that which tastes is called the tongue; that which touches is called the body; and that which cognizes is called the mind. Thus, the fifteenth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "It refers to the sense of seeing."

Hearing the object of meaning, smelling the object of meaning, tasting the object of meaning, touching the object of meaning, and knowing the object of meaning—these are called the "establishment of the sense bases" (*indriya-pratiṣṭhāna*) in terms of the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound, as they both encompass the faculty and its corresponding objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
Regarding the six objects such as form: that which is traversed by the eye is called "form" (*rūpa*), and those apprehended by the ear and so forth are called "sound" (*śabda*) and so on;

these are also *karmadhāraya* compounds. As for the six consciousnesses: they are designated as "eye-consciousness" and so forth because they depend upon those respective faculties and take those respective objects as their conditions. (*Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*)

The second [explanation] says: it has the nature of discerning based on the eye and conditioned by visible forms, and so on, up to having the nature of discerning based on the mind and conditioned by mental objects (*dharma*).
"The eye and so forth" refers to the bases (*āśraya*); "visible forms and so forth" refers to their respective objects; "discerning" refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of consciousness.
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 5, it may also be called "consciousness of form" and so forth, named after its object. This is the "mixed" [classification].

The collection [of consciousness] arises from the faculties; it is merely named after the eye and so forth, following the designation of its basis. All such cases are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 51, states: "Just as fire burns by depending on grass, chaff, or wood shavings, it receives their names and is thus called 'grass-fire' and so forth."
An illustration will clarify this.

Second, regarding the identification of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), there are briefly four types: first, in relation to the hundred dharmas; second, in relation to the three categories (*triskandha*); third, in relation to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*);
and fourth, in relation to the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*). First, concerning the hundred dharmas: the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) of form are among the eleven types of matter.
The sense-faculties have form as their substance. The mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) has as its substance the six past types of mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and the seventh and eighth mind-kings.

The *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states: "As for the mind-element (*manas-dhātu*), it consists of those [consciousnesses] that have just ceased without interval. The phrase "those" refers to the six consciousnesses.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*): it does not refer to the seventh or eighth [consciousnesses], as they are not objects of further desire and so on. Alternatively, the seventh and eighth may also be the same as the six consciousnesses:

that which was past is called the *manas*, while that which is present is termed *manovijñāna*. Since the designation *manovijñāna* is broad in scope, it encompasses seeds of the future as well as those of the past and present.

All of these constitute the essence of the *dhātu*. Thus, the first chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "It refers to the eye that has previously seen or currently sees forms, as well as its seeds.

The [eye] that has previously seen forms maintains the meaning of the past consciousness’s experience; the [eye] currently seeing forms maintains the meaning of the present consciousness’s experience.
As for these seeds, they either project the future eye-faculty or, having already been accomplished, produce the present one."

Regarding the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), these two types are called the "eye-element" (*cakṣur-dhātu*) because they are the causes for the arising of the eye. This excludes seeds of the eye that will never arise;

the same should be understood up to the mind-element (*mano-dhātu*). As for the five material elements (*rūpa-dhātu*), their substance consists of the five—form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects—among the one hundred dharmas.
The dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*) consists of the five types of form within the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) among the one hundred dharmas, as well as the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*).
All phenomena consist of twenty-four types of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and six types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

However, with the exception of the unconditioned, the remainder pertain to all three time periods. Although space lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is an object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and is therefore subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*);
furthermore, it likewise lacks past and future [distinctions]. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "All forms previously seen by the eye, as well as the eye-faculty, increase in this regard..."
Above. This is the characteristic of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the predominance (*adhipatibala*) of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) therein:

it means that because external objects arise based on the predominance of the physical sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), this [eye-faculty] is predominant because it is superior in producing consciousness from the faculty and establishing the seeds of the object.
As for the seeds of form and those of the future, they are not the objective domain of the eye; therefore, they are omitted here without discussion. In reality, however, these too are indeed form.
From the *dhātu* up to the *dharmadhātu*, the same applies to their major divisions. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (56), it is also stated in this same way:

"If that which is produced through the predominance (*adhipati*) of a material faculty (*rūpindriya*), or if that [faculty] is predominant with respect to it, this is called the 'form realm' (*rūpadhātu*);

it also extends across the three periods of time. The third fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* asks: "How many are already arisen? It replies: "All of the past and present, and one part of everything else."
How many are not already arisen? This refers to all future phenomena (*anāgata-dharma*) and a portion of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (56): Question: What is the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*)? Answer: It is the eye that has not yet been severed, or which, having been severed, is still sustained by the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Just as it is with the eye-element, so too should one know it to be for the elements from the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñāna-dhātu*) up to a portion of the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*). Thus it is transmitted.

The Tripitaka Master explains: For ordinary beings and those still in training (*śaikṣa*), [the seeds] have not yet been severed; for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they have already been severed.

Nevertheless, because they are sustained by the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and thus attain continuity, it is said that the life-faculty performs the function of sustaining them. In reality, however, it is the ālayavijñāna that sustains them.
This is explained in terms of what has not yet been severed from its objective fetters (*ālambana-bandhana*) and what has already been severed. Now, it is further explained:

if the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) has not been severed, that which is not the final eye-faculty of an Arhat is called "not yet severed. Alternatively, regarding "having already been severed," this refers to having been acquired and then lost;

or it refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) and so forth, whose current eye-faculty is severed, and is thus termed "already severed. As for "sustained by the life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya-parigṛhīta*): [End of excerpt]

Because it sustains those seeds, it is capable of bringing about rebirth. Regarding its inclusion within the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*): since the life-faculty is established based on the eighth consciousness, it is called the "life-faculty.
Thus, the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Apart from this life-faculty, the commonality of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) and so forth cannot be found.

The six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, refer to the six—namely, the manifest consciousnesses and their seeds—within the hundred dharmas; these are the seven mind-kings (*cittarāja*).

The eighth [consciousness] is of two kinds. According to the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, it is subsumed under the mind-element (*manodhātu*). Alternatively, it may pertain to both elements, as previously analyzed.
Some say that the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states it is subsumed under the six consciousness-elements because it maintains their seeds;

the Tripiṭaka Master’s commentary explains that this refers to the six [elements] by following the function from its essence. However, speaking according to the actual reality, it is subsumed under the mind-element. Furthermore, it is said to maintain all...

The seeds of the elements (*dhātu*) should also pertain to the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). Since this is not the case here, how could it be so there? Alternatively, one might grant that although they maintain those seeds, they do not count as being subsumed under them because they are not of the nature of mind.

Furthermore, another interpretation is that the treatise relies on the perspective of "concomitant transformation" (*anuvartana*), or explains according to the simultaneous presence of sense-faculties and objects, thereby dividing the mind into the six consciousness-elements (*vijñānadhātu*).
The substance of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) can be understood by analogy with the elements; therefore, I shall not elaborate further.
Thus it is stated. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* says: "Question: What are the characteristics of the locus? Answer: It should be explained as in the case of the elements (*dhātu*).

However, the past is excluded; that is to say, one should explain according to the meaning: 'the eye that shall see form,' along with its seeds, etc. Regarding the word "etc.," it refers to the eye that shall see form, the present eye, and the seeds.
By "etc.," one includes what has already been seen, what is being seen, and their respective seeds; these should be explained according to the meaning. Those seven minds...

The elements (*dhātu*) are also designated as the sense bases (*āyatana*), such as the mind base (*manāyatana*). Therefore, it is said that they should be explained according to their respective meanings. If the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56, states:

"That is to say, if a faculty has already been acquired and not yet abandoned, and its immediate essence is not of a nature subject to cessation—just as with the characteristics of the eye base (*cakṣurāyatana*), so too should the intrinsic nature of the other bases be understood.
'Already acquired and not yet abandoned' means, excluding those that have arisen and perished, [it refers to] the immediate essence."

Regarding those phenomena that are not subject to cessation: with the exception of the final eye-faculty and so forth of an Arhat, the various bases are definitively incapable of producing visual consciousness and the like.

This is the same as the case regarding the faculties and their objects. Regarding the two [categories] in relation to the three aggregates (*skandha*): the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter two, states: "The aggregate of form consists of ten elements (*dhātu*):
the five faculties such as the eye, the five objects such as visible form, and a portion of the dharma-element; as do the aggregates of feeling and perception."
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is one part of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*); since it does not encompass the entire essence of the dharma-element, it is said to be "one part.

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) consists of the seven consciousness-elements (*vijñānadhātu*), namely the six consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and so forth—and the mind-element (*manodhātu*). Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the aggregate of consciousness is the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*);

the others are to be understood according to the explanation of the elements. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter three, asks: "What is established as a base (*āyatana*)? It refers to the ten material elements (*rūpadhātu*). This means:

The ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) [are included in the aggregate of form]. The seven consciousnesses are the mind base (*manāyatana*). The element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is the phenomena base (*dharmāyatana*).

This is also the same as what is stated in the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*. Third, regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): all [of these] are equally pervasive and take the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as their essence.

Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the element of phenomena and the phenomena base each constitute one part, but they do not constitute its essence. All remaining [factors] are pervasive, because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are not produced by conditions.

Therefore, the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) takes as its essence one portion each of the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) and the dharma-base (dharmāyatana). It consists solely of the six unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), as no others are applicable.
This is according to the gate of the permanent and the impermanent; if categorized by the outflowing and the non-outflowing, it comprises one portion of all [phenomena].
It also has perfect accomplishment as its essence (*svabhāva*), because its nature is free from inversion and its function (*vṛtti*) is all-pervasive. Fourth, regarding the five dharmas:

all [of these] are "characteristics" (*nimitta*) and are what is expressed; the portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) is called the "essence," because it consists of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*), which are the expressers and their basis.

When the provisional is subsumed under the real, it belongs only to the form-element (*rūpadhātu*). If the provisional and the real are discussed separately, then there is one [instance] in each of the two elements.

It is a portion. The seven consciousness-elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*), the mind-base (*manāyatana*), the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*), and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) each have one portion whose essence is discrimination.

This excludes the untainted (*anāsrava*); thus, their essence is the correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) previously excluded, taken as a perfected whole (*pariniṣpanna*), as explained in the context of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Regarding the third point concerning the underlying intent, there are three further expositions. First, it is to reveal that the four conditions (*pratyaya*) are subsumed within three conditions, and thus the two categories of *dhātu* and *āyatana* are established in their respective order.
Thus, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* (Treatise on the Five and Six) states: "Question: For the sake of revealing what meaning are the *dhātus* established? Answer:

To reveal the meaning of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), as well as the meaning of the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and experience (*upabhoga*), the *dhātus* are established. This intention reveals that the six [internal] bases are established as the sense faculties.

Six [bases] are established to manifest the objects; six are established for the sake of enjoyment. However, as for the conditions: the name manifests the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of the faculties, while the object manifests the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Enjoyment manifests the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). For the purpose of clarifying what meaning, are the bases (*āyatana*) established?
They are established to demonstrate the three types of conditions: the immediately preceding, the objective, and the dominant. Thus, the immediately preceding...

The object-condition establishes the objective sphere; the dominant condition establishes six [faculties]. However, since the preceding [explanation] already manifested the immediate condition as the basis for establishing the faculties, it is itself the sixth faculty.
Alternatively, five [faculties] are established by way of the dominant condition, with two [the mind and mental factors] serving to manifest the grasper and the grasped, as well as their seeds.
Furthermore, because there are the grasper and the grasped, the "divisions" (dhātu) are established. Thus, the second chapter of the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states:

"In order to manifest the meaning of the seeds of those divisions—the grasper and the grasped—the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are established: the six sense-faculty elements as the grasper and their seeds; the six object elements as the grasped and their seeds;
and the six consciousness elements as the divisions thereof and their seeds. Therefore, that verse says: "The grasper, the grasped, and their..."
"Taking up" refers to the meaning of "seed," which is termed a *dhātu*. The term "one kind" below applies throughout the three preceding [categories].

To manifest the functional gate of that which experiences and the object to be cognized, the twelve *āyatanas* are established. Now, the meaning of the functional gate of experiencing refers to the six internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).

If the meaning of the functional gate of the objects to be cognized is intended, these are the six external bases (*bāhyāyatana*). Thus, the verse says: "The capacity to experience and the objects to be cognized... regarding their function.

The meaning of "gate" (*dvāra*) is "locus" (*āyatana*). This is also the same in the second major section of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. The third [section] explains the meaning of the gate of contact as the cause for the arising of object, consciousness, and sensation.

The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (XIV) states: "To contemplate the three factors—sense faculty, object, and consciousness—in conjunction as arising from their own causes is called 'skillfulness regarding the elements' (*dhātu-kauśalya*).
Because those various phenomena have flowed forth since beginningless time, they arise from their own seeds; because they arise frequently, and because of the seeds..."

Because the arising of the various types [of consciousness] is not from a single realm, but rather from various realms, one establishes the twelve bases (*āyatana*)—namely, the sense faculties and their objects—by means of well-understood wisdom regarding the meaning of the "gateways of contact" (*sparśāyatana*), as explained at length.
This is called skill in the bases (*āyatanakauśalya*). There are slight differences among the three versions of the text.

The general meaning is entirely the same: [these views] are all intended to refute the false conception of a self (*ātman*) that serves as the cause of all phenomena, as well as the nature of the experiencer.

Thus, the first verse of the *Madhyāntavibhāga* states: "The view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, which clings to them as being a single entity, the cause, the experiencer, the agent, that which acts with sovereignty, the dominant factor, the permanent, the basis of defilement and purification, and the nature of one who is bound or liberated—this is the clinging to unity."
1. The nature of a single essence; 2. the nature of being the cause of grasping; 3. the nature of the grasper; 4. the nature of the agent; 5. the nature of independent sovereignty;
6. the nature of supreme authority; 7. the nature of permanence; 8. the nature of being the basis for defilement and purification;
9. the nature of the practitioner; and 10. the nature of the one who is bound or liberated. It is for the purpose of counteracting these ten kinds of self-view that [the following is taught].

One cultivates skillfulness in the ten categories, beginning with the aggregates (*skandha*). These two—elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*)—serve as the antidotes to the grasping at a causal nature and the grasping at a recipient nature.
That is to say, it is to counteract the grasping at a self-soul (*ātman*), or Īśvara and so forth, as the cause of all phenomena, or the grasping at a self as the recipient nature.
It clarifies that the sixfold set, such as the eye and so forth, serves as the generative cause, while the six faculties, such as the eye and so forth, serve as the recipients.
This refers to the absence of a distinct self (*ātman*) or an *īśvara* (Lord), or else it serves to refute the doctrine of causelessness; therefore, it speaks of the "elements" (*dhātu*).

The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (XIV) states: "Because worldly fools are deluded regarding the body, they give rise to delusion concerning its primary cause, thereby clinging to an unequal cause—namely, a permanent *īśvara*, Brahmā, and so forth—or they speak of causelessness, which is the denial of [any such cause]."
The essence of all generative causes and the application (*yoga*) of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) likewise refute the self (*ātman*).
Regarding the fourth sequence, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle 2, states: "Because it proceeds according to the distinctions of worldly affairs.
That is to say, in the world, people first see one another; having seen one another, they exchange greetings; having exchanged greetings, they then receive [hospitality]."
Having bathed, applied fragrant unguents, and donned flower garlands, he next partakes of various kinds of exquisite food and drink; then he enjoys various kinds of bedding and female attendants.
Subsequently, the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) discriminates in various places; because of the sequence of the internal bases (*ādhyātmikadhātu*), the external bases (*bāhyadhātu*) are established.

The consciousness element (*vijñāna-dhātu*) is established according to this sequence; the remainder can be understood accordingly. Because the mind element (*manas-dhātu*) performs pervasive discernment throughout all preceding locations, it is mentioned last.

The external objects follow the sequence of the faculties (*indriya*); the sequence of the bases (*āyatana*) upon which consciousness relies—namely the faculties and their objects—is likewise as described.
Just as with the sequence of the elements (*dhātu*), so it is with the bases (*āyatana*). If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56:

There are seven successive explanations. First, the sequence is established based on the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). There are six further sequences within this. As that treatise’s verse states:
"Because they are numerous, conform to worldly convention, provide joy, serve as adornment, and follow two types of activity, they are taught in this order.
Because the power [of sight] arises repeatedly, the eye is mentioned first; the others are to be understood by analogy to it, hence they are called 'numerous. Second...
The sequence is the same as previously explained. Because joy and bliss arise according to this sequence and not otherwise, this is the fourth cause.
Furthermore, because all sentient beings first rely upon the two types of action—body and speech—and whether pure or impure, they diligently seek food and drink through skillful means;
once they are satiated with food and drink, they then cultivate and indulge in various desires. This is the fifth cause. Moreover...

As for the agent of action: by means of the eye, one purely sees various forms—whether moving or stationary, whether recognized or not—and [discerns] enemies, friends, neutrals, power, play, and so forth.
By means of the ear, one can hear various sounds, giving rise to all manner of discourse and exquisite music.
The nose-element can smell various fragrances; following the scent, it moves toward them, experiencing various joys and pleasures, and nourishing the physical body. The tongue...
The element of the tongue can taste various flavors; the rest is explained as for the nose. The element of the body can touch various tangible objects and experience various joys and pleasures;
however, the instruments of such pleasure may sometimes harm the body. Furthermore, compared to the preceding ones, each subsequent one becomes increasingly narrow and inferior;
therefore, they are mentioned later. The sequence throughout is to be understood according to the elements (*dhātu*).

Regarding the fifth point, the establishment and abolition [of categories], the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle 1, states: Question: For what reason are there only eighteen elements (*dhātu*)? Answer:

Because the body, the instruments, and so forth, are able to maintain the six modes of activity of the past and present, and because they possess the nature of experience. "Body" refers to the six faculties, such as the eye. "Instruments" refers to the six objects, such as form.
"The experience of the six modes of activity of the past and present" refers to the six consciousnesses. "That which is able to maintain" refers to the six... [faculties].

The six faculties and their six objects are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they can support the six consciousnesses by serving as their bases and objects, and because the past and present six consciousnesses, as the experiencers, do not abandon their own characteristics;
thus, they are termed "elements" in the sense of being supports. Question: For what reason are there only twelve bases (*āyatana*)? Answer:
It is solely because the body and its equipment serve as the gateways for the growth and arising of the future six types of experiential activity; that is to say:

Just as the sixfold aspect of experience in the past and present is supported by the eye and other faculties, so too is the sixfold aspect of experience in the future—resembling both the sense-faculties and their objects—the gateway for their growth.
As for the term "only" (*mātra*), it means that the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are established based solely on the faculties and their objects, and not based on the sixfold aspect of experience.
Regarding consciousness, it is said to "support" (*dhṛti*) in the past and present, and to "arise" (*utpatti*) in the future.
The term "gate" (*dvāra*) is used because [the object] is manifest. Therefore, it is said to be likewise. Otherwise, how could it be so?

If [the object] were not a gate of growth in the past or present, then the locus (*sthāna*) would not extend through the past and present; this would contradict the various treatises which establish that the locus extends through the three periods of time.
In the past, [the object] has already grown; in the present, it is currently growing. The meaning of "object" (*artha*) refers to the sense of being an objective field.
The sixth section, the analysis by way of various categories, consists of: 1. the nominal and the substantial; 2. the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*); 3.

the appropriated (*upātta*) and the non-appropriated (*anupātta*); 4. the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and the partially homogeneous (*tatsabhāga*); 5. the knowable (*jñeya*) and the unknowable (*ajñeya*); 6. the cognizable (*vijñeya*) and the non-cognizable (*avijñeya*); 7.

the penetrable (*prameya*) and the non-penetrable (*aprameya*); 8. the resistant (*sapratigha*) and the non-resistant (*apratigha*); 9. the visible (*sanidarśana*) and the invisible (*anidarśana*); 10. the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); 11. the three [times].
Regarding the elements (*dhātu*): twelve are abandoned by the three [types of] abandonment; thirteen pertain to the three trainings; fourteen are analyzed according to four propositions.
First, regarding the analysis of the conventional and the real: the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56, states: "The answer is that they are substantially existent—either seventeen or twelve.
This is because six are unified as one, and one is divided into six. This is based on the principle of conventional establishment, wherein those six are subsumed [into one]."

Because of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), one [element] is said to be conventional (*prajñapti*). Alternatively, since those six [consciousnesses] are divided from the mind-element, the twelve [elements] are real (*dravya*).

To elaborate on this distinction between the conventional and the real, as well as the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), one should consult the Chapter on the Five Aggregates (*pañcaskandhaka*);

it may be fully understood by following that. Regarding the distinction between the appropriated (*upātta*) and the non-appropriated (*anupātta*): it refers to those phenomena upon which the acquisition of sensation arises; however, with the exception of the mind itself, this is the meaning of "appropriated."
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle five, states: "Because it is the matter that serves as the basis for the arising of sensation (*vedanā*), it has the meaning of 'appropriation' (*upātta*).
If sensation arises in dependence upon this matter, it is called 'appropriated. If the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle two, says: 'It is appropriated by consciousness;

it is taken up as its own substance because they share the same security and peril, and thus it is called 'appropriated. This is the sequential exposition of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, whereas the *Vijñaptimātratā* [treatise] provides a comprehensive exposition.

To speak in terms of ultimate reality: "appropriation" (*upādāna*) refers to the sensation of being born. Because consciousness maintains [the body] so that it does not decay, and because there is the sensation of being born, it is called "appropriation.

There is no distinction between this and that; it comprises the entirety of the five sense-faculties (*indriya*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the bases (*āyatana*), as well as a portion of the four objects (*viṣaya*).
This "portion of the four objects" refers to those forms, odors, tastes, tangibles, and sounds that are inseparable from the faculties. Their substance is hollow and porous.

Because they arise and immediately depart from their substrate, they do not involve appropriation (*upātta*). When certain sources state that "five [elements] are partially [appropriated]," this refers to sound while it has not yet departed from its internal primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Regarding the statement that "four are both *sabhāga* and *tatsabhāga*," the term *sabhāga* (homogeneous) means that the sense faculty and consciousness function together in a similar manner, arising in a continuous stream with respect to their respective objects. This is based on the meaning of the faculty and consciousness functioning in a mutually similar way.

This is termed "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā). When the sense faculties arise in a continuous succession that is similar to its own kind even when separated from consciousness, and because they arise in a continuous succession that is similar to their own nature alone—distinct from the union with consciousness—the meaning of the similarity of the faculties is called "that which is homogeneous" (tat-sabhāga).

This is also stated in the *Pañcāśatka* (Treatise on the Fifty): "Of the fifty-six [categories], only a portion of the five faculties within the elements and bases is both homogeneous and that which is homogeneous. Therefore, it is so.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, fascicle five, states: "One portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)—namely, the five [faculties] such as the eye—and one portion of these same elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), are both 'homogeneous' (*sabhāga*) and 'non-homogeneous' (*tatsabhāga*).
The remainder do not necessarily function simultaneously with consciousness. This is because the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-base (*mana-āyatana*) are indeterminate;

they may share the same object as consciousness, or they may have an object even when consciousness is absent. The five sense-faculties are not like this. Alternatively, according to the perspective of the 'concomitant gate,' by way of the mind-element and mind-base..."

It does not coexist with consciousness (*vijñāna*), nor is it said to be equivalent to it. According to the actual principle of reality, since the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] are both subsumed within the sphere of the mind (*manodhātu*) and its base (*manāyatana*), when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) occasionally shares the same object as them, it may be termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). When they do not arise simultaneously, it is termed "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra, Chapter 56. It merely excludes external [objects], speaking of the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and so forth; it does not exclude the internal. As it says:
"Only among the internal elements (*dhātu*) comprised by the sense faculties (*indriya*) does one deliberate upon the homogeneous and the 'partially homogeneous' (*tatsabhāga*);

this is not the case for the external elements such as form (*rūpa*), etc. (1) That which is known is not that which is known; (2) that which is cognized is not that which is cognized; (3) that which is realized is not...

Regarding "that which is reached": it refers to that which is universally accessible and known by consciousness. Wisdom (*jñāna*) taking an object is called "knowledge" (*jñā*); the mind (*citta*) taking an object is called "consciousness" (*vijñā*);

and universal accessibility in taking an object is called "reaching" (*prati*). Wisdom, mind, and universal accessibility each have many varieties, as explained extensively in the treatises. Regarding the distinction between the eight types of "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and "without resistance" (*apratigha*):

these consist of the five faculties and five objective spheres of the desire realm, excluding all faculties and objects belonging to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm; [these constitute] six.
Regarding "transformation of consciousness": all the remaining [factors] are, in one sense, with resistance (*sapratigha*). Thus, the *Pañcavastuka* (Treatise on the Five Categories), verse 56, asks:

"In what sense and how many aggregates are with resistance? The answer is: "The sense of being with resistance consists in mutual contact, according to the meaning of location (*deśa*), and according to the meaning of grossness (*audārika*).
As for the meaning of grossness, it should be understood as being free from three kinds of subtlety. These three kinds of subtlety are as previously described.

It should be known that one part of one aggregate (skandha) is with resistance (sapratigha). Regarding the three kinds of subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*), the *Pañcavastuka* (Treatise on the Five Categories), section 54, states:

1. Subtlety by way of reduction (*apacaya-sūkṣmatā*): This refers to the analytical division of gross matter down to the level of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*). 2. Subtlety by way of kind (*prakāra-sūkṣmatā*):

This refers to the matter of wind and so forth, as well as the matter of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*). 3. Subtlety by way of mastery over the mind (*cittavaśavarti-sūkṣmatā*): This refers to the two realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding "all forms" (*rūpa*), that which constitutes "one part of one aggregate" refers to one part of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

According to the second chapter of the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, there are three reasons for explaining that [form] is "with resistance" (*sapratigha*): first, by way of its category, because it is of the nature of resistance;

second, by way of accumulation, meaning that atoms accumulate so that a single atom is known to be non-obstructive; and third, by way of being unrefined, meaning it is not refined through meditative concentration. Based on this, then...

Excluding the dharma-element and the dharma-base, [the remaining] forms are not composed of atoms because they are cultivated through meditative refinement. These two treatises both rely on coarse and manifest phenomena;

they do not speak exhaustively of the principle. To speak in detail, the forms produced by karma within the form realm—the five faculties and five objects—as well as the faculties and objects of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), those transformed by meditative mastery, and edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) and so forth, are all characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*). As the *Pañcaṣaṣṭikā* states, this is based on their spatial location.
Because "meaning" (*artha*) also possesses resistance (*sapratigha*). These [terms] are all spoken of in reference to location and because they possess the sense of being coarse and large;

thus, one distinguishes them from these [other things]. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, fascicle three, states: "That which can obstruct coming and going is the meaning of 'resistance' (*pratigha*).
Fish, rice, gold, silver, and so forth, which have practical utility, all obstruct coming and going. If it were otherwise, they would lack practical utility.

Therefore, it is further stated: "All that is visible is obstructive. This is because the matter of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), as well as the matter of the two upper realms, can all be seen.
Although these various texts differ, they do not exceed three types [of visibility]: first, contact and opposition; second, extreme coarseness and manifestation; and third, location.

First, "contact and opposition" excludes the matter produced by meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in the intermediate state. Second, "extreme coarseness and manifestation" excludes wind and other such elements.

Regarding the arising of form and karma in the higher realms, the three [categories] are established based on what is reached. As for "that which is visible," this refers generally to all forms (*rūpa*).
Having cited various scriptural passages, they should be analyzed accordingly. Thirteen: the distinction between the visible and the invisible.

The eye faculty and the objects of consciousness—based on the conditions of consciousness and as can be inferred from the *Cintāmayī Bhūmi*—are termed "visible. Other than these, the remainder are termed "invisible. 13.

Regarding the two bases of phenomena (*dharma*) and the classification of the twelve [bases] as being abandoned by three [types of] insight (*darśana-prahātavya*):

all afflictions (*kleśa*) arising from the classification of "one part" of everything, along with the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) associated with them, and the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) based upon them;

the realms and bases produced by the karma of the three evil destinies; the continent of Uttarakuru; the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*); and those without form or with both forms—all these are abandoned by insight. Therefore.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle 4, states: "It refers to the defiled views and doubts arising from conceptual discrimination;

the bases of views and the bases of doubt; the wrong practices undertaken with respect to views and so forth; the primary afflictions and secondary afflictions; and the bodily, vocal, and mental karma produced by views and so forth."
Furthermore, all aggregates, bases, and elements of the evil destinies and so forth are the locus of views (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*) that is abandoned.

This refers to abandonment by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*saṃprayoga*), and the disappearance of cause and fruit—these three types of abandonment. It is described as the locus of views and the locus of doubt (*vicikitsā-sthāna*).

Since these arise from the objective realm transformed by oneself, when the subject that perceives (*ālambaka*) no longer exists, the object perceived (*ālambana*) is also abandoned; this is also subsumed under the "disappearance of cause. If one speaks of abandonment based on the disappearance of the support (*āśraya*), that refers to the body.

Those [factors] that arise from it—such as the eleven wholesome factors and so forth—are also abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). Since that body no longer exists, those [factors] arising in dependence upon the body cannot exist either.

With the exception of what was previously abandoned [by insight], all remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, chapter four, states:

"That is to say, with the exception of the defiled views and so forth arising from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), the remaining contaminated phenomena are [abandoned by cultivation]. Contaminated phenomena...
This also includes the wholesome states conducive to the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), because they are accompanied by the latent predispositions (*dausthulya*).

A portion of all [phenomena] is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). As for this "portion," it excludes those to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) as well as untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).

That is to say, all untainted phenomena—excluding the wholesome states conducive to penetration—are not to be abandoned. Untainted phenomena refer to the supramundane noble path (*āryamārga*) and that which follows it.

It is attained. Together with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of the aggregates (*skandha*) are not to be abandoned (*apraheyā*).
They are not designated as "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) based on being free from bondage or arising from an outflow-free body; rather, they are outflow-free by their very nature (*svabhāva-anāsrava*).

Otherwise, other elements and bases would also have to be called outflow-free. It is only because bodily and vocal actions consisting solely of form and sound are preeminent in manifesting the outflow-free that they are so described.
It is not "non-abandonable" (*aprahātavya*). If that were not the case, for what reason would the others not also be so designated?

However, the statement that the ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and the unlearned (*aśaikṣa*) bodily and vocal [actions] are non-abandonable is not a statement that exhausts the full reasoning; it is spoken according to coarse characteristics.

To speak according to reality, a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the base (*āyatana*), as well as the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of all bodily and vocal actions induced by the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state once one has entered the vision [of the truths], are all not [abandonable].

"Abandonment" (prahāṇa) refers generally to the untainted (anāsrava), because it is that which is induced [by the path]. However, regarding what was previously mentioned as "afflictions abandoned along with their co-nascent factors," these are abandonment by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-prahāṇa);

the mind and other factors associated with them are abandonment by way of association (saṃprayoga-prahāṇa); and the remaining objects of perception are abandonment by way of dissociation (ālambana-prahāṇa).

One should explain accordingly how the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and so forth are acquired. Regarding the thirteenth section, the distinction of the three trainings (śikṣā): from the stage of the aids to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) onwards, up to the moment immediately preceding the diamond-like concentration (vajropamasamādhi).
Regarding the path that has been attained: all those of a virtuous nature that accord with the noble paths sought by the three vehicles are called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*).

Specifically, this refers to the five faculties (*indriya*) belonging to this stage; the entirety of the three spheres of objects (*viṣaya-āyatana*); the seven mind-spheres (*citta-dhātu*), the mind-sphere (*manas-āyatana*), and one portion of the dharma-sphere (*dharma-dhātu*);
and the remainder—all these, whether by their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*samprayoga*), co-arising (*samutthāna*), or manifest action (*vijñapti*), are "those in training."

According to what is appropriate, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle 4, states: "From the stage of accumulating the provisions (*saṃbhāra*) onwards, ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of the aggregates (*skandha*) are 'in training' (*śaikṣa*).

Regarding the ten elements, these refer to the seven consciousness elements (*vijñānadhātu*), the element of form (*rūpadhātu*), the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*), and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding the four bases, these refer to the bases of form, sound, mind (*manas*), and phenomena. Therefore, from the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) following the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) onwards, all [of these]...
Wholesome dharmas that accord with those beyond training are all termed "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). The abbreviated explanation is as before. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter four, states:
"All wholesome dharmas belonging to one who has attained the ultimate perfection in the various points of training (*śikṣāpada*) constitute the meaning of 'beyond training.

Because Arhats and others have already attained the ultimate perfection in the higher trainings of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), they are called 'beyond training. [The ten realms and four...]

That which resides in a portion of the aggregates (*skandha*) is "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). This refers to what was previously excluded, as well as all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);

these are all subsumed under that which is neither-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*). Defiled states, neutral states (*avyākṛta*), and other such unconditioned phenomena are not practiced by those in training (*śaikṣa*).

Although the attainment of cessation is practiced, it is because it relies upon *nirvāṇa* and is a state of total quiescence; thus, it is neither training nor beyond training. This is not [the state of] exhaustion.

This is the principle. This is explained according to minor characteristics; however, speaking according to reality, if it pertains to the body of a Buddha, all seventeen elements (*dhātu*) and a small portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) constitute the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*).

Among the elements and bases (*āyatana*), this excludes the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Regarding the fourfold logical analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the fourteenth [topic]:

Is that which is the eye also the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)? Or is that which is the eye-element also the eye? This concerns the relationship between their breadth and narrowness (*viśāla-saṃkucita-lakṣaṇa*).
Because they appear similar, the answer is given in four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). There are cases that are the eye but not the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*):

namely, the eye at the final moment of an Arhat, because immediately thereafter one enters the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-dhātu*) and thus currently lacks causal function; therefore, it is not an element. There are cases that are the eye-element but not the eye:
namely, when one is in the eggshell, during the *kalala* stage, or during the *peśī* stage while remaining in the mother’s womb, provided that [the eye] has not yet been obtained.

Regarding the eye: even if it has been acquired and subsequently lost, as well as the causes for the eye of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there exist the causes capable of producing it;
therefore, the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) exists. However, because the eye is not currently present, it is not [considered] the eye. According to the *Pañcaṣaṣṭikā-śāstra*, it further states:

"Alternatively, when the eye has ceased without interval, or has already ceased without interval, it exists in the past. Because it was once able to see forms and can act as a cause, it is not [the eye] in the present."

Because it is seen: there are cases where something is both the eye and the eye-element, namely, all remaining states excluding those previously mentioned and excluding noble beings born in the formless realm (*ārūpya*).

There are cases where something is neither the eye nor the eye-element, namely, those in the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) and all noble beings born in the formless realm;
for in these cases, the body and consciousness are entirely absent. Although noble beings in the formless realm possess the seeds of that [eye], they will never arise. Thus it is said.
This is not the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*). Furthermore, it is said [in the *Abhidharmakośa*] at verse 56: "The eye of an Arhat has already perished, or the eye does not arise.

As it is with the eye and the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), so it should be understood accordingly for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and so forth. However, there are those who possess the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) but do not possess the body:

namely, formless beings (*ārūpya*) and beings born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*) and so on. Because they possess a body in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there are those who possess the mind (*manas*) but do not possess the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
"Is [the mind]? refers to the final mind of an Arhat, because it lacks the sense of being a cause.

"There is a mind-element that is not mind" refers to the mind of one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), excluding those in the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), because they possess a defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*).

This is stated with reference to the seventh consciousness as the defiled portion; otherwise, this phrase would not exist. "There is a mind that is also a mind-element" excludes the aforementioned cases.

And regarding the state of "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*) and other states: that which is neither the mind (*manas*) nor the mind-element (*manodhātu*) refers to those who have already entered the state of "without remainder.
The eye-element and so forth should be understood accordingly. Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*): there may be that which is the eye but not the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*).

This refers to when the eye has been acquired and not yet relinquished, yet it is a phenomenon subject to immediate cessation. Because phenomena subject to immediate cessation are weak in force, they are currently determined [not to function].
It can serve as the gateway for the arising of consciousness, yet after it has ceased without interval, it cannot serve as the gateway for the arising of subsequent consciousness.
This excludes the final eye-faculty, etc., of an Arhat. There are locations that are not the eye, namely those remaining locations characterized by their state of abiding.

There are cases that are both the eye and the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*), namely when the eye has been acquired and not relinquished, and is not a phenomenon that has just ceased. There are cases that are not the eye.

It is not the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*). That is to say, it refers to when the eye is not obtained, or having been obtained, is lost, as well as other bases such as the ear that do not abide in the characteristics of a location.

Although the text does not explicitly state that one enters the nirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), this phrase also possesses various detailed categories. Fearing prolixity, I shall cease here.

The seventh question and answer first addresses the elements (*dhātu*). Within the single question regarding names, it is asked elsewhere that the term "body" (*kāya*) is used in the sense of an accumulation (*caya*) and so forth;
how then can that which is capable of touching (*spraṣṭavya*) be called a "body"? Answer: The name "accumulation" applies generally to all [the elements], yet they are all called "bodies.

Now, based on a specific meaning, that which is capable of touching is designated as a "body. Question: Is it not the same for form (*rūpa*)? Or perhaps it is because the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), although...

This is a general designation, which is also a specific name. This cannot be said of the "body" (*kāya*). If one were to rely on the term "body," then the mind-element (*manodhātu*) would also have to be called a "body.
Alternatively, if the name "body" were applied equally to form (*rūpa*), there would be no such confusion, as "mind" (*manas*) is defined by the act of cogitation (*manana*).
If that were so, then the five consciousnesses that have just ceased would not be the mind-element, because they lack cogitation. Therefore, the former interpretation is superior. (2)

Question: Since [the visual consciousness] relies on the faculty (*indriya*) and has form (*rūpa*) as its object, why is it designated solely by relying on the faculty and not given a name derived from the object?

Answer: There are five reasons. It receives its name because the faculty is predominant. What are these five reasons? Because it relies upon the eye-consciousness; because it is produced by the eye; because it belongs to the eye-consciousness;
because it assists the eye-consciousness; and because it is like the eye-consciousness itself. This explanation is made based on what is most frequent; however, according to the actual fact...

It is said: they are also called "form-consciousness" (*rūpa-vijñāna*) and so forth. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* quotes a verse stating: "One should admit that there are consciousnesses of form and consciousnesses that are not of form.
Among the three inquiries regarding their essential nature, why are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) established within the *dhātus* and *āyatanas*, but not within the *skandhas*?

The answer is: since a *skandha* (aggregate) refers to a collection or accumulation, and unconditioned phenomena are not such, they are excluded from the *skandhas*. However, because they are categorized according to the subject and object of cognition (*grāhaka-grāhya*), they are included within the *dhātus* and *āyatanas*.
Regarding the *dhātu* and *āyatana*: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56, states: "That which is subsumed under the *nirvāṇa-dhātu* sustains the non-arising of suffering.

It asks: "Is it subsumed under the *ākāśa-dhātu*? It answers: "Space has no accumulation; it is not grasped as an aggregate (*skandha*). Because it sustains the movement and function of the body, it is subsumed under the *dhātu* and *āyatana*.
Fascicle 56 further states: "Because it sustains the movement and function of the eyes and so forth of the body. Question 5: Regarding the establishment of the mind (*manas*), what...

Therefore, why are the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) each explained separately? The answer is: it is because one wishes to cause the sentient beings to be converted to develop skillfulness regarding both the extensive and concise methods.
Within the method of the aggregates, consciousness and form are presented concisely; within the method of the elements, consciousness and form are extensively analyzed;

within the method of the bases, only form is extensively explained; and within the method of the aggregates, only mental factors (caitta) are extensively explained, while the elements and bases are presented concisely.
Because it is taught that there is only one element (dhātu) and one base (āyatana). Among the six questions concerning the establishment or rejection [of categories], it is asked:
since the eyes, ears, and noses each have two locations, why are twenty-one elements not established? If, although they are each twofold, the elements are not distinct—why is this so?
Their characteristics are similar, as both possess the characteristic of being an eye. Their functions are similar, as both perform the same function for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
In this way, the nose and tongue may be understood by analogy with the eye. Although these—the mind and the eyes, etc.—each have two [organs], they both apprehend a single object.

Since they arise from the same single consciousness, they constitute a single realm (*dhātu*). [Question: If that were so, since the mind (*manas*) is capable of producing the six [consciousnesses] and takes the six objects as its conditions, it should be subsumed under the six bases (*āyatana*).
[Answer: If the past six consciousnesses were divided into six [separate bases], there would be the fault of confusion (*saṃkara*).

For instance, if that which has just ceased immediately after visual consciousness were called the "eye-faculty," it would be confused with the eye-faculty that perceives visible forms; furthermore, it lacks any superior capacity. It does not.

It is called "eye" alone because the eye illuminates and gazes. Among the sense organs (*rūpīndriya*), five possess this quality and may thus be named individually. The others follow this same principle, as they do not abandon their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, because they possess the capacity for deliberation (*manana*) and the function of generating [consciousness], they are collectively termed the "mind element" (*manodhātu*).

Alternatively, following the Hīnayāna, the past five consciousnesses are also collectively termed the mind element. According to the Mahāyāna, however, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are termed the mind element.

The remainder are the six consciousness-elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*). This is not so; for the six consciousness-elements do not extend across the three periods of time. This is because that which is past is collectively designated as the "mind" (*manas*).
Even though the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) serves as the support for defilement, purity, and so forth, and also gives rise to the various consciousnesses, the aforementioned difficulty remains.

The answer is: because that [the mind-faculty] is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), whereas this [the consciousness-element] is common (*sādhāraṇa*) in its production, they are not comparable. Question 8: If [the consciousness] has already passed, such as visual consciousness and the rest...

Because they do not abandon their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, they are given the same name, "mind-element" (*manodhātu*). If that were the case, then the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) would also constitute a single element, as the three meanings [of being a basis, a support, and a cause] would likewise be equal.

Answer: Taking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as the cause, two of these meanings may indeed be equal; however, they do not share the same name of "illumination," such as hearing, smelling, and so forth.

Therefore, they are distinct realms. If one follows the latter interpretation, this objection does not apply. Question 9: Since the object and consciousness perform the same function, why do the eyes, ears, and noses each arise as two?

Answer: For the sake of beauty, each arises as two. Question 10: Although animals also have two [of these], how could they be beautiful? Originally there was only one; who would say that it is ugly? Answer: [This refers to the human context.

Regarding the statement "originally there was only one": who says it is ugly? [In the case of humans, the symmetry is for the sake of beauty. (Note: The final answer addresses the implicit objection regarding the necessity of two organs in humans versus the lack of such need in animals.)
If animals were to be born as a single individual, they would not appear dignified. Furthermore, even if they were originally one, why should it be considered improper to say they are "ugly"?

Some say that the nature of cause and effect is such that they are arranged in this way, like the upper and lower roots; how can one fully criticize this? Question 11: Each of the three [faculties] has two [aspects].
Does consciousness arise based on one, or does it arise based on two? Answer: It arises based on one, and it arises based on two; there is no logical contradiction in either case. [End of section.]
One may also obtain them. Since seeing, hearing, smelling, and so forth allow for the arising of two consciousnesses, they obtain clarity and intensity. Regarding the twelve [faculties], it is asked:
can the eye and ear sometimes simultaneously possess three types—namely, those born of maturation (*vipāka*), those through nourishment (*aupacayika*), and the divine eye and ear?

As for the others, each possesses two, excluding those produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāja*). Since there are these many types, do they occupy the same location or are they distinct? The answer is: those produced by cultivation and the other two [types] occupy different locations.

They share the same locus of support; yet, just as sand in water differs according to its coarseness or fineness, there are distinctions between the locations of the nourished (*aupacayika*) and the ripened (*vipākaja*).
The nourished is external, like a city wall that protects what is within. (13) Question: How is it that the nose, tongue, and so forth lack the cultivated and the innate?
Answer: Because they are not supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). (14) Question: For what reason are the three—the nose, tongue, and body—not supernormal powers?

Answer: It is impossible to know an object at a distance through the combined operation [of the senses]. Question 15: If this is so, why do the nose and other faculties of the desire realm perceive the odors and so forth of the form realm?
Answer: Because they function reciprocally; because it is an object of wisdom; and because of the power of the dharmas. Question 16:

There are six consciousnesses that possess faculties and objects, and based on these, the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) are established. Since the seventh and eighth consciousnesses also possess faculties and objects, why are there not twenty elements?
4. Answer: Based on the distinction between faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are taught. Seven [of these] have not yet transformed their basis (*āśraya*);

they perceive only the eighth [consciousness], and since that faculty is itself the object, it cannot be established separately. The eighth consciousness does not differ from the sixth in its reliance upon a faculty, and since it lacks a distinct objective referent (*ālambana*), it likewise cannot be so established.
17. Question: How many elements are capable of apprehension through combination, and how many do not involve combined cognition? Answer: The elements of nose, tongue, and body—these...

The three consciousness-elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*) are all capable of apprehending when combined [with their respective bases]. The eye, ear, and their corresponding consciousnesses—these four—are capable of apprehension when separated [from their objects]. The single element of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-dhātu*) apprehends both when combined and when not combined.
Therefore, the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā* (Treatise on the Five Categories) states: "Six [elements] are capable of apprehension when combined; four are not capable of apprehension when combined;

five and a small portion of one are not capable of apprehension. One element, whether combined or not combined, is capable of apprehension in both cases. This is the intended meaning of the question regarding the eighteen elements.
[Question: Among these, the six [consciousnesses] that have ceased immediately prior (anantara-niruddha) are both capable of synthesis and non-synthesis; why are they not mentioned? [Answer:

Although those that have ceased immediately prior were once capable of synthesizing and taking [objects], they currently lack the capacity for such grasping; therefore, they are not mentioned. [Question 19:

Regarding the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, since they are also included within the sphere of mind (manodhātu), what is their mode of grasping? [Answer: The seventh [consciousness] exclusively takes the eighth as its object; thus, it is one that takes itself as its own object.

Regarding the mind-element (*manodhātu*): it does not establish its object separately, nor is its conjunction or separation analyzed. In the twenty questions concerning the retributive condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*), it is asked whether the mind-element is conjoined with or separate [from its object].

The answer is that conjunction and separation are analyzed in a general sense based on the faculties (*indriya*). Since this faculty and its object are one, how can one analyze conjunction and separation?

Speaking in terms of consciousness: since it is devoid of form and obstruction, how can one distinguish between conjunction and separation? Furthermore, if the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) have neither conjunction nor separation, how could consciousness—which depends upon them—possess conjunction or separation?
Moreover, even if conjunction and separation were applicable [to consciousness], what harm would there be? The twenty-first question:

When the sixth [consciousness] and the eighth [consciousness] both take the sense organ and the object as their conditions, do they do so in conjunction or in separation? Answer: The sixth and eighth are both [conditioned by] the seventh as their root. The seventh does not take those [the sixth and eighth] as its conditions.

Regarding the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*, the *trika*): if one distinguishes their combination or separation based on the faculties, since the faculties do not exist [as discrete entities], consciousness would not be divided.

Alternatively, if they were both combined and separated, what flaw would there be in principle? (The twenty-second question: If the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is both combined and separate, why is it spoken of as only one?

Answer: One [consciousness] takes the whole as well as the individual sense organs and objects; because these are manifest, they are so described. It is not that there are no individual sense organs or objects at all; because they are hidden, they are not analyzed.

Alternatively, this is according to the conventional gate (*anuvartana-mukha*). The seven [mental consciousnesses] do not take others as their objects; this is stated based on the state prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

If the basis has already been transformed, they can also take the five consciousnesses and their sense organs as objects. Regarding the analysis of conjunction and separation, this is stated for the time being based on the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*); if one reaches the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), they all universally pervade.

Regarding conjunction and disjunction: if it were not so, there would be no universal knowledge. This is the twenty-third question. Within the dharma-dhātu, as for the mental factors (caitta), are they conjoined with or separate from their objects?

The answer distinguishes between conjunction and disjunction based on the faculties and consciousnesses as they relate to their objects. Since those [mental factors] abide within the object itself, how could one distinguish conjunction and disjunction therein?

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the previous statement was made according to what is predominant, merely distinguishing the faculties and consciousnesses. If one were to speak exhaustively according to the principle, it should be...

According to their respective bases, they are subsumed under both the combined and the separated categories. As for how many are exclusively capable [of grasping] and so forth, one may understand this by inferring from the thought-process. Regarding the twenty-four questions:

how many are capable of grasping by virtue of their associates, and how many are capable of grasping alone? Answer: The five sense-faculties, the consciousness-elements, and a small portion of the dharma-element.

Because they assist the grasper through the conjunction of the sense-faculties and consciousness, a portion of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the entirety of the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are capable of grasping independently.

The mind-element is distinguished as such because it is the immediately preceding cessation of the five [sensory consciousnesses]; furthermore, a portion of what is called "mind" (*manas*)—which is not conjoined with the sense-faculties and consciousness—is also capable of grasping.

Alternatively, there are five reasons why the sense-faculties are led by the mind: because of the conjunction with consciousness, because of their dependence on the sovereign (consciousness), and because the mind only grasps when assisted [by these factors].
Regarding the consciousness of the elements (*dhātu-vijñāna*): it does not grasp [its object] solely by means of projection. Question 25:

Why is it that in other places eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*) or ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are taught, or only two are mentioned, while here twelve are taught? Answer: This is to destroy the grasping at a self as an experiencer.

Based on the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), and according to their distinct functional capacities and the characteristics of the mind and its states, there is an increase or decrease [in the number].

Question 26: Regarding the conventional and the ultimate, if—as the teachers of the Hīnayāna maintain—there are only six consciousnesses, and the mental element (*manodhātu*) is said to be the immediate succession of these six consciousnesses, then it is possible for six to become one, and from this [one], six arise;
thus it is possible for one to become six. Why is it that in the Mahāyāna there are eight consciousnesses? Answer:

Some say that this is according to the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-yukti*), which is a method of following the flow of phenomena (*anuvartana-naya*). Such is the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate.

Regarding the principle of ultimate reality (*tattva*), all eighteen [elements] are real; however, we now maintain that this is not so. From the perspective of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), all eighteen are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*), existing as illusory manifestations arising through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

This is as explained according to linguistic expression. According to the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), by way of the gate of conforming reasoning, there are six abodes of mental nature.

All are termed the mind-element (*manodhātu*). The Sarvāstivādins state that the eighteen elements exist throughout the three periods of time; therefore, according to the faculties and their objects, a single mind is divided into six.

Such is the distinction between the provisional and the real. This [classification of] the provisional and the real regarding the mind-element serves to subsume the other elements and, furthermore, constitutes this very element itself.

These may be called "provisional" (*prajñapti*), while not grasping at anything else, they abide in their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-dhātu*) and are thus described as "real" (*tattva*). According to the Mahāyāna, eleven elements (*dhātu*) are real;

the five sense organs and the six consciousnesses are [included therein], while the remainder are both provisional and real. As for the mental element (*manas-dhātu*), it has no substantial entity (*avastuka*) immediately following [the cessation of] that [preceding moment].

The mental faculty (*manas*) is designated by conventional name (*prajñapti*). The remainder is fully explained as in the chapter on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Regarding the twenty-seventh question:

within the *dharmadhātu*, are the two types—vitarka and vicāra—exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*), or do they also extend to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*)? Answer: They also extend to the outflow-free.
This is because right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is said to be outflow-free, and this right thought has vitarka and vicāra as its essential nature (*svabhāva*). Or...

Its essence is volition (*cetanā*). However, in the state prior to final realization, when one teaches the Dharma to others within the wisdom attained subsequent to meditative equipoise (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one must necessarily rely upon vitarka and vicāra;
therefore, they also pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*). Question 28: If this is so, why does the *Yogācārabhūmi* state that they are subsumed under discrimination (*vikalpa*)? Answer:

Although it is said that vitarka and vicāra are necessarily discrimination, it is not definitively stated that they belong exclusively to discrimination [in the case of] the wisdom attained subsequent to meditative equipoise (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-samyagjñāna*).
[This] is because there is also discrimination within [the category of] "intermediate. Question twenty-nine:

Regarding the section on "appropriation" (*upātta*), according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga Practice), fascicle 56, there are five types of appropriated and non-appropriated [objects], which encompass all five sense objects (*viṣaya*). Why, then, does the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Compendium of Abhidharma) mention only four?
Answer: In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, because matter is described as being sparse and detached from its substrate (*rūpa*), it is said to be "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*).

In the fifty-sixth [treatise], because it is not yet detached from its substrate, it is categorized as "appropriated" (*upātta*). Thus, there is no contradiction between them. Regarding the thirty questions, within the section on the "objects of cognition" (*ālambana*), how many elements (*dhātu*) and how many consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) cognize them?
Answer: According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects are cognized by two types of consciousness.
Regarding the objects of cognition (*ālambana*): all other thirteen realms are exclusively objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

According to the Mahāyāna, based on the view that they correspond respectively to their causes, there are five, three, six, and two; six, one, and one are indeterminate; and these are distinguished according to the sovereign [consciousnesses] and so forth.

Since this refers to the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) at the stage of the cause, it is said that they correspond respectively to their causes. As for "five, three": the five sense-objects correspondingly add six or eight conditions.
