Regarding "six have two": the five faculties, such as the eye, each serve as the sixth and eighth conditions for [their respective consciousnesses]. The mental faculty (*manas*) serves as the condition for the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. Regarding "one has six":
the six consciousness-elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*) are conditioned solely by the sixth [mental] faculty. Regarding "one is indeterminate": this refers to the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*).

When the faculties face their objects, the six consciousnesses and various faculties may function interchangeably; thus it may be conditioned by all five consciousnesses, or by the seventh consciousness, or—

Because the six consciousnesses take them as objects, they are said to be "indeterminate. Regarding the "discrimination by mastery" and so forth: if one reaches the stage of fruition, one obtains the capacity to take all of them as objects as appropriate;

therefore, they are called "the discriminated. The term "and so forth" refers to the power of the consciousness-dharmas and so on, which are to be discriminated according to their respective capacities.
Question thirty-one: Within the gate of "having vision" and "lacking vision," does the eye see, or does consciousness see? Answer:

It is not the eye that sees, nor is it consciousness and so forth, because all phenomena are devoid of functional activity (*nirvyāpāra*). It is by virtue of their conjunction that "seeing" is conventionally designated.

If one follows worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*), one may say that the eye sees, for [the eye] is superior to the six consciousnesses in four respects: first, because consciousness arises dependent upon it;
second, because it is the cause for the arising of a single consciousness; third, because it is constant and of a uniform nature; and fourth, because it does not depend on an object.

[It is] a synthesis, because it arises moment by moment. Fifth, it is due to the adornment of the basis-body (*āśraya*). Sixth, it is due to the sacred teaching (*āgama*), as stated in the Sūtra: "The eye can see forms. The other five [faculties] are to be understood accordingly.
If one relies on the ultimate meaning (*tattvārtha*), seeing is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) established upon the synthesis [of conditions], yet the name "seeing" is applied to it.

As the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* states: "In this context, the ultimate meaning is that it is only with respect to 'seeing' and so forth that one speaks of a 'seer' and so forth; [this is] a grasping [of a convention]."

Regarding the thirty-two questions concerning hearing, smelling, and so forth: do they take as their objects only those of their own level for the eye-consciousness of that same level, or can they also take other levels as objects?

The same applies to the questions regarding hearing and the rest. The answer is: the faculties (roots) may pertain to their own level, a lower level, or a higher level; the consciousness follows the faculty accordingly.

For example, humans and devas of the desire realm may perceive the forms and sounds of the Brahma realm, and they may experience the edible food transformed by the fruit of supernormal power (*ṛddhiphala*). This refers to the eighth [consciousness] of the desire realm.

The divine eye and other such faculties do not take higher realms as their objects. Regarding those who have attained a higher realm but possess lower ones: the eyes and ears take lower realms as their objects; this is clearly stated in various authentic texts.

As for the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body, it is as in the case of birth in the Form Realm. Do the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages not rely on consciousness to perceive the two lower objects?

The body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) itself does not require external conditions; it is able to cognize through contact and functions with sovereign mutual independence, which is not contrary to principle.

Therefore, it can also take lower objects. While the eight higher [consciousnesses] take lower objects through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth, this merely excludes the power of karma, because such states as meditative concentration are associated with defilement (*kliṣṭa*).

The consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and body are known to pervade all [levels]. As for the two consciousnesses of the nose and tongue, they do not take lower levels as their objects, because those [objects] do not exist in higher stages.

If one is in the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), where untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses are "lent" to these stages, there is no obstruction whatsoever, because they can take everything as an object.

The *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* speaks mostly in accordance with coarse distinctions; it is not a statement that exhausts the full principle. Regarding the thirty-three questions: for the consciousness of its own stage, it takes its own stage as its support.

Question: Is this also the case for the sense-faculties (*indriya*)? Answer: The five consciousnesses rely on their own level or a higher level; a higher consciousness does not rely on a lower one. However, the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), as well as the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses], may also rely on a lower level.

This is because after an outflow-tainted state (*sāsrava*), an outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) arises, and that outflow-free state further relies on the desire realm, the seventh, or the eighth [consciousness].

Thus, when a Bodhisattva of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is born into the fourth dhyāna and gives rise to the six outflow-free [consciousnesses], the sixth and seventh consciousnesses serve as [the support].
Regarding the eighth point, "by way of dependence": the sense faculties such as the eye are superior material faculties; they cannot be abandoned because they depend upon that which is inferior.
Thirty-fourth question: Are the five faculties, such as the eye, necessarily of the same level as the body faculty, or do they extend across higher and lower levels?

Answer: The eye and ear faculties both reach upward; the nose and tongue do not reach upward or downward. If the mental element (*manodhātu*) is considered in relation to the body, it reaches both downward and upward.

If the eighth consciousness is considered, it does not reach upward or downward. Regarding that which has just ceased (*anantarātīta*), there is no obstruction whatsoever. This applies to the consciousness and its objects in relation to the body.

One may consider this accordingly. If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, the answers to the first three questions differ entirely from these. That work contains a verse which says: "The eye is not lower than the body;
color and consciousness are not higher than the eye. Color is [not lower] than consciousness in all cases; the same applies to the other two in relation to the body."

As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear. The next three [faculties] all belong to their own level (*svabhūmi*). The body-consciousness belongs to its own level or a lower level. It should be known that the mental faculty (*manas*) is indeterminate.

Regarding the ear and the subsequent gates, as well as their essential natures (*svabhāva*) and so forth, they are all distinct from those [preceding ones]; fearing prolixity, I shall not analyze them here.

Among the thirty-five questions, there are times when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes a single realm (*dhātu*) as its object, or when eighteen [factors] are taken individually by the mental consciousness, or when it takes them collectively in the present.

Regarding inference (*anumāna*): its nature is manifest and can be known. Alternatively, does it follow one of the five [sensory consciousnesses] and, taking other realms as objects, become a present or inferential cognition?

Answer: It is explained according to the predominant object. If the five sensory objects are powerful, it manifests together with the five [consciousnesses]. If the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is powerful, then although the five [objects] are being perceived simultaneously, the mental consciousness may be inferential.
If the objects are equal in strength, it follows the five and also manifests; because it takes the object with clarity while sharing the same objects as the five, it follows [the five].

The five [senses] are manifest. However, as for the statement that the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are not objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this is said based on their predominant conditions.

Furthermore, it is explained that while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes all eighteen realms (*dhātu*) as its objects, it is admitted that the five [sense-consciousnesses] share the same objects; yet, the objects of the five [senses] are superior. Moreover, the realm of mental consciousness encompasses both direct perception and inference (*anumāna*).

Since the essence of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is one, while its seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) has manifold capacities and gives rise to various functions, what logical fault could there be? Furthermore, it is stated that the five sense-faculties are not... [text truncated].

Because it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As for what the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says—"or that which is neither valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), and whose fruit is not self-cognition"—this refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), which at times is exclusively valid cognition and at other times is exclusively non-valid cognition, but is not so at all times.
This [passage] intends to exclude both the state of being both valid and non-valid cognition, as well as the state of being exclusively valid cognition.
Therefore, it is not their fruit. Both explanations present difficulties, which the wise should examine carefully. Question thirty-six:

Within the section on the realms of bondage (*dhātu-bandhana*), why is it that those born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)—who have already attained detachment from sense objects—still give rise to the two realms of the nose and tongue?

Answer: It is so that the body upon which they rely may be made dignified and beautiful; furthermore, it is because they have not yet attained detachment from the faculties (*indriya*). Question thirty-seven.
Since one has already become free from craving regarding other objects as well, why speak of only these two? Answer: These two types of objects cause desire to increase particularly;
because one has already abandoned craving for food, they alone are mentioned. Whether the six objects exist or not is explained in the chapter on the five objects (Pañcavastuka).

In the thirty-eighth question, within the section on the three types of abandonment, if it refers only to the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the untainted bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), it is said to be "not abandoned."

Question: For what reason does the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, chapter seven, state that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), are both categorized as "not to be abandoned" (*aprahātavya*)?

Answer: That [text] refers to them as "not to be abandoned" based on the fact that their binding objects have already been severed; it does not mean that they are untainted (*anāsrava*) by nature and thus inherently not to be abandoned.

Therefore, he further states: "If that which has already been abandoned is called 'not to be abandoned,' then the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) would also pertain to what is not to be abandoned.

Since sorrow (*daurmanasya*) can induce the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), it is also said to pertain [to both]. He says: 'Furthermore, it is not like sorrow, which is permanently liberated from defilement;

only that which is directly induced by the outflow-free also pertains to what is not to be abandoned. Then, the essence of painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) could also pertain [to both], as could matter (*rūpa*)."

Analyze this in detail as explained in the *Sandaṃśa* (The Three-Part Compendium). Regarding the thirty-ninth question: "Why are Nirvāṇa and space called 'elements' (*dhātu*) because they maintain cessation and movement?
If the final mind of an Arhat also maintains its own nature, why is it not an element? Answer: That [final mind] is said to maintain cessation and movement;

it is not merely that it maintains [the nature], but it also maintains the cause of movement. In reality, it is also capable of serving as an object for the arising of consciousness. Therefore, that...
Although consciousness arises, it is not [included among] the six consciousnesses because it is the eighth. Alternatively, although it manifests, it lacks the function of further production;

therefore, it is not called a "realm" (*dhātu*). Or rather, the sense of "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*) also receives the name "realm," yet because this [eighth consciousness] acts as a cause for that [sustenance], it is said not to be a realm.
(Question 40: Why, among the eighteen realms, is this eye not a realm, but is only described as the "eye-base" (*cakṣur-āyatana*) of an Arhat’s final moment?

Is it then also a *dhātu*? Answer: A *dhātu* is established based on being a cause. That [past object] lacks causal efficacy; as for a *āyatana*, it is that which currently produces consciousness. A sense faculty (*indriya*) that has ceased in the immediate past is inferior and does not produce consciousness;
therefore, it is also not an *āyatana*. However, because it still exists as a seed, it can be called a *dhātu*. It serves as a cause for what follows. Thus, it may be designated as a *dhātu*.

Thus far, the inquiry has primarily relied upon the *dhātus*; the *āyatanas* may be understood by analogy. Within these *dhātus* and *āyatanas*, there are extensive inquiries and various question-and-answer exchanges;
I have provided a rough outline of the main points for fear of excessive prolixity, so those who are extensively learned should investigate them in detail themselves.
The Forest of Meanings of the Five Aggregates.

The five aggregates are briefly analyzed through six sections: first, the explanation of names; second, the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*); third, their sequential order; and fourth, their establishment and exclusion.
Five: The Various Gates; Six: Resolving Objections.

First, regarding the explanation of the names, there is first the enumeration and then the explanation. As for the enumeration: they are the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Regarding the explanation of the names, there is first the general and then the specific. The general name is *pañca-skandha* in Sanskrit; *pañca* means "five."

*Skandha* is translated as "accumulation" (*yun*). The older name was "aggregate" (*yin*). Although commentators claim it means "to accumulate," this completely contradicts the etymology of the character.
Why is this? If "aggregate" (*yin*) here carries the sense of "covering" or "obscuring," then in the Sanskrit original it should be *prāvṛta*.
According to the character "aggregate" (*yin*), it should instead be the "yin" of "yin-yang" (the female principle). In recent times...
There are alternative explanations. Some say it is like calling a collection of "bland" things a "bland aggregate" (*skandha*).
This explanation is not correct; medical treatises speak of "bland drinks," but they do not speak of a "bland aggregate. There are further alternative explanations that cannot be fully related here.

If one says that *skandha* means "the place where the vital breaths (*vāyu*) are stored," this is indeed the sense of "collection. While taking this as a metaphorical name may roughly suffice, the phonetic values of the characters differ. Alternatively, some say:
Although there is no error in the meaning of "five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*), it deviates from the Sanskrit original.

In the Sanskrit language, the term is *saṃgha*, which is translated here as "assembly" (*zhòng*) or "collection" (*jù*). This [interpretation] is also incorrect. If one were to call them a "collection," the Sanskrit original should have been *āgama*.
Since the Sanskrit original is actually *pañca-skandha*, translating it as "aggregates" (*yùn*) is correct. "Five" is the number; that which is accumulated is called an "aggregate."

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (56) states: "The meaning of 'accumulation' (*caya*) is the meaning of 'aggregate' (*skandha*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (3) states: "Because it has the sense of accumulation, like a hoard of wealth;
this refers to the accumulation of its own substance. It further states: "Because the characteristic of suffering is vast, it is called an aggregate, like a great forest;
for by depending on form (*rūpa*) and so forth, the vast suffering of birth and so forth arises. This refers to the object [of accumulation].

Furthermore, it is said that they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*) because they bear the burden of afflictions (*saṃkleśa*). Just as one carries a load on the shoulders, these phenomena—form and so forth—are able to bear the burden of the afflictions of defilement;
they weigh down the practitioner, causing them to sink into the river of birth and death, unable to cross over toward the mountain of Nirvāṇa.
Thus, they are sometimes called "burdens. In the West, the term is used for the shoulder as well as for places where things are accumulated, such as a courtyard or field. All [of these]...

They are called "aggregates" (*skandha*). The first [explanation] applies universally to both the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the tainted (*sāsrava*); the latter two rely upon the tainted. That which is untainted is not a basis for suffering, nor does it bear the burden of afflictions (*kleśa*).

All three [types of aggregates] apply to all three time periods. If one speaks of the "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*), they are likewise exclusively tainted, because they are conjoined with the characteristics of clinging.
Therefore, they are called the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*). This refers to all desire and lust (*chandarāga*) within the aggregates;

that is, regarding the aggregates of future and present phenomena, it is that which draws them forth and prevents their relinquishment. It desires and hankers for the future, drawing those future aggregates so as to cause them to manifest;

it greedily stains the present entity, causing one not to abandon it. These two—desire and lust—are collectively termed the "aggregates of clinging," because they are drawn forth and stained by desire and lust.
Therefore, they are called the "appropriated aggregates" (*upādāna-skandha*). [The *Abhidharmakośa*] omits the past [aggregates]; its three explanations are too extensive to be related in full here.

The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* explains the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) through three senses. The verse states: "Because they are not one, because they are a collection, and because they are a delimited portion, they are called 'aggregates'.
Regarding "not one": this refers to all forms (*rūpa*), whether past, or even distant or near; since these types are not one, they are so named.

Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*): according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the meanings of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also to be understood accordingly. Second, as for the general summarized meaning:

because such [factors] as the past and so forth are briefly condensed into a single collection, they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*). If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, the summarized meaning does not refer to the substance itself, because the three time periods are distinct.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna, there is no substance that can be summarized, because the past and future are merely provisionally established within the present dharma. Third.

The meaning of "segmentation" (*skandha*) refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form (*rūpa*), which are called "aggregates" because they establish the respective characteristics of form and so forth individually.

This is consistent with the first two interpretations in the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*. The four meanings for explaining "accumulation" (*caya*) in the fourteenth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*) are as follows:

the first two are identical to the first two meanings in the *Madhyānta-vibhāga*; the third is the sense of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*); and the fourth is the sense of "superimposition and denial" (*samāropa-apavāda*). [Aggregates] arise together through various conditions, or are harmonized...

"Arising in combination" is called "arising in common. This refers to arising and ceasing, as well as nourishment and augmentation, and opposition and diminution; "augmentation and diminution" is the meaning here.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 56), the explanation of the aggregate (*skandha*) also has four meanings: first, the sense of being the entity summoned by various [names].

First, that which is summoned by various names and serves as a name, based on the meaning of substance (*dravya*) and collection (*samudāya*). Second, the meaning of mutual intermingling and functioning, which is the meaning of functioning together (*sahabhū-vṛtti*).
Third, the meaning of a general summary of a single category. Fourth, the meaning of superimposition (*samāropa*) and negation (*apavāda*), explained in the same manner as before.

Within the six types of compound analysis (*vigraha*), when a number is included in the name, "feeling" (*vedanā*) and so forth are the aggregates (*skandha*); this refers to the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Fifth.
This is the enumeration. Since the five dharmas are the aggregates (*skandha*), they encompass both [categories]. Regarding the second point, the explanation of their individual names:

because they can be planted and increased, can be pointed out as "this" or "that," and possess resistance (*pratigha*), they are called "form" (*rūpa*). As the *Pañcāśatikā* states: "In various locations..."

Because they are planted, grow, and possess the quality of transformation and resistance (*rūpaṇa*): when touched by the hand and so forth, they are "transformed" (*rūpyate*) as they perish; they are "resistant" (*pratighāta*) because they obstruct coming and going.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* is likewise. That which definitely arises within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), which can be pointed out as "this" or "that," and which is derived from form—namely, the form induced by volition (*vijñapti-rūpa*), the form that obstructs other forms, and the form consisting of brief, distinct, and pervasive conceptualization—is all termed "form" (*rūpa*) because it originates from matter. That which experiences is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). [The others] are established...

The objective sphere, its image, name, and conceptualization are called form (*rūpa*). Volitional activity and the flux of conditioned phenomena are called formations (*saṃskāra*). The discernment of objects is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). The term "aggregate" (*skandha*) is used as a collective designation.

Second, regarding the essential nature [of these aggregates], there are four general types: first, in terms of the hundred dharmas; second, in terms of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*); third, in terms of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Regarding the four gates—namely, subsuming characteristics into nature and so forth—in relation to the five dharmas, they are not mentioned here because those categories are broader.

Regarding the hundred dharmas, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) takes eleven types of form as its essential nature. Thus, the *Fifty-three* [Treatise] asks: "What is the self-nature of the aggregate of form?
It answers: "Briefly, there are eleven, namely the ten bases of form, such as the eye, and that which is subsumed under the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)."

Matter (*rūpa*). Furthermore, it is generally divided into two: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*). It is also called the "five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*). What is the aggregate of matter?
It refers to the four great elements and all forms derived from the four great elements. Regarding the nature of the first five faculties, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (First Chapter) states:
"The pure matter (*rūpaprasāda*) derived from the four great elements that serves as the basis for visual consciousness and the others is called the 'eye' and so forth."
Regarding the sense faculties (*indriya*): The *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* asks, "What is the eye-faculty? It is the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) that has visible form as its object.

The *Abhidharma-samuccaya* clarifies this by presenting both the essence and the cause-and-effect relationship. The *Pañcaskandhaka* treats them in terms of their objects and their essence, each according to one specific meaning.

Since the eye and other faculties cannot be apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they are elucidated by citing their causes, effects, and objects. Alternatively, some distinguish them based on their cause, namely, that they are composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

It is composed of the essence of translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*), distinguished from both the sense-faculties that support the organs and their respective objects; thus it is termed "translucent matter. Regarding the five objects:

according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, visible form (*rūpa*) is derived from the four great elements and is the objective domain of the eye-faculty. The other four [objects] are to be understood accordingly.

However, while the faculties are presented by way of their specific functions, the objects are presented by way of their objective characteristics—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, high, and low. If...

The twenty-five types of color (*varṇa*)—namely, correct and incorrect, light and shadow, brightness and darkness, clouds, smoke, dust, and mist, distant color and manifest color, and the single pervasive color of space—are collectively twenty-five.
The *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states: "That which is the objective domain of the eye: manifest color, shape-color, and informative color (*vijñapti-rūpa*), etc.

The former [section] cites cause and effect along with the essence of manifest color; the latter refers only to the essence of the fruit along with the essence of manifest color. This is the first [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
There are twenty-four [types of color], excluding *prabhā* (luminous space). Since *prabhā* is merely a specific variety of *varṇa* (manifest color), it is not established separately.
According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, there are twenty-five types of color; excluding *prabhā*, the reflection (*pratibimba*) is added.

Some say that when an image appears in a mirror or similar surface resembling its substance, this is reflection-color (*pratibimba-varṇa*). When light and so forth are manifested, a color of darkness arises that does not resemble [the original object].

The "original object" (*pratibimba*) refers to the color-form (*rūpa*). Now, it is said that by means of a mirror or similar medium, one perceives the original object in reverse; the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) thus carried along is called the "reflected image. The *Pañcaskandhaprakaraṇa* states:
"It refers to the objects of the eye—color-form (*varṇarūpa*), shape-form (*saṃsthānarūpa*), and informative form (*vijñaptirūpa*), as well as distinct color-form.

Regarding sound: it is produced from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and is the object apprehended by the auditory faculty (*śrotrindriya*). There are eleven kinds of sound, namely: agreeable, disagreeable, [and so forth]... [text truncated]

Agreeable, disagreeable, and both contrary [to these]. [Sound] has as its cause the primary elements that are appropriated (*upātta-mahābhūta-hetuka*), as its cause the primary elements that are not appropriated (*anupātta-mahābhūta-hetuka*), and as its cause both types of primary elements.

It is established by common worldly consensus, is produced by what is brought about (*abhinirhṛta*), is arisen from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), and is included within authoritative speech (*āptavāda*) or not included within authoritative speech.
The *Pañcaskandhaka* states three types, namely: sound caused by appropriated primary elements, and so forth. As for odor, the *Abhidharma* states six types, namely: pleasant and unpleasant.
They are equal, co-arising, conjoined, and subject to transformation; the five aggregates are likewise. Regarding tastes:

while the five aggregates are said to be six—sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and bland—the Abhidharma speaks of twelve, by adding the agreeable and the disagreeable to those six within the five aggregates.
Regarding "contradictory," "co-arising," "conjunction," and "transformation": according to the Abhidharma treatises, there are twenty-six types of contact (*spraṣṭavya*).

These are the four great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which act as the creators, and the derived qualities: smoothness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, warmth, laxity, tension, cold, hunger, thirst, and satiety.
Power, inferiority, exhaustion, nourishment, stickiness, illness, old age, death, fatigue, and respiration. The statement "and so forth" in the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* is likewise the same here.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 54) states that there are twenty-four types of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*), excluding laxity (*śithila*) and tension (*tīvra*). Laxity is subsumed under softness (*mṛdu*), while tension is subsumed under heaviness (*guru*).

Heaviness is conventionally established based on the solidity and substantiality of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); tension is itself this solidity and substantiality. Regarding the matter (*rūpa*) subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* speaks of five types:

namely, the extremely condensed (*paricchinna*), the extremely remote (*dūra*), that which is led by feeling (*vedanā-anuvidhāyin*), that which arises from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), and that which is produced by mastery (*vaśitā-janita*). These are the five.

The explanation of the aggregates (*skandha*) is the same. Thus, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), briefly stated, consists of two parts: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and eleven types of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).

Extensively, there are eighty-five, as listed in full. This is the essence of the aggregate of form; a detailed analysis of these eighty-five dharmas shall be further examined in the chapter on the five objects (*viṣaya*).
As for the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), its essence is the category of feeling among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).

The first [section] of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*: The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) refers to the six groups of feeling, namely, feeling produced by eye-contact, up to feeling produced by mind-contact.

Alternatively, they are threefold: suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. Furthermore, there are many varieties, as explained in detail therein; however, they do not transcend these three: pleasure, suffering, and equanimity.
The five aggregates are also described in terms of suffering and pleasure, which are said to be threefold. That which brings satisfaction to body and mind is called...

That which is neither pleasant nor unpleasant is called the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). In total, these three sets of six constitute the essence of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).

As for the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), it likewise consists of the omnipresent perception (*sarvatraga-saṃjñā*). It is stated that there are also six types, as further explained previously.

These are designated as the six perceptions according to their arising from the six contacts (*sparśa*). Furthermore, six [types] are taught: first, perception with signs (*sanimitta-saṃjñā*); second, perception without signs (*animitta-saṃjñā*).

[The six perceptions are: first, the perception of the limited; second, the perception of the immeasurable; third, the perception of the narrow and few; fourth, the perception of the vast; fifth, the perception of the infinite; and sixth, the perception of nothingness.

These are distinguished according to the realms, stages, and sentient beings. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* also provides these two sets of six names, which are identical to this [text]. The *Pañcāśatka* states:

Furthermore, there are briefly two types: first, mundane perception (*saṃjñā*); second, supramundane perception. These are distinguished according to whether they are with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Taken as a whole, their essence consists of two sets of six and two [factors]. Regarding the essence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is stated in the *Pañcāśatka* that this also comprises six kinds, which should be understood as previously described.

This refers to the pervasive volition (*cetanā*) that follows contact; it is divided into six as the essence of the aggregate of formations. The *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* is the same. [This] is cited.

Because the superior obscures the inferior, only volition (*cetanā*) is mentioned. In reality, however, with the exception of form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), all others constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "Furthermore, this very volition—excluding feeling and perception—together with the remaining mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), is collectively termed the aggregate of formations.
Although feeling and perception are excluded, [it refers to] all mental factors and the formations dissociated from mind.
One should practice; all [factors] are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). However, volition (*cetanā*) is preeminent, as it serves as the leader of all formations.

Therefore, it is specifically mentioned. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on the Demonstration of Consciousness-Only), Volume Three, states: "Because volition is the primary and most excellent factor within the aggregate of formations, this is cited to encompass the rest."

Thus, one should know that with the exception of the four aggregates (*skandha*), all others are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The five aggregates are likewise [to be understood].

In total, seventy-three dharmas constitute the essence of the aggregate of formations: namely, the three universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific factors (*viśeṣa*), the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala*), the six primary afflictions (*kleśa-mūla*), the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), and the twenty dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). This elaborates upon the mental factors (*caitta*) and the dissociated formations.
As explained in a separate chapter, regarding the essence of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*): the eight mind-kings constitute the essence of the aggregate of consciousness.

Thus, the second fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* asks: "How is the aggregate of consciousness established? It states that "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are each distinct.

"Mind" refers to the eighth [consciousness], because it is able to accumulate all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). "Intellect" refers to that which, at all times, takes the ālayavijñāna as its object and engages in cogitation.
Nature. This is the seventh [topic]. "Consciousness" refers to the six groups of consciousness, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.

Eye-consciousness has the nature of discerning based on the eye and having visible form as its object; the others are to be understood accordingly, with their essential natures distinguished by their dependence on the respective faculties and objects.

The *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states: "With respect to the object of cognition, its nature is that of discernment (*vijñapti*). This is the general definition. What follows below provides a specific explanation by addressing difficulties regarding mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*), which does not contradict this.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 53, speaks only of the six consciousnesses; this is based on the commonality of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and thus the other two [the storehouse consciousness and the afflicted mind] are concealed.
Second, regarding the determination of the essence (*svabhāva*) in terms of the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*): the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of ten elements and ten bases.

The entirety [of the aggregate of form] consists of the whole of the dharma-dhātu and the dharma-āyatana, as well as a small portion of each. That is to say, within the dharma-dhātu and dharma-āyatana, there are the most concise (paramāṇu) and the most remote (dūre-deśa) forms and so forth.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 54, states: "The aggregate of form comprises the ten elements (dhātu) and ten bases (āyatana) in their entirety, and a small portion of one element and one base.

The two aggregates of feeling and perception likewise consist of the dharma-dhātu and dharma-āyatana, because they are the two dharmas of feeling and perception. Fascicle 54 further states: "Feeling and perception are mentioned together..."

A portion of one element and one base. Excluding the two—feeling and perception—from within the element and base of formations (*saṃskāra-dhātu-āyatana*), as well as the six unconditioned phenomena and the five [material] forms, all the remainder belongs to the aggregate of formations.
The *Pañcavastuka* (Treatise on the Five Categories) states: "The aggregate of formations comprises a portion of one element and one base.

As for the essence of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), it is the element of mind-consciousness (*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*), because it is the totality of the mental base (*manāyatana*). The *Pañcavastuka* states: "The aggregate of consciousness comprises seven elements."

Complete. Complete in one place. The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the Abhidharma are all explained in this same way. Regarding the third point, concerning the essence of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*):

some say that because the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is a non-existent phenomenon, it is not subsumed within the aggregates. This explanation is incorrect; it encompasses all three natures.

That which is falsely conceived as truly existent has the first nature as its essence. That which arises from various conditions has the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its essence. It is non-existent...
The outflows (*āsrava*) are free from inversion; their essence is perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna*). Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 8, asks:

"How do the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) subsume the six categories of phenomena (*ṣaḍdharma*)? Within those six categories, all possess the three natures. This is because form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) all possess the nature of being falsely imagined and dependently arisen.
Question: Since the essence of false imagination (*parikalpita*) is non-existent, how can it constitute the meaning of an aggregate (*piṇḍārtha*)? Answer: It is falsely imagined as...
There is. There is the sense of a collection of delusions (*mṛṣā-saṃcaya*). If it were not so, how could it be that all things, such as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), are said to be empty?
That which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is called "existent" (*sat*); "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*) are called "non-existent" (*asat*).

As stated in various treatises, the Dharma taught by the Buddha is unique among non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): what exists is declared to exist, and what does not exist is declared not to exist. Since the aggregates exist through the conditions of arising, how can they be said [to be non-existent]?

Emptiness, as well as the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), should be subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Since the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) does not exist, how could it ever constitute the aggregates?

Regarding the fourth [section], the definition of the five dharmas: the five dharmas are the characteristics (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*). Excluding the perfected nature [from the dependent nature].

All four have the four [factors] as their substance. Although the five dharmas are explained differently regarding their essential nature, when considered generally, all four are subsumed within them.

If one speaks of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), names (*nāman*), and substance (*vastu*) based on dependent origination, then the five aggregates (*skandha*) are all characteristics, while a small portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) constitutes the name as substance.

In the combined discussion of the provisional and the real: a small portion of the aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) have "function" as their essence; this is because the two phenomena of name (*nāman*) and sound (*śabda*) are subsumed under distinct aggregates.

The three [aggregates] of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), along with a small portion of the aggregate of formations, have "discrimination" as their essence; this is because only the eight types of mind and all mental factors (*caitta*) are of the nature of discrimination.

The five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) may have four [of these categories] as their essence, because they include both the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and its semblance, which function as both the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*). As for the capacity...

That which transforms them has correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) as its essence; it is untainted (*anāsrava*), free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), and has perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna*) as its essence.

Regarding the three gates of the permanent and the impermanent, with the exception of the perfectly accomplished nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), or that which is free from conceptual proliferation, these are not names for those [impermanent] characteristics. Although there are both the signifier and the signified, all have correct cognition as their essence.
This is based on *nirvāṇa*: having abandoned impermanent form (*rūpa*), one attains permanent form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise [transformed].
Thus it is. Furthermore, according to the third master’s interpretation in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) constitutes the essence of the five aggregates.

For the first two masters, however, it does not constitute the essence of the aggregates. For now, the essence has been established according to the first gate of the *Vijñaptimātratā*; the remaining cases should be understood by applying the same principle as appropriate.

The third [section] has nine successive stages; the second [chapter] of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* has three successive stages: first, based on the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and consciousness itself;
second, regarding its functioning as a basis, by virtue of the power of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*);

and third, because feeling arises in accordance [with contact] and experiences it, one grasps the characteristics of what is experienced; according to the corresponding perceptions, one performs various karmic actions, and in accordance with those actions, [one undergoes rebirth].

Consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is so called because it cognizes objects before it and undergoes transformation as it moves toward other realms of existence (*gati*). Third, regarding the basis of defilement and purity:

this refers to how the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) serve as the conditions for defilement and purity. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The appearance of confusion and the essence of confusion...

if one does not exist, the other also does not exist. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is predominant in the arising of mind. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* explains that perception depends upon the sense faculties and objects, and is either defiled or undefiled. There are two types of feeling (*vedanā*).

[It] arises. Depending on what is experienced through feeling (*vedanā*), one grasps signs and engages in formative activity (*abhisamskāra*). That is to say, by means of the appropriate (*yoniśas*) and the inappropriate (*ayoniśas*), there is respectively defilement and purification.

That which is defiled or purified is precisely the mind (*citta*), because it possesses heaviness (*dausthulya*) or is free from heaviness. (Yogācārabhūmi, *Bhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, Chapter 54) There are six successive expositions:
first, the order of arising—initially form (*rūpa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), formations (*saṃskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). Therefore, that...
The treatise states: "With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; and so on, up to: with the mind and mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises.

Here, it first mentions form, then consciousness, and then, due to the conjunction of these three, contact (*sparśa*); conditioned by contact, feeling (*vedanā*) and the others arise. This is called the sequential order of the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Therefore, the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on Establishing Consciousness-Only), fascicle 3, says: "Contact refers to the conjunction of the three, which is a conceptual transformation."

[It is] different. Its nature is that which causes the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) to contact their objects; its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.

Second, regarding the basis for overcoming perversions (*viparyāsa*): these are form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*). Thus, that treatise states:

"In order to counteract the four perversions—conceiving the impure as pure, suffering as pleasure, non-self as self, and the impermanent as permanent—this [treatise] first explains form, feeling, and consciousness. Consciousness...

Next, one contemplates the two [aspects of] formations. Third, regarding the basis for the process of transmigration: with the sense faculties as the objective domain, through the two types of aggregates, various defilements arise;
because they experience and grasp at objects, they perform wholesome and unwholesome deeds, giving rise to all subsequent defilements such as future rebirths.

Consciousness is that which is defiled; therefore, it is mentioned last. This constitutes one portion of the defilement and purification of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. The four bases of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) are the same as in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
The five bases of establishment (*pañcasthāna-vyavasthāna*) refers to how, when people in the world see one another, they first perceive their physical form (*rūpa*).

Next, one knows their advancement and retreat, whether they experience suffering or pleasure; next, by knowing their such names and categories; next, one knows their faculties and dispositions, their dullness or wisdom, and their superiority or inferiority;
finally, through the recognition of the aggregates, one establishes an internal self, [perceiving] the six bases as belonging to the self and the objects as pertaining to the self.
That is to say, I depend upon the body to experience pleasure and pain regarding various objects and subsequently give rise to verbal expressions.

These two types [of actions] are accumulated only through what is lawful (*dharma*) and what is unlawful (*adharma*), arising from volition (*cetanā*) and through performance (*abhisamskāra*); I possess these in their respective order.
I shall explain this later. Because these factors of the self (*ātman*) depend upon the self, they are explained first.

Regarding the four preceding [aggregates] as "mine" (*ātmīya*) and the fifth as the "self-entity" (*ātma-vastu*), the explanations of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness found in various sūtras and śāstras do not follow the order of their arising nor the sequence for counteracting specific inversions.
Therefore, the sequence before and after is not fixed; such explanations are made according to the occasion to treat specific afflictions. If both...

In the first fascicle of the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, it is explained four times. Thus, its verse states: "According to coarseness, defilement, vessel, and so forth, the realms are established in their respective order.

Although this differs from the tenets of our own school, there is no harm in mentioning it. Since there are already many [such divergent views] of our own, I shall desist for fear of excessive prolixity.
Regarding the fourth point, "refutation and establishment," the preceding sequence should likewise be refuted and established. How is this known?

Within the fifty-four [sections], in the sixth section, namely the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it states that the aggregates (*skandha*) have only five causes. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says: "Question: For what reason are there only five aggregates? Answer:
To manifest the five matters of the self (*ātman*). That is to say, to manifest the matters of the self as the body, its instruments, and enjoyment."
The entity of the self; the entity of the self as expressed in speech; the entity of the self that constructs all phenomena (dharma) and non-phenomena (adharma);

and the entity of the self’s own essence which serves as their basis. It continues until it says: "For what reason? Because sentient beings in the world mostly conceive of the aggregate of consciousness as the self, and conceive of the remaining aggregates as 'self' and 'belonging to self'.
This explains the five reasons; therefore, the aggregates are not five [in number] regarding the self.

It increases but does not decrease; by this one may know that the same applies to their establishment and abandonment. Furthermore, regarding the principles of establishment and abandonment: the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are both of the nature of form (*rūpa*), and thus they are combined into the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

The eight consciousnesses are of a similar class, and thus they are combined into a single aggregate. Within the mental factors (*caitta*), feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established separately because they serve as the fundamental basis for purity and the cause of birth and death.
For householders attached to desire, feeling is the root of contention; for those who have left the home life, it is perception.

They serve as the roots of contention: through feeling (*vedanā*), greed arises because of attachment to sensual pleasures; through perception (*saṃjñā*), views arise because of the production of clinging.

These lead to mutual anger and rivalry. As for the cause of birth and death: through internal and external feelings, two types of delusion are initiated, namely, delusion regarding the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

And there is delusion regarding the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*). Based on these, one conceptually establishes the characteristics of limits through either appropriate or inappropriate mental engagement (*yoniśo-ayoniśo-manasikāra*), and accordingly performs various karmas.
All other [factors] lack any distinct superior capacity and are all characterized by flux (*saṃskāra*); therefore, they constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Although volition (*cetanā*) possesses superior capacity, it is established as the aggregate of formations because its primary function is to perform formative activity; thus, performing activity and being subject to flux share the same meaning as "formations."

Fifth, the analysis by way of various categories (*yogācāra*) consists of fifty-six [sections] in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the third, fourth, and fifth [chapters] of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, which extensively elaborate upon many categories.

Here, I shall briefly describe three; the detailed explanations are as found therein. First, the category of the conventional and the real; second, the category of the outflowing and the non-outflowing (*sāsrava-anāsrava*).

The third section concerns the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). First, regarding the provisional and the real: First, concerning dependence on or independence from verbal designations (*nāma-paññatti*).

That which depends on verbal designations holds that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all provisional. That which does not depend on verbal designations holds that the five aggregates are all real. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter three, states:

"That which does not depend on verbal designations—namely, these other faculties and objects—is the meaning of being substantially existent (*dravya-sat*). Consequently, everything is substantially existent.

This means that they depend upon linguistic expression (*nāma-vyavahāra*). These remaining faculties and objects are of the nature of conventional existence (*prajñapti-sat*). All of them are conventional. Why?
Because both the cognition of linguistic expression and the linguistic expression itself depend upon common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), not upon specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Common characteristics are merely superimpositions (*adhyāropa*) based upon specific characteristics; they possess no separate essence. Therefore, they are conventionally existent. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Second Chapter) states: "Conventional..."
Wisdom and its designations function solely in reliance upon the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. Second, regarding the relationship between appearance and substance:

in the eighth consciousness at the stage of the cause, the fivefold number of objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) are all provisional, as they lack real seeds. Since the subjective part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the meaning-part (*artha-bhāga*) share the same objects as the sovereign [consciousness], they pertain to all five aggregates.

This applies to both seeds and manifestations; it is not limited to seeds and manifestations alone. If it were limited to only seeds and manifestations, the inclusion of the aggregates would be incomplete. (8)

Regarding the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*): those [objects] that take the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as their object are all provisional (*prajñapti*), because they are similar to the king’s (*citta-rāja*) objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Those that take the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their object may be either provisional or real. However, the objective aspects of mental factors (*caitta*) are also invariably provisional. As for the objects of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), their substance (*dravya*) may be either provisional or real;

since the objective aspect follows its substance, it may thus be either provisional or real. Regarding the seventh consciousness, both the king and its mental factors share a real substance, because at all times it is constant.

Regarding the eighth [consciousness], its *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) produces the substantial appearance (*dravya-lakṣaṇa*) of that eighth consciousness. Its fruit may be either provisional (*prajñapti*) or real (*dravya*), which can be understood by analogy with the eighth consciousness.

Regarding the causal and resultant stages of the sixth [consciousness], both its cause and fruit are common to both the provisional and the real, because both its cause and fruit take all objects as their conditions.

Regarding the causal aspect of the five consciousnesses, there is one interpretation that it is common to both the provisional and the real, because it is accepted that they take provisional forms such as long and short as their objects. There is another interpretation that it is exclusively real, as the five [consciousnesses] do not accept [provisional objects].

Because consciousness is conditioned by the provisional (*prajñapti*), this principle is explained in detail as it is taught in the "Chapter on the Five Objects" (*Pañcaviṣaya-varga*). Depending on the specific case, the characteristics of the provisional and the real (*dravya*) arise.

When serving as a basis (*āśraya*), its substance is likewise either provisional or real. To state the general characteristics of the three [aggregates]: the three aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all substantially real.

The two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) encompass both the provisional and the real. Now, within the aggregate of form, the five faculties such as the eye, and four among the [six] contacts...
"Great! All are substantially existent. (Abhidharmasamuccaya) 54 states: "Among the forms subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), nine types are substantially existent (*dravyasat*);

one should know that the remainder are merely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*). Because the five faculties (*indriya*) have their characteristics clearly manifest, they are not mentioned separately.

Among the five objective spheres (*viṣaya*), blue, yellow, red, and white—these four are real colors (*bhūtavarṇa*). The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states: 'Among the twenty-five types of form, blue...'"
The four types—yellow, red, white, and [the remaining]—are substantial; all others are merely nominal. Among the eight kinds of sound, only those that can be [perceived as] real are substantial.
Wherever "echo-sound" is mentioned, one should know that it is nominal. Among the six kinds of fragrance, "combined fragrance" is nominal. As stated in [Treatise on the Five Aggregates, Chapter] 54:

"In the winds moving through space, there is no co-nascent fragrance and so forth; there is only that which is nominally combined. Since it says "nominally combined," it is clearly known that [this is not substantial].
This is conventional; the rest may all be real. Among the twelve types of taste, those that are composite should be understood as conventional by analogy with odor; the rest are all real.

Within the matter of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), the four types—extreme reduction, extreme distance, that which arises from conceptual construction, and matter derived from mental volition—are all conventional.

It should be known that the aggregate of matter produced by meditative concentration is real. As it says in [the *Abhidharma-kośa*] 54: "If there is a meditative concentration possessing majestic power..."

The objects of their activity are like transformations (*nirmāṇa*). Those fruits, those objects, and the objects of the consciousnesses associated with them—namely, material form (*rūpa*)—are substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
If that were so, then the material forms of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and restraint (*saṃvara*) would all be merely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*);

since he did not state that the material forms produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are nominally existent, it is clear they are substantially existent. Furthermore, he explains: "If material form is produced by the power of meditative concentration, it is substantially existent."

The provisional forms (*prajñapti-rūpa*) and so forth produced by other meditative concentrations are merely provisionally existent (*prajñaptisat*). This treatise speaks according to what is predominant; it does not speak exhaustively of all possibilities.

Otherwise, even "extreme reduction" (*atyanta-saṃkṣepa*) and the like would have to be considered substantially existent (*dravyasat*). However, there is a judgment that states: "Forms arising from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) encompass both the provisional and the substantial.

Because one does not clearly and directly perceive their objects, they are termed "pervasive conceptualization. Although they are called "pervasive," they nevertheless serve as the seeds and roots for the formation [of phenomena].

[Objection: It is reckoned as being merely conventionally existent (*prajñapti-sat*). [Response: This explanation is not correct. If it can establish a seed (*bīja*), it must certainly be substantially real (*dravya-sat*). A conventional phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*) is like non-existence, for it is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Alternatively, that which is the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpya*) is each subsumed under its own respective category; thus, when the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is established, it is subsumed under the category of pervasive conceptualized form (*parikalpita-rūpa*).

However, to say that pervasive conceptualization is "shadow-form" (*chāyā-rūpa*) does not mean it is the shadow of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*); rather, it is the nature of pervasive conceptualized form, which resembles the mind of grasping (*grāhaka-citta*).

What appears is called a "reflection" (*chāyā*) as well as the "discriminating mental consciousness" (*vikalpa-manovijñāna*). When this consciousness alone takes such things as "flowers in the sky" as its object, because they lack substantial reality (*dravya*), there is only a reflected image;

it manifests solely from the deluded mind and is therefore termed "universal construction" (*parikalpita*). If one were to claim that when the mind takes these as objects, they belong to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), then the five sense faculties would not exist, for the five faculties are also objects of the mental consciousness and so forth. Thus, these are merely objects of the mind and are not the domains of the other [sensory] faculties.

It is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), because it can universally take other sense bases and their objects as its cognitive range. Therefore, it is distinguished [from the other faculties] by this alone.

This explanation accords with the profound principle. Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), all non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*). They pervade all three types of specific objects.

All [of these] are real. Among the eleven wholesome factors, the three—equanimity (*upekṣā*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*)—are nominal. Among the six root afflictions, unwholesome wisdom (*daurprajñā*) is nominal.

Among the twenty secondary afflictions, the ten minor ones and the three major ones—heedlessness (*pramāda*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*)—are also nominal.

Among the four indeterminate categories, vitarka and vicāra are all conventional (prajñapti); the remainder are substantial (dravya). This is stated according to the correct principle; otherwise, they are indeterminate.

Regarding the second gate of the outflows (āsrava) and the non-outflows (anāsrava): within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), there are the five faculties and their objects belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

The matter of non-restraint (*asaṃvara-rūpa*), the unwholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) of the intermediate state, the non-informative matter of mundane wholesomeness, the matter arising from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), and the matter arising from a distinct mind in the desire realm—all these are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).

If that which exists within the gate of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) is called "outflow-free," then, excluding the non-informative matter of non-restraint and the unwholesome matter of the intermediate state, the remainder is called "outflow-free. This refers to the karma-born matter of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Regarding the five sense faculties and their objects, which are forms: with the exception of the five faculties, such as the eye, produced by a Buddha, the five [faculties], the eight [unmanifests], and the five objects are all exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

As for the sixth and seventh characteristics, the forms of the five objects, the extremely subtle forms, the distinct forms, and the unmanifests concomitant with meditative concentration, these arise from both meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

They are both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), because they arise from distinct tainted and untainted minds. Within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), suffering (*duḥkha*) and grief (*daurmanasya*) are tainted;

joy (*prīti*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and pleasure (*sukha*)—these three—are both tainted and untainted. Perception (*saṃjñā*) follows the five types of feeling. Volition (*cetanā*) may be inferred accordingly. Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*):

The universal [mental factors], the object-specific ones, and the eleven [factors] including joy; the indeterminate [factors] such as vitarka and vicāra; acquisition (prāpti), non-acquisition (aprāpti), characteristics (lakṣaṇa), life-force (jīvita), names (nāman), phrases (pada), and syllables (vyañjana);

homogeneity (sabhāgatā); and the ten [factors] beginning with the process of transmigration (pravṛtti)—these are both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava). As appropriate, they arise in association with contaminated or uncontaminated minds because they are concomitant (sahabhū) with them.

Furthermore, there are the fundamental and secondary [unwholesome states] such as regret (kaukṛtya), sleep (middha), and the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), as well as the maturation of non-perception (asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka).

Together with the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), these are all exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*). As for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), its essence is exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) also extends to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated;

this can be understood by analogy with the preceding [discussion]. Regarding the third [section], the analysis of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva-vibhāga*): namely, the wholesome (*kuśala*), the unwholesome (*akuśala*), and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature.

Within the wholesome, there are two types: those produced through application (*prāyogika*) and those acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*). There are six types of indeterminate: obscured (*nivṛta*), ripening (*vipāka*), and deportment (*airyāpathika*)... [and so forth].

Regarding the categories: ritual, craftsmanship, transformation, and intrinsic nature—these constitute nine distinct doors. Together with the door of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), there are ten types of aggregates (*skandha*).
In the Hīnayāna, there are only nine, as it lacks the aggregate of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-skandha*). As for the first, "virtue through application" (*prayoga-kuśala*):

that which must be produced through the exertion of effort and cultivation is called virtue of application; this includes, within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), visible form, sound, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), the extremely subtle (*paramāṇu*), the extremely remote (*dūra*), and those pertaining to spatial direction.
It is so because it is matter and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) arising from a mind associated with skillful means (*upāya*); thus, it is pervasive. Its nature is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*).

The three types of mundane wisdom (*prajñā*)—those that are extremely concise, extremely remote, and impure—are also all contemplative. Neutral non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that is intermediate, as well as the non-informative matter of the vows (*saṃvara*), are skillful through application (*prayoga-kuśala*).
Although innate [skillfulness] is intermediate, it is inferior and does not give rise to non-informative matter. The production of matter through mastery is solely through skillful means.

Excluding those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and those arising from preparatory effort (*prayoga*), within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), there are eight pervasive and specific factors,

eleven wholesome factors, and four indeterminate factors. Because regret (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) exist during the stages of hearing and reflection, as well as their concomitants, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness, the acquisitions (*prāpti*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), names, phrases, and syllables,
the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and the ten such as the "flowing equally" of the mental factors— all these are also added according to their respective applicability.

One practices virtue. Regarding the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the first six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), both [the sixth consciousness and the five sensory consciousnesses] are absent. For the latter two [powers], both are absent; for the former six, both are present—the meaning of this should be understood.

How is it known that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, exist? Because they arise for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness, there are consciousnesses associated with the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear.

This is "virtue acquired through application" (*prayoga-kuśala*). Furthermore, another explanation states that it refers to the virtues produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) arising on the eighth stage and above;

these are also virtue acquired through application. Second, "virtue acquired at birth" (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) is so called because it is obtained immediately upon birth and is not a virtue produced by an applied mind (*prāyogika-citta*).
This refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)—namely, visible forms and sounds—emitted by such a virtuous mind.

There are two types [of wholesome states]. Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), there are those that pervade all three [realms], as well as the five specific object-oriented mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*), the ten wholesome [mental factors], regret (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*), along with their associated aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the various dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) based upon these; these are the "wholesome by birth" (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*).

All others are not. Third, regarding the unwholesome nature (*akuśala-svabhāva*): it is that which contradicts reason, harms things, possesses a superior intrinsic nature, and brings about future results; this is called [the unwholesome].

Regarding the nature of the unwholesome (*akuśala*): within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it consists of the two types—visible form and sound—as well as non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), and a portion of form arising from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).

Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it includes all discriminative thoughts among the primary and secondary afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as those innate afflictions that give rise to unwholesome karma;
furthermore, it includes the associated aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness. [These] pervade the three [categories of mental factors], the specific objects, and the... [incomplete].
The four [mental factors] within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as well as the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) based upon them, are all unwholesome (*akuśala*);

the remainder are not. Regarding the fourth category, the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*): defiled wisdom that obscures and obstructs the ultimate truth is called "obscured" (*nivṛta*); because it does not bring about karmic maturation (*vipāka*), it is called "unspecified" (*avyākṛta*).
This refers to both form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*), which are categorized as obscured according to the motivating mind; thus, the afflictions (*kleśa*) follow from such motivation.

Only within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) do the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) arise. [However,] it may also extend to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as evidenced by the deceptive speech and physical gestures of Brahmā toward Aśvajit, which constitute obscured (*nivṛta*) karma.

Furthermore, the three types of mistaken transgressions (*viparyaya-āpatti*) of body, speech, and mind, as well as those arising from ignorance regarding objects of knowledge, are also pervasive obscured states.
Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), the innate (*sahaja*) greed, delusion, and pride of the desire realm that do not give rise to karma are both innate [obscured states].

[The first category] is "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). Within the two upper realms, all primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) associated with this [view], as well as the three universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyata*), the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), the triad of feeling, perception, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-vijñāna*), and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) based upon these, are all of an obscured nature (*nivṛta*).
All others are not. Regarding the fifth, the "ripened neutral" (*vipākāvyākṛta*): its essential nature is neutral, indicating that it is the result of wholesome or unwholesome causes.

That which is induced by diverse [karmas] is called "maturation" (*vipāka*). Within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the five sense organs and the five objects are maturation only when they are induced by karma;

all others are not. The eighth consciousness induced by karma, the six consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness, their associated aggregates of feeling and perception, the three universals, the five particulars, the three indeterminate factors, and the various non-associated formations that depend upon these—these are [maturation].

It is of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*). All the remainder are not. Regarding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) of the sixth [category], the deportments (*airyāpathika*), such as walking and standing, and the arts (*śailpasthānika*):
although these pertain to all three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate), those that are wholesome or unwholesome are subsumed under their respective preceding categories.

Here, only the non-defiled indeterminate is taken; that is, within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the four objects—form and so forth—if they constitute the substance of deportment, are exclusively informative form (*vijñapti-rūpa*). This is what is taken.

Because it is separated [from its object] and because this is its condition, it thus pervades the four sensory objects (*viṣaya*). The substance of sound is empty and sparse, and thus it arises even when separated from its material basis; furthermore, it does not depend on this [specific] condition.

It is not said that it pervades the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-skandha*), nor that it arises in association with the mental states of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*) produced by the sixth consciousness.

Furthermore, those associated with these non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are also modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*). Some say that, excluding feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that coexist with them.

As for the visual and other consciousnesses, the eleven wholesome [mental factors], the two types of afflictions (fundamental and secondary), the two mindless absorptions, the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vedayita*), life-force (*jīvita*), the nature of maturation (*vipāka-dharmatā*), and the sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), as well as other non-associated formations based upon these—all of these are not [modes of deportment].

Regarding this inclusion: some say that the four consciousnesses which take postures (*īryāpatha*) as their object are also included within the category of postures; this is the same as the Sarvāstivāda school.
However, in the Mahāyāna tradition, those indeterminate states taking postures as their object are instead included within the category of "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).

Because the Vaibhāṣika category of "posture" is narrow while the Mahāyāna category of "maturation-mind" is broad, their respective inclusions differ. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, fascicle five, states: "Like the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), the seventh..."

Regarding "craftsmanship" (*śilpa*): "craft" (*śila*) refers to industrial skill, and "mastery" (*pa*) refers to expedient means. The presence of carvings, engravings, and so forth, as well as these images, is termed "craftsmanship.

To the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), sound is added because it is craftsmanship regarding speech. Within the category of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), names, phrases, and phonemes are added.

The rest is the same as the meaning of "majesty" (*vibhūti*). Regarding the eighth, "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*): the conversion of one's essential nature is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*); that which suddenly appears where there was nothing is called "manifestation" (*nirmita*). Only...
Regarding the arising of transformations for the purpose of play: because they are subsumed under the nature of the wholesome, they arise for the sake of benefit and happiness.
