fourth, by manifesting through divisions; fifth, by means of discrimination; and sixth, by means of question-and-answer analysis.

First, regarding consciousness: if various consciousnesses exist within the state of Buddhahood or in the *vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*, they are all exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whether they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

However, regarding contaminated concentration (*samādhi*), there are briefly two interpretations. First, in the case of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), such as the contemplation of fire (*tejodhātu-bhāvanā*) and so forth, if the provisional image (*parikalpita-nimitta*) has not yet been established, it is not subsumed under direct perception; if the provisional image is established, it is indeed direct perception.
The *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the *Yogācārabhūmi*, and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā* all state: "In this context, the establishment of the objective sphere (*ālambana*) refers to grasping the foundational object.
It is not a conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) produced by mental fabrication. Regarding the objects of the various elements (*dhātu*), such as the earth element and so forth:

if the understanding is not yet matured, it is established through mental fabrication; if the understanding is fully matured, it is no longer a mental fabrication. This is what is meant by 'established through mental fabrication' [in contrast to] 'not through mental fabrication.'"

Because it is accomplished through mental construction (*vikalpa*), it is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Second, it is said that all conceptualizations (*parikalpita-saṃjñā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are termed "unaccomplished" and are merely called "pseudo-direct-perception.
All meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) of the higher realms are accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); thus, these conceptualizations are termed "accomplished.

While the mental activity of the desire realm may serve as a preliminary means (*upāya*), the latter of the two interpretations is superior. If one is in a state of distraction (*vikṣepa*), [the faculties] are five or eight respectively.

The seventh [consciousness] is not both; the sixth is common to both. When it functions together with the five [sensory consciousnesses] as their object, being free from all conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it is subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Although it shares the same objects as the five, if it apprehends them through conceptualization and thus does not correspond to the original object, it is subsumed under non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*).

If the cognition corresponds to its object, it is subsumed under inference (*anumāna*). To apprehend a single, conventionally established cause that extends to others is called "conceptualization"; this does not refer to...
All such conventional designations are produced solely by the sixth [consciousness]. Therefore, inference (*anumāna*) resides only in the sixth;
direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) pervades all eight, as previously analyzed according to their respective applications.

Second, regarding the clarification by way of the mind (*citta*): this refers to the five types of mind—sudden (*ābhoga*), investigative (*paryeṣaka*), determinative (*niścita*), defiled-pure (*kliṣṭa-śuddha*), and outflowing (*naiṣyandika*).
In general, these five minds all pertain to both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). If explained individually, the details would be too extensive and cumbersome;

therefore, we shall distinguish the mind by way of consciousness (*vijñāna*), for the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is easily understood in accordance with consciousness. To distinguish them by way of consciousness: in the causal stage of the eighth [consciousness], there are only three types of mind.

The *sutarāṃ-niścita-citta* (decisive mind) and the *niṣyanda-citta* (outflowing mind) arise for the first time in a different realm, as well as when subsequent objects appear; this is because they possess the *ābhoga-citta* (sudden or impulsive mind).
Regarding this decisive mind, there are two interpretations. One states that within this very mental state there exists a decisive mind that differs from the five [sensory consciousnesses].

Following the investigation by the mental consciousness (*manas*) and having reached a decision, one subsequently engages in minds that are defiled, pure, or neither-defiled-nor-pure; it is not itself wholesome.
Because it is unwholesome. One interpretation holds that the mind of the first moment consists solely of *sutarika* (sudden occurrence), as its nature of maturation (*vipāka*) is inferior.

Furthermore, explaining this according to its meaning: the first is called *sutarika* because it has just passed over the object; the subsequent moments, such as investigation (*paryeṣaṇa*), are the second moment. Regarding this second moment, there are also two interpretations. One interpretation explains the mind according to its meaning:
the first is called *sutarika* because it has just crossed over the object, while the second moment is then called "determination" (*niścaya*). This is precisely...
Thereafter, its nature is no longer distinct; arising in accordance with its preceding nature, it is called a "consequent mind" (*niṣyanda-citta*).

This differs from the five consciousnesses, because at the time of determination, its nature is not yet fixed. Alternatively, it is designated as "determined" based on its function; only at the third moment is it properly termed a "consequent mind.

One interpretation holds that while there is a consequent mind, the "determined mind" arises from vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), whereas the eight [types of consciousness] lack such seeking.
Therefore, there is no fixed determination. This is because it arises from the same nature as the preceding [state] and is termed a "mind of outflow" (*niṣyanda-citta*).

Even if there were a fixed determination, it would be figuratively described as such with respect to the mind of outflow; for example, when hearing a sound while in meditative absorption, it is figuratively described as a "sudden" (*ābhoga*) mind with respect to the mind of outflow.
At that time, it should not be called merely "sudden" (*tātkālika*), because one has not yet abandoned the meditative object.

From this point onward, all subsequent "sudden" moments constitute the second moment; furthermore, all subsequent states of determinate mind (*niścaya-citta*) are designated as "evolutionary" (*naiṣyandika*) minds, because they arise separately with intervals and continuities in their objects.
If one is in the state of Buddhahood, four types of mind may be present, with the exception of [the aforementioned].
In the search [for liberation], among the eight causes, the objective condition is not universal; it conditions only three objects, excluding the uncontaminated state.

Therefore, in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), there is a sudden mind (*ābhoga-citta*). Regarding this very mind, it is metaphorically designated as "decisive" (*niyata*) and "defiled or pure" (*kliṣṭa-śubha*).
Otherwise, this stage would not be wholesome or defiled. The second moment is called "consequent flow" (*nisyanda*); there is no further suddenness or decisiveness.

In the meditative states (*samāpatti*), both defiled and pure objects have already been experienced; they are apprehended spontaneously according to their preceding nature. Therefore, the first four [mental factors] are absent.
This differs from the causal state, where, upon first encountering an object, one must first deliberate before determining its nature and only then giving rise to a wholesome or defiled mind.

Since this [meditative] mind constantly functions for benefit and happiness, it possesses determination (*niyata*) as well as wholesome and defiled aspects. There are further alternative interpretations, which are too numerous to recount here. The seventh [mental factor] exists.

Regarding the outflows (*āsrava*), there are only four types of mind. The eighth [mind] of a different realm is encountered for the first time; thus, although it newly encounters an object, it immediately grasps it as "self.

Because the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is continuous, one does not seek further. It is also explained according to this principle that within a sudden, impulsive mind (*tātkālika-citta*), there can exist minds that are determinate or defiled/pure;
it is not that the impulsive mind itself does not grasp [the object] as "self. Otherwise, the grasping at a self would be subject to interruption.
Therefore, some say: "There is no fixed determination, yet there is defilement and purification. It cannot be said that because one does not seek [them], there is no fixed determination;
for if there were no fixed determination, defilement and purification would likewise not arise. If defilement and purification do not arise, there should be no resultant flow (*niṣyanda*).
If defilement and purification exist by virtue of one's own conceptualization (*vikalpa*), they must also exist by virtue of one's own definitive discernment (*pariccheda*). Or perhaps it may be so.

Their nature is eternally established; they do not newly arise at present. There can only be two types: the *sutarāṃ-utpanna* (sudden) and the *nisyanda* (outflowing). Among these, the three [other] types are absent.

If one is in the untainted state (*anāsrava*) within the stage of Buddhahood, there are likewise four types of mind. This is because the *ādarśa-jñāna* (mirror-like wisdom) initially arises as a sudden occurrence.

The remaining wisdoms are as previously explained regarding the eighth consciousness. In the causal stage, there are five types, because the untainted objects are new; thus, the *sutarāṃ-utpanna* is present. [This concludes the section on] the eight.

From the stages above the Grounds (*bhūmi*), although one occupies a position of mastery, one must still rely on seeking [remedies] regarding medicines and illnesses. The seventh consciousness follows the six, and as it shares the same objects of perception as them, it may likewise involve seeking.
The latter three [consciousnesses] can be fully understood in this regard. As for the sixth consciousness, its state at the stage of Buddhahood is the same as previously described;

however, during the causal stage, it possesses both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) aspects. During the causal stage, the five sensory consciousnesses possess only two types of mind, excluding the nature of the middle three minds.
Because there is no investigation of the object, there is no seeking; because there is no seeking, there is no determination;

because there is no conceptualization, there is neither defilement nor purity. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "By means of the arising of visual consciousness, three types of mind are obtained, which follow one another in sequence:

namely, the sudden mind (*ābhoga-citta*), the seeking mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*), and the determining mind (*niścaya-citta*). The first is visual consciousness; the second and the third belong to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Regarding the determining mind:
Subsequently, there is defilement and purity; only after this does the resultant eye-consciousness arise, functioning as wholesome or unwholesome.

Since it has been stated that defilement and purity occur only after a determinate mind (*niyata-citta*), and that the subsequent resultant eye-consciousness is clearly of only two types [wholesome or unwholesome], some maintain that the five sensory consciousnesses also possess defilement and purity, because they become defiled or pure despite being devoid of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). This is not mentioned in the first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Regarding the five types of existence (*bhava*), they are induced by others and thus possess both defilement and purity. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that this mind, whether defiled or pure, arises due to two conditions:
first, what was previously induced; second, through conceptualization (*vikalpa*). One interpretation holds that the five sensory consciousnesses may possess all five [mental factors].

It is said that the "seeking mind" (*paryeṣaka-citta*) operates in conjunction with desire (*chanda*). Since the five sensory consciousnesses operate in conjunction with desire—because they aspire toward their objects—they can possess seeking. Although [the sensory consciousnesses] are themselves...
There is non-conceptual seeking, yet there is spontaneous seeking; or there is non-constructive seeking, yet there is also conceptual seeking.

It is taught that the five consciousnesses possess conceptual afflictions because they are induced by the mental faculty (*manas*). Otherwise, the five [types of] afflictions would not be subject to abandonment through insight (*darśana-heya*).

According to one interpretation, the five consciousnesses lack conceptual afflictions; as for the teaching that they possess conceptual seeking, it applies to those [afflictions] abandoned through insight.

Because the cause has ceased, it is described as "annihilation. These afflictions of the five consciousnesses are induced by the conceptual afflictions of the conditioned mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

When the inducing [consciousness] is eliminated through insight (*darśana*), that which is induced is subsequently severed. Of these two interpretations, the former is superior. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that both conceptual and innate greed and other afflictions pervade all five types of sensation;

furthermore, the five [sensory consciousnesses] are induced by the mental consciousness, and while the mental consciousness performs investigation, the five sensory consciousnesses cannot do so immediately.
Regarding the determination of the outflow of defilement and purity: if this were to occur only in the subsequent stage, it would not be induced by the mind (*manas*).

Since it is indeed induced by the mind—just as in the case of mental seeking and so forth—the same applies to the five consciousnesses. Furthermore, one cannot claim that although there is "seeking," the five [consciousnesses] are still merely "sudden" (*ābhoga*), because their objects are not newly encountered.
If they were in a state of autonomy, seeking would not be required; for the five do not follow the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

It is also because it takes the faculties and natures of sentient beings as its object. If it takes the six objects as its object, the six [consciousnesses] do not seek them; the same applies to the five consciousnesses.

If it pertains to the state of Buddhahood, it is also as previously explained. Having understood the universality and limitation of the mind, one can fully comprehend the presence or absence of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Third, regarding the mental factors (*caitta*), it should be understood that the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viniyata*) factors, as well as the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*) factors, pertain to both types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As for the six fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*) and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) in their entirety, along with a portion of the remaining four, do not pertain to both types of valid cognition;

rather, they correspond to either view (*dṛṣṭi*) or doubt, as they are not themselves the two types of valid cognition. If greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*) occur within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), they are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); if they occur in... [the mental consciousness].

Mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), as well as greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—whether conceptual (*vikalpita*) or innate (*sahaja*)—are all generally encompassed by both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

If it is associated with the five [sensory] consciousnesses and does not involve arbitrary conceptualization (*parikalpa*), it is subsumed under direct perception. The *Nyāyamukha* states that "that which is remote from all things, up to the various types of conceptual differentiation (*vibhāga-vikalpa"), is false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa-vikalpa).
This refers to false conceptualization, and not merely to the conceptualization of qualities such as beauty or ugliness regarding an object; the latter is also excluded by that [definition]. If...

If it were not so, then the two types—vitarka and vicāra—would not be applicable to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As for the remainder: either they are inference (*anumāna*), non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*), or indeterminate;
or they may be those that arise simultaneously with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), or those that coexist with the five [sensory] consciousnesses, which could be direct perception.

However, those arising through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) are also not direct perception, because the *Nyāyamukha* states that "all [cognitions] are excluded from conceptual construction. Between these two interpretations, the former is superior. Twenty follow.

The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) arise following the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), either simultaneously with them or subsequently. Like the root afflictions, they are accessed through both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
Among the indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is accessed only through inference or, alternatively, through non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*);

it does not involve direct perception. It occurs only within the distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because its object is the past. Sleep (*middha*) involves only the present and the past; it occurs solely within the distracted mental consciousness. It does not [occur] otherwise.

The clear and distinct condition (*viniścaya-pratyaya*) is also not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is admitted that all [mental factors] are associated with volition (*cetanā*). Among these, the wholesome may include both inference (*anumāna*) and the two types of investigation (*vitarka* and *vicāra*).

If they occur within a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), they are entirely direct perception; if they occur within a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), those that arise simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are likewise direct perception.

To apprehend the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an object is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To take a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object is either inference (*anumāna*) or non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*).

Regarding the fourth point, the analysis of the "aspects" (*bhāga*), that is, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and so forth: first, the various schools and Mahāyāna masters establish the similarities and differences in their presentation of these aspects;
next, regarding the analysis of the aspects and valid cognition, there are the teachers of the various Hīnayāna schools, excluding the Sarvāstivādins.
19. All [schools] establish the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part), yet lack the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective part), with the exception of the Saṃmitīya school.

Although they all speak of "objects," these are actually the *nimitta-bhāgas*—all that serves as the objective condition (*ālambana*)—which function as the *ākāra* (mental aspect). The *darśana-bhāga* is termed the "substance" (*vastu*). Their establishment of the *ākāra* corresponds to the *nimitta-bhāga* established in the Mahāyāna.
However, their fundamental tenet holds that the *ākāra* belongs to the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) that act as the perceiver; thus, it is established as being "only" [the mind].

The second chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "For those who realize that there are no objects apart from consciousness, the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) is the object-condition (*ālambana*), the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) is the mode-of-apprehension (*ākāra*), and the self-substance is termed the 'entity' (*vastu*).
The Saṃmitīya school maintains that the mind directly grasps the object and possesses no further mode-of-apprehension.

However, some commentaries explain that, with the exception of the Saṃmitīya school, there is no [school] that lacks a mode-of-apprehension; among the other nineteen schools, all establish the existence of the *nimitta-bhāga*.

This is because it is not a tenable thesis. Within the Mahāyāna, the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka maintains that within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is the view of the non-existence of both [subject and object], as only illusory phenomenal appearances manifest; how then could there be a mind?

Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), as well as in the Ekavyāvahārika school of the Hīnayāna, both the seeing and the appearance are non-existent. The Ekavyāvahārika explanation states: "All phenomena exist only as designations."
As for names, they have no intrinsic substance. According to Bhāviveka’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all things are empty; thus, the *Tattvaviniścaya* (Pal-zhen lun) states:
"In true nature, conditioned phenomena are empty because they arise dependently like illusions; unconditioned phenomena lack reality, being non-arising like flowers in the sky.

If one follows Vasubandhu and others, both the conventional and the ultimate possess the perceived and the perceiver (*grāhya-grāhaka*), establishing two parts; therein, the perceived part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is taken as the object.

Regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is established as the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and wisdom (*jñāna*) itself is the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

Therefore, in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, the Bodhisattva Dignāga establishes three parts. As his verse states: "The object of cognition (*prameya*) is that which possesses an appearance resembling the external object;

the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the result (*phala*) are the aspects of seeing and self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*). These three are not distinct in essence. Taking the object as the object of cognition and the aspect of seeing as the means of cognition, it follows that..."

Because there must be a result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is established. For example, when cloth and the like are the object of cognition (*prameya*), seeing and so forth are the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the subsequent knowledge that records them is the result of cognition.
If there were no such recording [cognition], one would be unable to recollect a past mind, for one cannot recollect what has never been experienced.
Therefore, the Bodhisattvas Dharmapāla and others later established four divisions by adding the "witnessing self-witnessing division" (*sākṣāt-svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

Regarding this intention— that the aspect of appearance (*nimittabhāga*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*), the aspect of seeing (*darśanabhāga*) is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is the fruit of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*)—
since self-awareness takes the aspect of seeing as its object of cognition and itself as the means of cognition, and since these mental factors are identical, how could there be no fruit?

It cannot be said that seeing constitutes the third fruit [of the path], because the self-attesting portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) always takes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as its object, whereas the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) is sometimes inferential (*anumāna*) or neither of the two [perceptions].
How, then, could it have only direct perception as its fruit? If that is so, why are inference and the "neither" category considered only direct perception?

Answer: The essence of self-cognizing consciousness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not the result of inference, because it is not an object of inference; nor is it the result of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Question:
If the divisions of consciousness are identical, there must necessarily be a result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). Of these four divisions, what serves as the result for the fourth? Answer:

The third division itself serves as the result for the fourth, because they are able to mutually cognize one another and both are of the nature of direct perception. No further [result] is established. All...
This is explained in detail as stated in the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. This refers to the different ways the various schools establish the divisions [of consciousness].

Next, regarding the determination of the divisions according to their nature and measure: although the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) is not itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is distinguished in accordance with the mind and thus encompasses both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

The causes of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) are termed "direct perception" and "inference. The seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the five [sensory consciousnesses] and the eighth [storehouse consciousness] both pertain to these two; their cause and effect are always manifest.

The seeing-portion of the seventh [manas-consciousness], when it is a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), is exclusively present; therefore, it does not constitute the two types of valid cognition. As for the seeing-portion of the sixth [mental consciousness], if it is in a concentrated mind...

Furthermore, the accomplishment of conventional characteristics (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*) is entirely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Regarding the concentration of the mind through desire and so forth, the two explanations of "conventional imagination" (*parikalpa*) should be understood as previously stated.
As for other distracted minds and their various mental factors (*caitta*), the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) is the same as before when clarified in terms of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so on;
the remaining two portions are entirely direct perception.

Fifth, regarding the clarification based on the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, we shall first distinguish them according to the two categories of the three and the seven types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) to clarify the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

First, we shall clarify the three types: namely, innate conceptualization (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), recollective conceptualization (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), and deliberative conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).

If one follows the second chapter of the *Saṃgīti-sūtra-nibandhana* (or *Abhidharma-samuccaya-bhāṣya*), which explains these in relation to the six consciousnesses, they exist only in the sixth consciousness; they are entirely absent in the five sensory consciousnesses. However, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptibhāṣya*...

In the Mahāyāna, within the refutation of the sixth consciousness relying upon the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*), it is stated everywhere that "the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would lack recollective and deliberative [discrimination]," but it does not say that it would lack intrinsic-nature discrimination (*svabhāvavikalpa*). Based on this, it is accepted that the five consciousnesses possess reliance upon material sense organs.

If this is so, why do various treatises appear to contradict one another? The answer has two interpretations. The first says: [The contradiction arises because] it is not admitted that [intrinsic-nature discrimination] exists within the five consciousnesses.

Regarding the existence of intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that the sixth consciousness arises due to three types of inducement; it does not say that the five [sensory] consciousnesses possess them.

As for the objection that "if they lacked these, there would be no intrinsic, recollective, or conceptual discrimination," this is merely a concession that intrinsic discrimination might exist [in the five senses];

however, since the two other types of discrimination are first refuted, there is no contradiction. It is not that we actually grant their existence. One interpretation holds that intrinsic discrimination is of two kinds.

They are not the same. First, vitarka and vicāra have these as their nature and take present objects as their domain. Second, the various consciousnesses themselves are capable of giving rise to cognitive deliberation;
taking the self-nature of objects is what is called "intrinsic discrimination" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*). Therefore, the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"The eight contaminated consciousnesses are all termed 'discrimination,' for they arise from delusive conditions and do not accord with reality. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* refers to the first [type] and speaks only of the [first] consciousness.

Sixth: Since the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises refer to the latter [type of conceptualization], they allow for the existence of five [types of direct perception]; this is likewise not contradictory.

If one were to maintain that there is absolutely no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) involving deliberative conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*), it would contradict the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, which states: "Deliberative conceptualization refers to [conceptualizing] objects of the past, future, and present that are not currently perceived."
Conceptual construction through reflection is said to be non-perceptual; this clarifies that while direct perception (pratyakṣa) is absent, inference (anumāna) may be present.

Although recollective cognition takes the past as its object, it does not distinguish between the states of concentration and distraction, as both are common to these two positions. When the concentrated mind takes the past as its object...
It can be subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). When a distracted mind takes the past as its object, it is subsumed under inference (*anumāna*).

If its intrinsic nature resides in the sixth consciousness, it possesses only direct perception. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "That is to say, it is the conceptualization of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the conditioned phenomena currently experienced.

Since it speaks of "conceptualization of specific characteristics," it is clear that there is no non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*) such as inference. [Inference] takes the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of objects as its domain and functions through comparative estimation and false construction.

Because it is not inference (*anumāna*). Alternatively, there is also inference; for the mind of inference cognizes its object by conforming to the nature of that object, which is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself.
Thus, it is also called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), and is not restricted solely to what is termed a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) upon the basis of its own substance.

For example, impermanence (*anityatā*) regarding an object may also be called a "particular characteristic," because its essence is impermanent. However, the former interpretation is superior: [it refers to] the mental activity (*ākāra*) that takes the particular characteristic as its object.

This is according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmasamuccaya* regarding the gate of rationality (*yukti-mukha*). As for the "intrinsic discrimination" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that even if one were to grant [the opponent's position], it would be the same as in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmasamuccaya*.

If one takes the object-field itself (*sva-viṣaya*) to be what is called "intrinsic," then this refers to the intrinsic discrimination of the five sensory consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness.

These are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The seventh [consciousness] is exclusively non-valid cognition (*anumāna*). This is all based on the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), not with reference to the latter two portions, because the latter two portions are exclusively direct perception.
Next, regarding the seven [types of discrimination], the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* state that the seven are distinct.

First, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* explains the seven types of discrimination in order to clarify the two types of valid cognition. The seven are: spontaneous, with-aspect (*sanimitta*), without-aspect (*animitta*), seeking (*paryeṣaka*), [discerning], [determining], and [recollection].
Investigation (*vicāra*) is either defiled or non-defiled. Spontaneous conceptualization (*svarasavāhin-vikalpa*) is exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

As the treatise itself states: "The five bodies [of consciousness] are like their objects; they lack discursive differentiation (*nirvikalpa*) because they function spontaneously within their own respective domains.

Among these, there are aspects that are both direct and inferential, namely, the conceptualizations of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa*). As for the five [mental factors] such as the signless (*animitta*), none possess direct perception.
It can be understood through inference (*anumāna*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that all five [mental factors] take conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the seventh [consciousness] in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it refers to those with signs (*sanimitta*), those without signs (*animitta*), spontaneous (*svarasa*), seeking (*paryeṣaka*), examining (*pratyavekṣaka*), defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).

However, these seven types exist only in the sixth consciousness and do not extend to other consciousnesses. This is because it is said to be the sixth [consciousness], which possesses eight unique characteristics (*āveṇika*). It is characterized by having signs.

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). This refers to the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that arises when the sense faculties have matured and one is skilled in linguistic conventions (*nāma-pada*) regarding an object previously experienced;

because it does not distinguish between the meditative and non-meditative states, it is also present in the signless (*animitta*). Non-conceptual [perception] (*nirvikalpa*) also extends to direct perception;

this refers to the conceptualization arising in those who follow what was previously induced, as well as in infants and others who are unskilled in linguistic conventions. Since the term "infants" is mentioned, it is clear that this does not apply solely to what was previously induced; however, it is simply... [text ends].
The term "wholesome" (*kuśala*) refers to its meaning. How could it not be in accord with the essence of the object? Furthermore, the interpretation [that it applies to all objects] is not tenable.

If an infant were to apprehend the essence of an object through a present one, that would be a spontaneous inclusion (*svataḥ-saṃgraha*), not an inclusion by way of the signless (*animitta*). Therefore, this [text] speaks only of objects in the past.

It is said to be spontaneous and exclusively a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it functions spontaneously according to the power of the object. Seeking (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) may apply to both direct perception and inference (*anumāna*); thus it is said regarding all...

The investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) consists of seeking (*vitarka*) and examination (*vicāra*). Because it does not distinguish between concentration and distraction, one seeks and examines all objects even within a state of meditative absorption.

Defiled [investigation] is common to both inference (*anumāna*) and does not extend to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it takes past and future worlds as its objects and is associated with afflictions;
regarding present objects, it is said to involve "clinging" (*abhiniveśa*). Non-defiled discrimination extends to both direct perception and inference, and extends to all objects.
The three periods of time are not associated with defilement; they are either associated with faith and so forth, or they are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).

Within the indeterminate nature, there are those that are transformative (*nairmāṇika*); these are fixed as results and are not entirely dispersed. A mind that is entirely dispersed can be an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
These two [categories]—the seven and the three—are analyzed in detail as in the *Cheng weishi shu*.

Regarding the sixth question and answer, concerning the identification of the essence [of the faculties]: within the five material faculties (*rūpa-svabhāva-indriya*), how are the subjective and objective aspects subsumed? Answer: These are objects known through inference (*anumāna*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For those in the causal stage of the Mahāyāna, as well as for practitioners of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), their existence is known through inference.

It is only the Tathāgata who knows them through direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*). As the first volume of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Based on the fact that they can give rise to consciousness, their existence is known through inference," according to other [authorities].

This is what is known; it is not restricted to the Buddha’s teaching. Alternatively, it may be that in the Mahāyāna, while at the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*), [the sense-cognitions] are within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because they function interdependently.

Since the visual and other consciousnesses take mental objects as their domain, they should not be limited to taking only the "form" (*rūpa*) within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) as their object. Question:
If the five faculties are not capable of direct perception, how is it that the *Vyākhyāyukti* and other texts state: "Question: Of what is such direct perception the property?"?

There is. The answer states: "The sense-faculties (*indriya*), direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and so forth. Furthermore, it explains: "The objective sphere (*gocara*) traversed by the five sense-faculties consists of the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), as previously described.
Regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of direct perception, the object is cited as the 'possessor' (*bhāva*); that which is possessed is the five sense-faculties.

If it were not direct perception, why would the existence of the object be required? The intended meaning of that passage is to cite the basis of the mind (*citta-saṃniśraya*) and the objects apprehended by the faculties (*indriya-grāhya-viṣaya*).

This is because it can possess direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it were not so, one might as well say that it is "the object traversed by all mental faculties" (*manas-indriya-gocara*); yet, how could one cite the object of the mind (*mano-artha*) and thereby take the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) itself?

[If one did so,] it would refer to the seventh consciousness and the past, which has already ceased. The seventh consciousness is exclusively non-valid cognition (*anumāna*), because it constantly clings to a self (*ātman*).

As for the past mind, since it no longer exists, what could be said to be "present"? Therefore, it refers only to the mind (*citta*). Question: Regarding its capacity with respect to specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)...

Regarding the mind that takes [an object] as its condition (*ālambana*), only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established: the semblance of inference (*anumānābhāsa*) and the semblance of direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). By which means of valid cognition is it apprehended? The answer has two interpretations. The first says:

both are subsumed under inference, because they take only the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as their object and not the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). As the *Nyāyamukha* states: "There is nothing apart from these two."

There may be objects to be measured; in order to cognize them, other means of measurement (*pramāṇa*) are further established. However, it is logical that there be a distinct understanding of the real and the pseudo.

Since the *Nyāyamukha* clarifies proof and refutation, the two types of pseudo-reasoning (*hetvābhāsa*) are not included within inference (*anumāna*). Nevertheless, in reality, they are indeed subsumed [within it].

One explanation states that they are subsumed under the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): direct perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna). From the perspective of the *Nyāyamukha*, these two are established because they are capable of cognizing their respective objects through reasoning.

Furthermore, the two means of valid cognition are established for the sake of one’s own realization and for the realization of others. Regarding the objects known by these means of valid cognition, they do not exceed the categories of the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa);

therefore, no other means are established. Apparent perception and apparent inference are not so established because they are incapable of cognizing those particular and universal characteristics, nor are they capable of establishing or refuting [theses].
Because one realizes [the nature of] oneself and others, two types are established based on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since that [other type] is not valid cognition, if it were inferential cognition (*anumāna*), then among the four principles found in various sūtras and śāstras, the establishment of phenomena through inference could not serve as a definitive standard, because it would pertain to what is non-valid and because it would be established incorrectly.

Question: If the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not fully encompass the mind, then because the seventh consciousness has not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), it would always be invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

Answer: The establishment of the two [means of valid cognition] is based on principle; it does not intend to exhaustively encompass all mental states. Even if they do not fully encompass them, what contradiction is there with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)?

Alternatively, if one relies on the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), it is not subsumed under the two means of valid cognition; however, if one relies on the self-witnessing aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), what mental state is not fully encompassed? For all are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Question: Since this is based on the two aspects...

Regarding the establishment [of cognition] through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), what is the essential nature of their specific (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) characteristics? Furthermore, how do they differ from the two types of characteristics mentioned in the sūtras?

In response, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* presents the interpretations of three masters: The first master says: "A concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) can universally apprehend both specific and general characteristics, and these are all instances of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

However, when the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Logic Treatise) speaks of apprehending the two kinds of characteristics—specific and general—it does so based on the state of a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*)."
The second [master] says: "The concentrated mind takes only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object;

however, because it is induced by the skillful means (*upāya*) of the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and since it is a principle manifested by various universal characteristics, it is described in terms of those skillful means as 'knowing the universal characteristic. That which is not so is called 'knowing the specific characteristic.'"
By this principle, some say that *tathatā* (suchness) is termed "emptiness" and "selflessness," which is the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena.

Others say that *tathatā* is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness and is not a universal characteristic. Thirdly, it is said: according to the true meaning, the two characteristics [the particular and the universal] as explained in the *Hetuvidyā* differ slightly from those in the sūtras.

The intent of the *Hetuvidyā* is that the real meaning of all phenomena—whether particular (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) or universal (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)—is designated as "particular" (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) when each adheres to its own essence.

Regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): if one establishes a single category based on a distracted mind that discriminates, wherein the signifier and the signified pervade all phenomena like a thread threading through flowers, this is called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
All concentrated minds (*samāhita-citta*), being free from such discrimination, take [the object] as its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);

these are all direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Although they take various phenomena—such as suffering, impermanence, and so forth—as their objects, each individual phenomenon exists separately; thus, they merely take [the specific] as their object.
Regarding its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*): the essence of suchness (*tathatā*) is the true nature of all phenomena; it is also subsumed under its own-characteristic.

Furthermore, although subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes as its object both names and the referents they signify, it does not grasp at those referents. While it necessarily involves names, it does not claim that names are fixedly attached to referents, because it illuminates names and referents as having distinct essences;
thus, it is also [an instance of] own-characteristic. The intent of the Sūtra is that [this constitutes] "wonderful observation" (*pratyavekṣaṇā*).

Wisdom that takes as its object the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—the essence of form, sound, and so forth—is called "taking intrinsic characteristics as its object. Wisdom that takes as its object the specific distinctions of phenomena (*dharma*), such as the meaning of permanence or impermanence, is called "taking common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
Therefore, they are not the same. Based on this, one understands that the essence of intrinsic and common characteristics is distinct according to the intent of the Sūtras and Śāstras. Question:

Regarding the common characteristics in this treatise and those taken as objects by a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), such as permanence, impermanence, and so forth, there are the image-aspects (*nimittabhāga*) they carry. [One hundred...]

What does "dharma" include? One answer says: because it lacks a substantial entity (*svabhāva*), it is not included among the one hundred dharmas. Another says: it is included within the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) category.

Now, I say that it can be understood as being included within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Depending on the transforming mind (*pariṇāma-citta*), it cannot be separated from the mind; therefore, it should be judged as belonging to the *sabhāga*.
The *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is established based on similarity among many phenomena, yet it possesses no substantial entity whatsoever.

As for this common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), if one were to rely on the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by conditions, one could say it has a substantial entity, because a direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) must necessarily exist.

However, it is not like other *nimitta-bhāgas*, whose entities are real and which share the same seed as the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect). In terms of its function as an object, it is divided [from the subjective aspect]. If one relies on the original essence (*bimba*), it is indeed without substance.

The objects of concentration, such as the permanent or the impermanent, are merely the manifestations of the mind’s direct realization (*abhisamaya*). As for the objects of inferential cognition (*anumāna*), they are general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*);
these are merely provisionally established by inferential cognition itself. If this were so, the Buddha would not take these general characteristics as objects of his inferential cognition.
However, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that the Buddha’s wisdom does not take inferential general characteristics as its objects. The answer is: [the Buddha] produces inferential cognition.

They are provisionally established as being non-different, yet the Buddha’s wisdom does not take them as its object. The Buddha possesses universal knowledge (*sarvajñā*), which takes those sentient beings as its object through an inferential cognition (*anumāna-citta*).

Based on this, he establishes their conduct and understanding. As for all their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), what fault would there be in principle if one were to understand them as being like the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)? Question:

What is the difference between the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inferential cognition (*anumāna*)—namely, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)—and the two aspects expressed by names and phrases (*nāma-pada*)? Answer: First, regarding the statement concerning inference:
The designation [of a term] is identical to a non-inferential designation; the two characteristics differ slightly.

For instance, when it is said that "sound" is its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the alternative expression "the name 'sound'" is called a particularity (*viśeṣa*). This does not require being established by mental application (*manasikāra*); rather, it pervades all phenomena.

Furthermore, both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inferential cognition (*anumāna*) universally take those two as their objects. Otherwise, how could it be said that "hearing" refers to inference? Regarding those two characteristics, for the sake of... [desire].
To fully comprehend the mental images, conceptualizations, and resolutions, and then to apply them analogically to other phenomena, is what is called inference (*anumāna*).

Because its object of apprehension is the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), it differs from the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*). Regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there are both similarities and differences between the two.

If names and phrases denote such things as form, sound, permanence, or impermanence, and direct perception also takes these as objects, then they may be considered similar. However, based on not relying on names while taking those two [specific and universal characteristics] as objects, they are distinct.

Regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): this is merely a slight distinction from reality. Names (*nāman*) express the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while phrases (*pada*) express differentiation.

These exist only as transformations of the mind; they lack an unchanging substantial nature and function according to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) carries with it realization. Those two types of characteristics are collectively termed "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*), which thus possess differentiation.

Furthermore, if the mind of direct perception were to give rise to verbal expression, its object of focus (*ālambana*) would likewise be the same. The mind that functions through conceptual understanding is termed... [text ends].

This is because it is conventional cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*). Both conventional cognition and its designations function in relation to the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.

Furthermore, even when a direct-perception mind (*pratyakṣa-citta*) investigates the phenomena designated by those names and expressions, although it does not definitively determine that the name belongs to the object and so forth, it still forms a conceptual engagement (*pratipatti*) that is identical to that [conventional cognition].
This is because cognition does not function where sound does not reach. Moreover, the Buddha’s wisdom knows that their essence is non-existent. Because...
Because they are universal objects of cognition (*sarvālambana*), they are also the same as those [preceding cases], with the exception of the aforementioned meanings.

When the five or eight consciousnesses exist in the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*) or within a meditative state (*samāhita-citta*), the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) they carry while cognizing various phenomena (*dharma*) may be either substantial (*savastuka*) or non-substantial (*avastuka*). These are what are expressed by names and phrases (*nāma-pada*).

All common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) are entirely without intrinsic nature and are non-conceptual; they directly realize suchness. These self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are distinct from them.
Accordingly, the two characteristics—the expressed meaning of names and phrases and the characteristics of the self and the common as taught in the sūtras—differ in their essential nature.
The sūtra refers to the substance of phenomena (*dharma-tattva*), whereas the names and phrases express that which is understood by the mind and the mental formations of perception.

[The opponent] stands up and asks: "If the nature of conventional designations (*prajñapti*) and the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) upon which they depend is non-existent, how can direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) apprehend them?
[The respondent] answers: "Direct perception also takes the non-existent as its object; it is simply not the same as discursive thought (*vikalpa*).

This is because names and conventions are fixedly attached to their referents, and referents are fixedly attached to words; therefore, it constitutes direct perception. [The opponent] asks: "Since the cognition that investigates names and conventions relies upon common characteristics,"
If the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) has no substantial reality, how can there be the perfuming of names and words (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*) capable of producing the fundamental substance?

Answer: When one investigates through the wisdom of names and words, the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is not non-existent. A mind that accords with this investigative understanding is able to produce the fundamental substance; however, it merely forms an understanding of color, sound, blue, yellow, and so forth upon that image.

This common characteristic, which is the object-condition (*ālambana*) of that understanding-mind, is by nature non-existent when compared to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the particular characteristic:

Because this is increased in the higher [stages]. Question: Does the Buddha’s wisdom universally take as its object that which is expressed by words based on common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)? Answer:

One view holds that it does not take such an object, yet gives rise to verbal expression that expresses what is based on common characteristics. This is because the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that the Buddha’s wisdom does not take these common characteristics as its object.

One explanation states: The Buddha’s wisdom also relies upon common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), all phenomena are established by superimposing conceptual marks upon their essential natures.

If this were not so, how could it be called "skillful means wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna*) that proclaims all phenomena? It is taught that [this wisdom] does not take common characteristics as its object and is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
it is understood through the provisional establishment (*prajñapti*) of a pervasive connection with other aspects. This common characteristic is not a single entity.
None of them would be objects of cognition at all; otherwise, even impermanence and so forth would not be objects of cognition.

Furthermore, if the Buddha’s wisdom did not form a conceptual understanding (*vikalpa*) of blue and so forth, yet he were to speak of "blue" and so forth, it would not constitute noble speech (*āryavākya*), because his words would contradict his own cognition. Moreover, [if he] did not form such an understanding...

Regarding the aspect of non-change and the consideration that it does not depend [on others], as well as its engagement with non-existent phenomena (*abhāva*), this interpretation is superior because their essence can be directly perceived.

Question: Among the various gates, when the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) perceives the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) in a single moment, is that consciousness at that time direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)?
Answer: There are two interpretations. One says it pertains to both; when the five consciousnesses perceive the same object, it is direct perception.

Inferential cognition (*anumāna*) takes the periphery of the five sense faculties as its object; this is precisely inference. It cannot be known by a wisdom that manifests through the five sense faculties, for that would contradict the treatises.
Question: How can the two types of valid cognition arise from a single moment of mind? Answer: The seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) is manifold; this is established in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The seventh fascicle states: "The [subjective] aspect (*nimitta*) and the [objective] appearance (*lakṣaṇa*) both exist together, because various appearances arise.

If both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) were to arise simultaneously, then the two views of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) should also arise together. Answer: Because the two types of grasping (*grāha*) are firm, violent, and mutually contradictory, they do not arise simultaneously.

However, direct perception and inference are not themselves forms of grasping; therefore, they can arise together. One opinion holds that it is not fixed, as the mind follows whichever of the five objects is predominant and is drawn along by it. Even so...

Taking the five sense-faculties as objects is also direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Even if the mental object is the same as that of the five [faculties], the mind is exclusively inference (*anumāna*).

If the two objects are equal, the power of direct perception is superior; thus, the mind follows direct perception. It is impossible for them to arise simultaneously with different degrees of intensity. They do not take the same objects, such as blue or yellow forms;
although the aspects of what is seen are manifold, the five [faculties] share the same direct and inferential [perceptions]. Therefore, there is no contradiction, and many may arise together.

It arises. Just as when two objects of grasping are both grasped as existing, they can arise together; or when one grasps [something] as non-existent, there is only the grasping of dharmas, and the two do not arise simultaneously.
If one grasps the objects of permanence or annihilation as either existent or non-existent, they do not arise together. Both interpretations present difficulties; you may choose whichever you prefer.
Alternatively, it takes the eighteen *dhātus* as its object; it may be a solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), or it may be associated with the five [sensory consciousnesses].
This would then not apply to the *manas-vijñāna*. If it were to take [the object] alone as its object, it would all be an inference (*anumāna*), and thus there would be no aforementioned obstacle.

Since there is no textual prohibition [against this], this interpretation is superior. Question: Regarding the seven types of discrimination (*vikalpa*), how do the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* differ?

Answer: This is fully and extensively reconciled in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā*. Among these various categories, there are many fine details; I have briefly cited one corner [of the matter]. The rest...

This may be inferred accordingly. ○ Regarding the meaning of the ten paths of action (*daśa-karmapatha*), they are analyzed by way of ten sections: first, the essential nature (*svabhāva*); second, the etymological explanation (*nirukti*); third, the differentiation of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); fourth, the classification of their expansion and contraction; [fifth, the order of their arising]; sixth, the determination of their gravity and lightness; seventh, the distinction between the preparatory, the actual, and the subsequent stages; eighth, the inclusion within the three types of action; ninth, the inclusion within the three roots; and tenth, the inclusion within the three karmas. First, the essential nature. Second, the etymological explanation. Third, the differentiation of characteristics. Fourth, the classification of expansion and contraction. [And so forth.]

1. Abolition and establishment; 2. The similarities and differences of the three vehicles; 3. The presence or absence of meditative concentration and distraction; 4. The presence or absence of the realms and destinies;
5. The basis and locus of the paths of action; 6. The distinctions in the attainment of fruits; 7. Questions and answers for detailed analysis.

Regarding the first [point], the essential nature: these ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) counteract the ten unwholesome paths; their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are mutually inverted.

In various sūtras and śāstras, they are frequently explained through such mutual inversion and correspondence. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle 7, states: "Furthermore, these three types of karma—of body, speech, and mind—are either wholesome or unwholesome.
The wholesome ones are precisely the ten paths of wholesome action. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 8, states: "These, moreover, are twofold..."
The types are the ten kinds of wholesome and unwholesome paths of action (*karmapatha*), namely: taking life, abstaining from taking life, and so forth.

The *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra* states: Question: Regarding one who is "distant from taking life," [the term] "taking life" and its associated factors are heard [in the context]. In the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*: [it says...]

This is also because they are explained in relation to one another. Now, the wholesome and unwholesome factors of the paths of action are discussed. Furthermore, the ten paths of action are subsumed within the three types of action (*trividha-karman*).

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on the Formation of Action) asks: "Why does the Sūtra speak of three types of action? It is to show that the three types of action encompass the ten paths of action. The *Abhidharma* also states:

"The first three [paths of action] correspond to the four [unwholesome] actions of body and speech, while the latter three correspond to the three [unwholesome] actions of mind; these follow their respective order. Thus, these are the bodily and vocal actions.

Regarding the characteristics of mental karma (*manas-karma*), ten types of karmic substance are distinguished based on the threefold division of karma. However, their substance is threefold: first, the essential nature (*svabhāva*); second, the retinue (*parivāra*);
and third, the conventional designation (*prajñapti*). These ten paths of wholesome and unwholesome karma all have volition (*cetanā*) as their substance.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "The volition that moves the body is called bodily karma; the volition that issues speech is called vocal [karma]."

Karma consists of two types of volition (*cetanā*): deliberative and decisive. Because it is associated with the mind and functions as a movement of the mind, it is called mental karma (*manas-karman*).
The *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* also states: "Karma is volition; its nature is that of differentiation. It further states: "There are three kinds of volition:

first, deliberative volition; second, decisive volition; third, impelling volition. If volition can move the body, it is designated as bodily karma (*kāya-karman*); the same applies by analogy to speech and mind."
It is known. The *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*, fascicle three, states: "It is mind alone that perceives karma and so forth; yet there is a distinction between good and evil.
If it is impulsive volition (*ceṣṭā-manasikāra*), it gives rise to greed and the like, which in turn incite the movement of body and speech.

If it is deliberative volition (*niścaya-manasikāra*), it gives rise to greed and the like, which cause the mind to move toward action as the ten unwholesome karmas. Conversely, non-greed and the like give rise to the movement of body and speech... [and so forth].
It is intended to prompt action for the sake of the ten wholesome courses of action. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle 8, states:

"Regarding the course of action of killing, greed, hatred, and delusion serve as the preliminary application (*prayoga*); it is brought to completion by hatred. As with killing, so it is with the course of action of harsh speech and malice."
The course of action of taking what is not given has greed, hatred, and delusion as its preliminary application (*prayoga*). It is brought to completion through greed.

As it is with taking what is not given, so it is with sexual misconduct and covetousness. The course of action of false speech has greed, hatred, and delusion as its preliminary application; among these three, [it is completed by whichever is predominant].
In some cases, an action is completed by a single factor. This is as with false speech; the same applies to divisive speech and frivolous speech.

Regarding the path of action of wrong view, greed, hatred, and delusion serve as the preliminary application (*prayoga*), while it is completed through delusion. The ten wholesome paths of action are the reverse of these, both in their preliminary application and their completion.

However, since it is volition (*cetanā*) that initiates the movement which constitutes bodily and vocal karma, there can be no confusion between them. Furthermore, since mental karma consists of two types of volition, how could two volitions ever arise simultaneously?

Regarding the paths of mental action (*manas-karmapatha*): according to reason, they should both definitely consist of a single volition (*cetanā*) as the path of mental action; otherwise, there would be multiple occurrences of mental action.
They are collectively termed "paths of action" because they are spoken of in accordance with their characteristics and because they are proximate preparatory stages.

Regarding the nature of the two retinues: those that arise in association with wholesome or unwholesome volitions are also wholesome or unwholesome karma. Thus it is stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, fascicle eight.

It is said: The associates of karma are also designated by the name "karma"; therefore, those factors associated with karma are also called karma. Regarding the third point, the provisional designation of their substance:
as in the Sarvāstivāda and other schools, the first three courses of action have bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) as their substance; the subsequent four have vocal intimation (*vāk-vijñapti*).

Because sound is its substance. The *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* states: "Furthermore, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct arise from volitional action (*cetanā-karman*) and are produced based on the body;

because they conform to worldly convention, they are also called 'bodily karma' (*kāya-karman*). In reality, their essence is neither virtuous nor non-virtuous, yet they are also [designated as such] according to worldly convention."
A name is provisionally established so that the world may, by means of this gateway, engage in the movement of wholesome and unwholesome volitions and practice cessation and activity.

Therefore, the names "wholesome" and "unwholesome" are used as provisional designations; non-informative action (*avijñapti*) does not follow others in being a provisional designation. Mental action has no such provisionality.

Most schools define action primarily as mental intention (*cetanā*), though there are differences among the non-Buddhist outsiders. Herein, the three types of action are distinguished according to the various schools, and furthermore—
Regarding manifest and non-manifest [action], they are explained in detail in works such as the *Karmasiddhi*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the *Abhidharmakośa*;

fearing prolixity, I shall not recount them here. Second, regarding the explanation of the names, there are two parts: first, the enumeration of the names; second, the explanation of the names. The enumeration of the names may be understood [from the text]. Regarding the explanation of the names, there are two [parts].

There are two aspects: the general and the specific. First, regarding the general explanation: "ten" refers to the number. "Wholesome" (*kuśala*) means that which accords with principle and benefits sentient beings;
therefore, it is called "wholesome. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because it is able to accord with and benefit this world and other worlds, it is called wholesome."

Regarding these minds and mental factors associated with grasping that coexist with faith and so forth: although they may produce the pleasant fruits of humans and devas and thus be conducive to this life, they are not so for future lives;
therefore, they are not termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*). This distinguishes them from the maturation (*vipāka*) summoned by wholesome karma, which is designated as "unwholesome" (*akuśala*).
That which contradicts reason and harms sentient beings is called unwholesome. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "It can [produce] results for this life and for other..."

Because they contradict and harm the present world, they are called "unwholesome" (*akuśala*). Although the bitter fruits of the miserable realms (*durgati*) contradict and harm this world, they are not [themselves] unwholesome.

The opposite case is to be understood by analogy with the preceding. The meaning here is that although the *vipāka* (maturation) they attract may provide benefit or harm in the present, it cannot be designated as wholesome or unwholesome because it lacks a future fruit (*phala*) that can be so predicted. It is only this volitional action (*cetanā-karman*) and its [resulting] action...

Regarding one's retinue, their benefit or harm to oneself, and the subsequent fruition they induce—those which are capable of bringing about benefit or harm are termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*) and "unwholesome" (*akuśala*).

Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), fascicle three, states: "The term 'determined' (*vyākṛta*) refers to the wholesome and the unwholesome, because they can be specifically designated as having desirable or undesirable fruits, as well as a distinguished self-nature (*svabhāva*).
The fruits of humans and devas are called 'desirable,' while the fruits of the three miserable realms are called 'undesirable. [The latter] refers to a distinguished self-nature."

This is the very nature of karma, or it is untainted (anāsrava) wholesome [karma]. Although it does not attract [retributive] fruit, it is nonetheless termed "wholesome. That which is performed is called "karma" (*karman*).

It is termed a "path" (*mārga*) because it encompasses both the sense of producing [results] and the sense of being traversed. Thus, the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* asks: "Furthermore, how is volition (*cetanā*) named a 'path of karma'?
Volition possesses the quality of performing [action], and is therefore called "karma"; furthermore, it serves as the path to the good and evil destinies, leading one to be born therein.
Therefore, they receive the name "paths of action" (*karmapatha*). According to the *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-śāstra*, the explanation is likewise the same. As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:

"The volition (*cetanā*) that gives rise to bodily and vocal [actions] and performs a construction is called 'action' (*karman*), because it is that which is traversed by the volition of deliberation and determination."

Because it universally produces the ripening fruits (*vipākaphala*) of both suffering and pleasure, it is also called a "path" (*mārga*). This is explained through three types of karma—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
There are two senses in which it is termed a "path. Regarding the two specific explanations: first, an explanation specifically concerning the three paths of action;

second, an explanation specifically concerning the ten paths of action. As for the explanation based on the three types of karma: within each of the three types of karma, there is first an analysis of the individual abstentions, followed by a collective explanation.

Furthermore, regarding bodily action (*kāyakarman*), the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* states: "Body" refers to that which has as its essence a specific combination of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). It is formed by accumulation; this is the meaning of "body.

This term applies generally to all five faculties, yet when used as a collective designation, it is specifically a name for the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), just as [the term] "form-base" (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth are used.
Alternatively, the use of the specific term serves to distinguish it from the eye and other faculties. Action is volition (*cetanā*), distinguished as...

Nature (*svabhāva*). Whatever is produced in accordance with the intention of the agent is the meaning of "action" (*karma*). To distinguish between the general and specific [definitions], one should follow the explanation provided for the preceding body.

Furthermore, because it takes up "predominant volition" (*cetana*), it is called "differentiation. This is an *aviśeṣa* (analytic) compound. Volition is able to move the body; thus it is called "bodily action" (*kāyakarma*).
That is, the action which moves the body is named "bodily action"; this is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* says: "In its full sense..."
One should say it is "action that moves the body. By omitting the word "moving," it is simply termed "bodily action" (*kāyakarman*).

It is like "power-oil," which is simply called "oil," or "dust-wind," which is simply called "wind"; this case is also like that. According to the *Siddhikarman-śāstra*, bodily action is itself the path;

this is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative compound). That [text] says it can serve as the path to the happy realms (*sugati*) and the miserable realms (*durgati*), because it leads one to be born there. Thus, it is established.

Regarding the term "path of action" (*karmapatha*): according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it may be interpreted either as a dependent compound (*tatpuruṣa*) or a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).
It is the path of volition (*cetanā*), because it is that which is traversed by volition; this is the combined explanation. "Speech" (*vāk*) has the nature of vocal sound.

It is called "speech" because it can express the meaning intended to be spoken. The meaning of "action" (*karman*) is as explained previously. This [explanation] subsumes the conventional designation under the ultimate reality. Furthermore, it is said that "speech" refers to syllables (*akṣara*) and so forth.

The basis [of speech] is called "speech" (*vāk*) because it can express meaning by means of phonemes (*akṣara*) and so forth; this is an analysis based on the distinction between the conventional and the real (*upapada-vigraha*).

The volition that initiates speech is called "vocal action" (*vāg-karman*); this too is the action that initiates speech, and is thus called "vocal action," which is a genitive compound (*tatpuruṣa*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise Establishing Action) states: "In its full form, one should say 'the action of initiating speech,' omitting the word 'initiating'."
These [two] are both termed vocal karma (*vāg-karman*). The metaphors for their explanation are as previously stated; the "path" (*mārga*) follows the pattern of bodily karma (*kāya-karman*).

This is the combined explanation. As for "mind" (*manas*), it refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*); because it is capable of deliberation (*santīraṇa*) and because it moves toward future births and objects, it is called "mind.

This explanation of "deliberation" applies in meaning to all eight consciousnesses. Because they move toward future births and objects, [the term "mind"] is used to distinguish [it from others]; the others do not [possess this specific function].
Because it intends toward rebirth and all objects, karma is likewise as previously explained; this concludes the analysis according to the *Ṣaṣṭhanirukti*.

Mental action (*manas-karma*) is so called because it is the activity of the mental faculty (*manas*). This is also the action of attention (*manasikāra*), and is thus termed mental action; this is an analysis based on the genitive compound (*tatpuruṣa*). The *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* states:
"In full, one should say 'the action of attention,' but by omitting the word 'attention,' it is simply called mental action. Alternatively, [it may be interpreted as] the mind...

Regarding "associated karma": excluding the word "associated," it is simply called mental karma (*manas-karma*). This is an explanation based on association (*saṃprayukta*): the essence of volition (*cetanā*) is karma, whereas the mind (*manas*) itself is not karma.

When one speaks of "mental karma," it refers to the meaning of volition being associated [with the mind], which is termed mental karma, just as in the case of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth.

The meaning of "path" (*mārga*) follows the previous [explanation]. If it is definitive volition, it acts as the agent by depending upon its basis; this admits of two explanations, for it is [the object] of deliberative volition (*tarka-cetanā*).

This is a combined explanation based on the term "traversing" (*yul-lam*). Alternatively, it is explained that the body which is moved constitutes the path of action (*karmapatha*) of volition (*cetanā*), because the three types of volitional action proceed in dependence upon it;
since this is the path of action, it is called a "path of action. The path itself is not the action. The meaning of the words should be understood accordingly.
The above explanation of its name was based on the actual action. Furthermore, it is explained that killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct arise from volitional action.
